3846: The petitioner in the special leave petition is a woman and was married to a man and a woman, who lived as husband and wife for a long spell. She had been living with her parents as husband and wives. The marriage was registered under the U.P. Marriage Registration Act, 1921. The petitioner filed an application before the Court for a decree of nullity of marriage on the ground that she was not his legally married wife. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the evidence produced by the petitioner did not establish that she was lawfully married to a person who lived in the same house as her husband. The High Court also rejected the contention of the petitioner that there was no valid marriage between the parties. Dismissing the special leave petitions, ^ HELD: (1) The presumption arises in favour of wedlock as husband and Wife. The onus of proving the factum of marriage lies on the party who asserts it. [813F] (2) In the instant case, the petitioner has failed to discharge this burden. The evidence adduced by her does not inspire confidence. The petitioner has failed on both counts to prove her marriage with the respondent. [814A B] (3) The petitioner has not led any satisfactory evidence to show that she was legally married to a woman who lived at her matrimonial home. The evidence produced by her does make out that she was married to the respondent in accordance with law. [815C]
5810: The petitioners, who were the appellants in this Court, had entered into a contract with the respondent for the sale of certain goods. The contracts were not completed and the work was not commenced. The respondent terminated the contracts by notice dated March 28, 1982. The petitioners filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the termination notice on various grounds including that the relevant documents had not been taken into consideration. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that it was not maintainable since the award did not contain any reference to the relevant documents. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in dismissing the petition as having no jurisdiction to deal with the question of validity of the unreasoned award. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court has rightly held that the award is not enforceable because the same was not made in accordance with law. [642F] 2.1 The award does not indicate that all relevant documents had been taken into account. The High Courts order shows that the award itself was not made available to the parties. The parties participated in the arbitration without demur. There was no allegation of violation of principles of natural justice. [641G H] 3. The award is an unreasoned one. It is not desirable, in the interest of justice, to keep this matter pending because some cases are pending here on the question of the validity of unreasoned award per se. [640A B] PG NO 641 PG NO 642 4. The award does contain non application of mind to relevant facts. The award cannot be said to be vitiated by reason of any error of law apparent on the face of it or gross mistake of fact resulting in miscarriage of justice. [652C D] 5. The award suffers from patent illegality appearing on the face thereof. [653D E] 6. The award fails on the ground that it contains non application of the mind to relevant factors. The award, therefore, is liable to be set aside. [654E F]

7131: The appellant assessee, a registered dealer under the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957, was assessed to sales tax for the assessment year 1972 73. The assessing authority in his order dated March 30, 1977, held that the amount of additional tax levied under section 5 (1) of the Act had remained unpaid and therefore, it was not leviable under section 20(3) of the Karnataka General Sales Tax Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the said order. The State Government filed an appeal before the High Court which reversed the findings of the authorities below on the ground that unpaid "not disputed" tax was the subject matter of the appeal. In the appeal by special leave to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that since the amount of the additional tax was determined with reference to the sales tax/purchase tax impost, the provisions of section 20(2)(a) of the KGST Act would not apply. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder including those relating to refund or exemption from tax are applicable to the levy, assessment and collection of the additional sales tax or purchase tax or both, as they apply in relation to the levy assessment and collection Of the additional tax under section 20 (3). [803 E] 2. Section 20(1) refers to the period of limitation. Sub section 3(A) of section 20 refers to the periods of limitation. The expression "tax" has been defined to mean a tax leviable under the provisions of the act and as such includes the additional tax levied thereunder. The additional tax is computed with reference to a sale tax/purchase price. When once the assessing authority determines the sales tax or purchases tax under the Act the additional tax is levied automatically and becomes part and parcel of the assessment order. The expression 'taxable turnover ' means the total turnover of a dealer liable to pay tax. [803 G H; 804 A B]
2907: The respondent, a member of a scheduled tribe, was granted a lease for the period from January 25, 1958 to June 30, 1963 for quarrying stone in a quarry. He paid the first installment of the lease amount and continued to pay the second installment till July 13, 1963. On July 13,1963, he declined to accept the settlement of the quarry. In his tender he offered to pay the balance of the lease money within 15 days but refused to accept it as arrears of land revenue. The Divisional Forest Officer accepted the tender and settled the lease with the respondent. The respondent 's appeal against the order of the Divisional Forest Officer was dismissed by the Conservator of Forests. The respondent then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court quashed the order of settlement on the ground that the amount claimed to be due from the respondent was not recoverable under the provisions of the Assam Forest Regulation VII of 1891 and passed an order quashing the proceeding for recovery. The State appealed to this Court with certificate. HELD : (i) The amount claimed to have been due from the appellant is not on account of the price of any forest produce or expenses incurred in the execution of the lease deed. It is a sum which the Government may consider to be entitled to recover as rent. [864 C] (ii) The rule does not give rise to any liability to pay a sum of money. It is, therefore, difficult to hold that stone is forest produce within the meaning of the Act. [865 D E] (iii) The amount alleged to be due is not on accounts of the price. of any forest produces. It is not a sum which is payable to the Government. [863 F G]
2986: The appellant was a citizen of India and had obtained a British passport. He was returning to India with his family in the year 1963. On the strength of that passport he was returning to Pakistan with his family. On his way he died on board the ship. According to the prosecution that passport came into the hands of the appellant. The appellant agreed to arrange his journey and also for that purpose to obtain a passport for him. The appellant, however, agreed to arrange for that purpose at Nairobi. On the basis of this passport he prepared an application before the Special Police Officer for a visa. The appellant was arrested and committed to the Sessions Court. The trial court convicted him under section 120B I.P.C. and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that no consent as required by sec. 196A(2) having been first obtained, the Magistrate took cognizance of the offence of abetment of an offence of criminal conspiracy and therefore, the committal order was without jurisdiction and had to be quashed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The Magistrate took cognizance not only of the offences charged but also of the offence under section 120 B I.P,C. and committed the case to the Sessions court. [864 C] (2) The offence of criminal conspirtion is made out from the facts and circumstances of each case. It may be either conspiracy or abetment. The offence of abetment is complete when the main object of conspiracy is fulfilled. [865 G] (3) The word 'attempts ' in sec. 196 A(2) does not mean instigation which is the common feature of all the five sections. It means instigate doing away or attempting to do so. [866 D]

The first proviso to sub section (1) empowers the assessing authority to allow a dealer to produce evidence at any stage if he is satisfied that the returns submitted are incorrect or incomplete. The second proviso requires the assessing authority, notwithstanding anything contained in sub section (2), to permit the production of any evidence even though the assessing authority has not been produced. 2023: The assessee was a British citizen of India and was a sovereign from January 26, 1950. He was a British subject in the United Kingdom and was assessed to income tax for the said two years. On his application, he was granted immunity from taxation under the International Law in respect of income which accrued or arose to him up to that date. In 1951, he was appointed Chief Commissioner of India and on his attaining the age of superannuation retired. In 1952, he was assessed to Income Tax for the said years. On March 31, 1956, he was served with an order assessing him to income tax. On March 25, 1958, he made an application to the Income tax Officer praying for the refund of the amount paid by him as immunity from payment of income tax levied on him under the Covenant entered into by him with the Government of India at the time of merger. The Income tax Officer rejected the application. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the assessment but the Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee. The High Court held that under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, the assessee being a sovereign from the time of his appointment became entitled to the exemption under the Covenants entered into between him and the Government of lndia. The question whether the assessee enjoyed immunity from taxation during the accounting year was not relevant because the assessee ceased to be a sovereign from December 26, 1950, when he merged in the United States of Hyderabad and was assessed for the said year. The High court also held that as the assessee continued to be a richer officer, he was exempt from liability to tax under the Covenances entered into by it with the Government Of India at thetime of merger. Held: (i) Under the International Law, the assessee was a richer individual and was not exempt from tax under the covenant entered into by the ruler with the Government. (ii)The assessee could not claim immunity from taxation in respect of his income which accrued to him during the accounting period. (iii)The assessee was not liable to tax under any treaty, agreement or convention whereby the rulers were bound to grant immunity from taxation. 2079: The appellants were convicted under section 353, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to three months ' rigorous imprisonment by the Munsif of Puri. The High Court set aside their conviction on the ground that there was no satisfactory evidence to justify the conviction of the appellants under sections 143/402, Indian Penal code. Held, that the two offences being fundamentally distinct in nature could be separately taken cognizance of. The High court erred in holding that there was a proper charge for the offence under section 186, Indian PenalCode. Section 195(1)(b), Criminal Procedure Code, does not bar the trial of the appellants for the distinct offence under section 352, Indian penal Code, though it is practically based on the same facts as for the prosecution under section 186. Section 195 (1) (b), Criminal Pro cedure Code, provides that no court shall take cognizance of any offence described in section 198 or punishable under section 205 or section 206 except upon a complaint in writing made by some person authorised by such person. The words "anything" in section 195(1) (a) are not used in a technical sense. They are words of limitation which cannot be cut down or whispered away except by clear words of legislation. In the present case, the Magistrate had before him the evidence of P.W. 2 who was an accomplice and whose testimony was corroborated by the other witnesses. The High COurt was therefore right in acquitting the appellants.
1076: The assessees were carrying on business principally in dyes and chemicals. They carried on business principals ' office, principal and agent, and the branch offices. In the years material to these appeals the I.T.O. disallowed the commission paid to the employees only if the turnover in dyes exceeded Rs. 1,00,000 net in any year but was subsequently reduced to 10% on sales on and after September 1, 1946. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed 5% of the net profits without deduction of Excess Profits Tax or Business Profits Tax, or 121% of the gross profit without deduction of any part of it. On reference, the High Court held that the commission paid by the I. T.O. to the agents was not deductible from the assessable income of the assessees as business profits. Held, that the disallowance of the amount of commission paid to agents was justified under Rule 12 of Schedule 1 of the Excess Profits Tax Act read with section 21 of the Excess Profit Tax Act. The object of the rule is to prevent evasion of tax. It is a device innovating to avoid evil and it is conceived with a view to avoid payment of tax by obtaining double taxation. The object is to prevent evaders of excess profits tax who are subjected to unjust enrichment. The object may be to prevent evaded taxes, but the rule is intended for ensuring that the taxpayer has not collected excess commission which he has failed to collect. The rule is not intended to prohibit the levy of excess profits Tax at a lesser rate than what was charged originally. The object being to prevent evictiveness of the I. P. Mills, the I. C. RayalooLessor and the I. D. Rayalee Agencies, the rule should be so construed as to effectuate the object.

2366: The appellant was convicted under section 5 (3) (a) of the Indian Explosives Act, 1884 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and also to pay a fine of Rs. 2,000 in default to undergo rigorous imprison ment for a further period of six months. The High Court allowed his appeal and convicted him under section 5(3)(a) of Act. It held that the three minor boys were employed and Gobardhan, in any event, was allowed to enter the premises licensed under r. 16 of the Rules for manufacture of explosives on April 28, 1960. Held:(i) The word "employment" in cl. 12 of the licence does not mean employment of an individual on daily wages but means employment of a group of persons who are employed for work connected with the manufacture or storage of explosives. In the context in which it occurs in cl. 11 of the licence, the word "employment " would include employment of a person who is employed in connection with the manufacture of explosives. (ii)The word "establishment" has been used in the sense of carrying out a contract of personal service or calling. The definition of "employment " given in the , is inclusive and includes employment of persons employed in connection With the manufacture or processing of articles or things. (iii)The word 'manufacturer ' in cl. 10 of the licence means a person who has undertaken the work of manufacturing any article or thing and includes a person who carries on the business of manufacturing such article or thing through any process whatsoever. (iv)The word `establishments ' in cls. 11 and 12 of the Licence must be construed as including employment of persons by persons who have undertaken the work. (v)The word . employment " in cl. 13 of the licence includes employment of a guest in a factory. (vi)The word employ shall have the same meaning as in the , and the rules made thereunder.

2511: The appellant was charged with offences under section 120B of the Indian Penal Code read with section 135 of the New Act and sections 23(IA) and 23B of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947. He pleaded that he was not concerned with the smuggling of gold and that he had been falsely implicated in the case. The Presidency Magistrate convicted him but the High Court acquitted him on the ground that the statements recorded by the customs authorities were admissible in evidence at the trial of persons accused of offences under section 23(IA), 23B and 23B. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the investigation conducted by the customs officers must be deemed to be under Chapter XIV read with section 5(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code and the statements so recorded could not be admitted in evidence; (ii) the statements recorded under section 161 of the new Act were inadmissible because they were not recorded in a manner prescribed by the new Act; (iii) the statements were inadmissible since they were not made in the course of investigation under the old Act; (iv) the statements of the appellant were inadmissible because the Customs Officers did not have the power to submit charge sheet under section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; (v) the statements under section 161 were not admissible in evidence as they were not in the nature of statements made by an officer in charge of a police station within the meaning of section 25 of the Evidence Act; and (vi) the statements in question were not voluntary and were not hit by section 162 of the Code. HELD: Dismissing the appeal, (i) The investigation was not a police officer within the meaning Of section 25 of . The statement of the appellant was not therefore admissible in evidence. [616 D E] (ii)The investigation was not by a police officer for the purpose of section 25. It was open to the Customs authorities to submit a charge sheet under the section. But the Customs Authorities could not proceed against the appellant without the sanction of the Government. [617 B C]

748: The respondent was employed in the Central Railway Workshop and Factory, Parel, Bombay, under a contractor. He claimed overtime wages for the period prior to May 19, 1953, on the ground that he had been working as a 'workman ' in the factory since 1948 and that he had not been paid overtime wages due to him from April 1, 1949, to September 30, 1954. The appellant denied that he was a worker within the meaning of section 2(1) of the said (LXIII of 1948), and contended that he was not a worker within section 2(i) of the Act. Held, that the claim made by the respondent was not barred by limitation. The claim was made by him after the expiry of three days of the date of his employment and the claim was made after the expiry or the extended time allowed by law. The claim could be made even after three days of his continuous employment. The claim having been made after three days were not governed by section 70 of the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1948, and the claim having been filed beyond three days of such continuous employment, it was not barred under section 70 of that Act.
2406: The appellants were the owners of certain plots of land in the State of Madhya Pradesh. They had two sons, Vishwasrao and Krishnarao. They jointly executed two mortgage deeds in that year, and in the mortgage deeds, mentioned that they were mortgaging the property which was described as 'Malguzari Mouza '. In 1939, the proprietary rights of the appellants were purchased by one Vinayakrao, so that under the law then in force, Shankerrao, the adopted son of Shamrao Ramachandrarao, became the ex proprietor occupancy tenant of his share in the plot. In 1942, when the proprietary rights in the plot were acquired by one Vinayanrao, he died and his heirs took over the possession of this plot. In 1945, when the proprietor of the plot sold the plot to the respondent, she filed a suit for restoration of possession of her occupancy rights. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants were not entitled to claim actual possession from the respondents. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellants had not been able to prove their title to the land in dispute. It further held that the respondents were not entitled, therefore, to claim actual posses sion of the land. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondents had become the occupancy tenants of the land in 1895, and that the appellants could not claim actual possession of the land from the respondents, because, they had become the ex proprietor, occupancy tenants of this land in the year 1895. HELD: (i) The respondents were not ex proprietors occupancy tenants. They were only holders of rent free lands. They had no right to remain in possession of these lands. [274 E] (ii) The respondents had not established their title to these lands. They were therefore not entitled to any actual possession from them. [273 F]

The holding Company shall pay the entire amount payable to the subscribers who were members of creditors association on the date when their claim applications were decided by the Kerala High Court together with interest there ough ting from the date they have been paid. [9D E] 2.1 The High Court was right in directing the holding
1257: The appellant was convicted under section 307, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. His appeal to the High Court failed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) A person commits an offence under section 308 when he has an intention to commit culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and if he does that act by doing so with intent to kill or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause death, he is liable for punishment under section 307. [708 F] (ii) The condition of acute emacia tion in which B is found on 5th June, 1956, is not due to any calculated starvation but it was on account of prolonged illness, the nature of which was not known to the accused till Dr. It follows therefore that a person committed an offence under s.308 when he had an intention to cause, in the natural and ordinary course of things, that he did something to accomplish that purpose. [709 G H]
4865: The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court set aside the acquittal of the appellant but confirmed the conviction of the appellant on the ground that the evidence of Bodu Lal was not corroborated by the recovery of the blood stained knife at his instance. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) It is impossible to agree with the view of the trial court as to the reliability of the evidence of the eye witnesses. The reasons given by the trial court for acquitting the appellant were cogent and they did not call for interference. [862 C] (ii) The High Court has specifically dealt with the reasons given by tho trial court in support of its order of acquittal passed by it. The High court has also specifically dealt with reasons given by it for setting aside the acquittal. [863 D E] (iii) The High court had carefully examined the evidence and came to the conclusion that the prosecution case was established beyond reasonable doubt. The High COurt was therefore justified in reversing the order of acquittal. [886 F G]
6063: The appellants are manufacturers of 'Supercem Water proof Cement Paint ', a chemical product and other allied products in their factory at Madras. In the course of their business they entered into an agreement with Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co., a registered firm, for sale of 'Appli cation No. 1 ' and other connected products. Clause (1) of this agreement provided that the selling agents shall sell to the purchaser Gillandras all kinds of cotton fabrics made out of cotton yarns of all types not only of the appellants but also of several other reputed manufacturers through their well staffed offices in all the States of India. Clause (2) of the agreement stated that the selling agent shall have the right to sell the goods on behalf of the manufacturer and to be sold to any person duly authorised by him in this behalf. Clause (3) of the said agreement stated that "the selling agent shall not sell the goods to any person other than the manufacturer or his duly authorised agent who is a party to the agreement". Clause (4) of the Agreement stated that "all orders, instructions, directions and writ which are being issued by the selling agent as aforesaid shall be deemed to be goods of the class or classes specified in the licence granted under the relevant provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder and shall continue to be so until repealed or amended. " The appellants were the manufacturers of ' Supercem Water Proof Cement Paint, a chemical products and other allied goods in their factory. They had been carrying on business at Madras and referred to as 'The Manufacturer ' and 'Gilanda ' and 'Selling Agent respectively. The appellants were manufacturing 'Supercematem Law delivery contracts ' and other allied con tracts. The appellants claimed that the price paid for the 'Appliances ' was not assessable under the terms of the agreement dated 1st May, 1962 and that the appellants were entitled to the value of the goods for levy of excise duty. The Assistant Collector rejected the contention of the appellants and held that the true character of the agreement was that it was an agreement for sole selling agency and not an agreement for sale. He held that the appellants had no concern with the manufacture of 'Superatem Law delivery contract '
3786: The appellant was born on January 1,1911. He joined the erstwhile State of Manipur as a junior clerk in 1935. He was appointed as a Subordinate Judge with effect from 25th Janu ary, 1960. In November 1962 he was served with a notice by the Government of India that he was required to retire from Government service with effect from 1 October 1966 in pursuance of the direc tions of the President in Paragraph 6 of the Government of Indi a Decision No. 23 noted below Fundamental Rule 56. The decision came into force on 1 December 1962. On the enactment of Manipur Courts Act 1955 the Court of Subordinate Judge was estab lished. The appellant did not earn good reports from superior officers. The appellant was served with notice dated 30 June 1966 that he was retired from Government serv ice with effect from January 1, 1966 in pursuance Of the directi bation of the President contained in Government of India 's letter No. 33/18/62 ESTS(A) dated 30 November 1962. The representation of the appellant for his being retained in service after the age of 55 years in public interest was rejected. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of compulsory retirement. The main contention of the appellant was that the impugned order of compulsory retr ospectively retiring him from service was null and void ab initio because the Fundamental Rule 56 at the material time contained no reservation of any powers in the appointing authority to retire an officer who had completed 55 years of qualifying service. The appellant also contended that the impugned orders were violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the impugned action taken against the appellant amounted to deprivation of reasonable opportunity to defend himself and that the order was therefore illegal. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The order of compulsory re instatement is not a punishment since it affects the public servant concerned. [864 C] (2) The order is not a penalty but only administrative order involving civil consequences. It does not affect the rights or privileges of a government servant. It adversely affects the status of the employee which is protected under Article 311 of the Constitution.[865 D]

1135: The appellants are the collieries situated in the Chhindwara District of Madhya Pradesh. They were carrying on business as coal dealers and were assessed to sales tax for coal manufactured at their mines. The respondent Sabha, acting under section 51 of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958, issued notices to the appellants calling upon them to pay the coal tax for coal supplied by them outside the State of Madhya Pradesh, which was levied and recovered from them under the provisions of the said Act. The appellants challenged the notices in the High Court. The High Court held that the appellants ' claims were barred by res judicata by reason of the earlier decision of this Court in the case of Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd. vs The Janapada Sabha, Chhindwara ; , and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellants had a vested right to continue the levy and recover the tax in question, and that the notice issued by the Sabha was not in accordance with law. HELD : (i) The appellants have no vested right to claim the benefit of the Constitution. [175 D] (ii) The appellants were not consumers of coal or their employees. They were not consumers within the meaning of the expression in the Indian Companies Act 1913. The appellants were consumers of coal and were liable to pay the tax. [176 E F] (iii) The appellants did not raise any dispute as to the liability to pay the said tax. They were only consumers of coal. The appellants could not be made to pay the price of coal charged by the Sabha. [177 G H]
5329: The respondent assessee was a manufacturer of tyres and tubes. It had claimed exemption from duty on the said goods under Notification No. 16/77 dated August 1, 1977. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim holding that the notification was not applicable to the case as it did not apply to the specified goods. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Assistant Collector. The High Court held that the notification dated July 14, 1978 was applicable only to the specified products and not to the specified articles and that there could be no double taxation with respect to the specified items. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the notification granting exemption from duty was intended to encourage the use of certain specified goods and not to allow any discrimination between specified goods and specified articles and therefore the notification granting benefit of exemption from duty to specified articles was not applicable in the instant case. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The notification dated August 1. 1976 is not applicable to specified goods. [857F] (2) The notification was issued in exercise of powers conferred by sub rule (1) of Rule 8 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. The notification dated July, 14, 1978 is not applicable in respect of specified goods. Therefore, the notification dated August 14, 1978 will have no application to the specified classes of specified goods mentioned in the notification dated June 16, 1975. [858G H; 859A] (3) The notification granting exemption to the extent of the duty paid on inputs should be applied first to the notification dated October 15, 1978 and then to the notification giving effect to it. [860B]

The g ings are then gintered and ginner is ginned along with gindy. [866D E] 3. The grading of the ginning
6421: The Bihar State Government by a Memorandum dated February 18, 1977 decided to merge the cadre of District Engineers with the Executive Engineers of the Public Works Department. In the said Memorandum it was stated that the cadre of the District Engineers would be merged with the equivalent/parallel cadre of Executive Engineers of Public Works Department and that the chances of promotion of Assistant Engineers would be affected. The said Memorandum also provided that the seniority of Assistant Engineers working in the Department would be maintained. By an executive order the Bihar Government created two new cadres of Executive Engineers viz., (i) the Bihar State Government and (ii) the Bihar Provincial Engineering Service. The Bihar Government by a memorandum dated February 18.1977 decided to merethe cadre of the Executive Engineers in the State of Bihar. The said decision was communicated to all the District Engi neers in the State who were working as Assistant Engineers in the Bihar Engineering Service, Class II. The said order was challenged before the Patna High Court on the ground that by merg ing the cadres, the chances ofpromotion of Assistant Engineers are likely to be adversely affected and as such merging the cadre of Executive Engineer with the equivalent cadre of Execu tive Engineer could not have been done. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the cadre was separate from the cadre of Assistant Engineers and that the promotional prospects of Assistant Engineers were likely to be prejudicially affected. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1. The impugned order is arbitrary and is liable to be quashed. The said rules cannot be changed retrospectively so as to affect their vested rights. The impugned orders do not violate any fundamental right or the petitioner has no legal right. [814E F] 3. The impugned merger order is not violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. [815A B] 3.1 The impugned merger Order does not suffer from any infirmity. It does not give any right to the petitioners to claim promotion to the post of Executive Engineers. The impugned mer ging the cadres are thus contrary to the 1939 Rules and as such cannot be sustained. [816
6116: The appellant, the successor in interest of the mort gagor of the suit property, filed a suit for redemption on 28.12.1973 and sought to meet the plea of limitation by urging that the son of the original mortgagee, while selling the property on 1.11.1913 had specifically acknowledged the right of the mortgagor to redeem the property. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the sale deed did not contain an acknowledgment of the right of redemption on the part of the mortgagor as on the date of the sale deed. The first appellate court affirmed the decree. In second appeal, the High Court held that the recitals in the document did not serve as an acknowledgement of the right to redeem the mortgage but only a right to sue for rendition of account. The High Court further held that the stipulation in the sale deed that the original mortgagee would be entitled to redeem the mortgaged land was not a mere formality but a condition precedent to the right to recover the amount of loan. The High COurt also held that the sale was not a transaction of mortgage simpliciter but was a transaction of sale simpliciter. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The stipulation in the mortgage deed that the mortgagor would be entitled only to the benefit of the mortgage and the rights and inter est in respect of the mortgage is not an acknowledgment of any right in the mortgagor 's favour. [614F] (2) The stipulation does not serve as a conditional acknowledgment of the title of the mortgagor. It merely says that what has been transferred to the purchaser is not only the right of recovery of the principal amounts and interest payable under the mortgage deed but also the right of renditioning the mortgaged land. If the sale deed contained an unequivocal promise to repay the borrowed money with interest, it could be said to have been made on behalf of the mortgagor and was binding on the mortgagor. [615B C] (3) The stipulation is not an integral part of the transaction itself. It is a provision which provides for the extinction or modification of the right which the mortgagor has in the mortgagor"s favour. The stipulation must be read alongwith the other provisions of the mortgage deed. [616D E]
1597: The appellant company was running a textile mill. It had a large number of employees and the question for consideration was whether the company could be said to have closed its business on account of the impending closure of its business. Held, that the company was not justified in refusing to make a gratuity scheme in respect of the employees of the appellant. The scheme was not based on any statutory enactment but was evolved by industrial adjudication as a step to achieve social justice. The provisions for payment of gratuity were never intended to be an incentive to the employer to start work in future. The scheme did not provide for the payment of gratuity to the employees at all. The scheme merely gave certain benefits to the employees who had put in more than 5 years service. The scheme also provided that the employees should be paid gratuity calculated on the average of the wages earned by them during the three calendar months immediately preceding the date of closure of the undertaking. The scheme further provided that the gratuity payable would be paid after deducting the amount of arrears from the total amount of gratuity payable to the employees. The scheme, therefore, was not designed to meet the liabilities of the employers arising out of the employment of the workmen. The scheme only contemplated a provision for gratuity and it was not meant to create a right in favour of the employees to get gratuity. The scheme had been framed because the employees had put in their full service and there was no scope for their being asked to retire voluntarily. The scheme could not be regarded as providing for the payment or the payment of Gratuity to the employees as the scheme itself contemplated only a small percentage of the workmen retire. The scheme made it clear that the employees were to be given gratuity only if they had completed 10 years service. In the present case, the scheme did not contain any condition that the employees must have put in more service. The employees were not entitled to gratuity under the scheme.
6094: % The appellants are manufacturers of beer and are covered by the provisions of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. They were assessed to tax under the Act on the value of packing material at the rate of 10 paise in the rupee at every point of sale other than at the point of last sale, at which point the rate is 5 paise per rupee. The appellants challenged the assessment orders before the High Court contending that the price charged by them was not the consideration for the sale of beer and so it was not assessable as tax. The High Court dismissed all the writ petitions filed by the appellants. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The price charged by the appellants to the dealer consist of the price of the contents, namely, beer or cement, but does not include the price of containers, that is the cartons, that is, the cartons are the different sale of the product with the transfer of the container without any sale consideration. [310G H] 1.2 The appellants are liable to pay sales tax on the value thereof at the rate applicable to the goods packed in the containers, thatis, the cartonies sold along with the goods and the cartons used for packing the goods. [311A B] 2.1 The appellants are entitled to exemption from payment of sales tax under section 6 A(b) of the Act. [312B] 3. The appellants have been rightly taxed by the assessing authority. [313C] 4. Section 6 C provides that where goods packed in any materials are sold or purchased, the materials i.e., beer or a carten or other thing subjected to the sale con tract would be taxable at the rate specified in the Third Schedule. The appellants are also liable to pay tax on the difference between the price of beer and the carton. [314D E]
6141: The appellant, a company registered under the Companies Act, was granted an application by the Central Government for the establishment of an industrial plant in the State of Rajasthan. The said application was rejected by the Central Govt. and the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated 20 9 88. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that it had no jurisdiction to pass any reasoned order. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the impugned order is vitiated as it merely sets out the bald conclusion of the officer concerned; (ii) the order has been passed by one Sri Vijayaraghavan whereas a personal oral hearing in the matter had been given by Sri S.S. This, coupled with change in personnel referred to above, has resulted in the denial of natural justice to the appellant; and (iii) the order is vitiated because of non supply of copies of documents at the personal hearing. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order dated 20.9.88 is not a reasoned or well considered order. [613F] 2. It is not a speaking order. The order does not deal with the contentions raised by the appellant. The order also does not indicate whether the appellant had applied its mind to all the relevant facts and circumstances. The order is silent on the question of the principles of natural justice. [614B C] 3. The order cannot be sustained. [615E F]
199: The Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was enacted to amend and codify the law relating to income tax. Section 13 of the Indian Finance Act, 1950, provided that "the Central Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, add to, amend or vary any provision of this Act. . . . . The Mysore Legislature passed the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1950. 4302: The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of certain shares in Mitra Prakashan Pvt. Ltd., which had been held by her as full owner thereof by virtue of provisions of section 14 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953. In Maya Press (P) Ltd. vs Commissioner of Estate Duty, , this Court held that the share scrips standing in the name of the wife of the deceased as benamidar were not property within the meaning of section 14 and were therefore liable to estate duty under section 64(1) of the Act. The appellant 's case was that these shares belonged to her husband as he was the real owner of those shares. The Assistant Controller of Estate Duty rejected the claim on the ground that the shares were held by the wife of his deceased son as benami and that the value of the shares could not be included in the principal value of the estate of the deceased. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Assistant Controller of Estates Tax but the High Court declined to answer questions other than those which were questions of law. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the view taken by the High Court was erroneous and that the two sections were mutually exclusive and they had independent fields of operation. HELD: (i) The two sections are mutually exclusive and so the question whether the shares were in the nature of benami or not must be determined with reference to the circumstances of each case. [864 G] (ii) The view taken by this Court is that the two Sections are mutually exclusive. It is only when there is conflict between the two judgments that the earlier judgment becomes the last authority. [865 C] (iii) The two Sections are inter entirely different. They deal with different situations and the Legislature has deliberately chosen to treat them as redundant and have introduced an altogether new provision. [866 D]

894: The appellant was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. He filed an election petition for a declaration that he had been duly elected. The respondent objected to the application on the ground that section 117 of the Act had not been complied with and that no appeal lay from such an order under section 90(3) of the Act. The Tribunal overruled the objection and held that it was not in terms of section 117 of that Act. The High Court, in revision, set aside the Tribunal 's order and directed the Tribunal to decide the election petition according to law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 117 does not require that every election petition should be accompanied by a Government Treasury Receipt showing that a deposit of Rs. 1,000 has been made by the petitioner infavour of the Secretary to the Election Commission as security for the costs of the petition. It is quite clear that the Tribunal had not been made under section 99. [520 B] (ii) The Tribunal had not committed any error of law which could have resulted in failure of justice. The Tribunal had only given its reasons for dismissing the election petition. [521 C] (iii) The order of the Tribunal dismissing the petition did not amount to an order under sections 98 or 99 of the Act and was therefore illegal. [522 D E]
6373: The appellant along with others were convicted for murdering Kumari Mangala in furtherance of their common intention and causing disappearance of evidence of the offence with the intention of screening themselves from legal punishment under section 302 read with Section 34 IPC and under Section 201 read with Section 120 B IPC. P.C., is empowered to enhance the sentence even in the absence of an appeal by the State against the inadequacy of the sentence as provided under Section 377 Cr. [773F G] Nadir Hussain & Anr. vs State of Maharashtra, [1979] 3 SCR 646; Nadir Hussein Mohammedali Rangwalla vs State of Bombay, ; ; Nadir Hasan Khan vs State (Delhi Admn.) ; ; Nallabothu Veerappa Mudaliar vs State of Maharastra, ; ; and Nadir Ahmed & Ors. vs State (Govt. of A.P. & Ors., [1988] Suppl. 1 S.C.R. 791, referred to.
1049: The petitioners, who were the owners of a bull or bullock in respect of which a certificate under section 3(1)(b) of the U.P. Prevention of Cow Slaughter (Amendment) Act, 1958 was issued by the District Animal Husbandry Officer, filed an appeal to the State Government against the order of the competent authority imposing the maximum limit of 20 years for slaughtering of such a bull or animal. The State Government referred the matter to the Director of Animal Husbandry and directed that the certificate should be issued after it had been certified that the bull or bullocks were over the age of 25 years. The petitioners contended that the certificate was invalid as the animal was over 25 years old and could not be slaughtered at all. Held, that the certificate must be treated as ineffective as it would have no effect on the validity of the slaughter of the bull or of the bullock. The certificate did not impose any conditions upon the animal or its owner nor imposed any restrictions on the slaughter of such a animal or its being over the age or the slaughtering of the animal. The certificate merely prescribed the period within which the animal should be slaughtered or the number of animals slaughtered. The animal was not slaughtered within the time specified in the certificate. The animal could not be said to be over 25 years and could not become permanently unfit for the purpose of breeding and therefore the certificate could not be effective.
1882: The appellant was convicted in two cases under section 467 read with section 471 and section 477A I.P.C., by the Sessions Judge on July 20, 1963 and was sentenced to three years rigorous imprisonment under section 409 IPC by Shri Dube, First Additional Sessions Judge Ujjain on July 20. 1963. In the fourth appeal, the High Court said : "The trial court has awarded a sentence of three years rigorous imprison ment to one of the offences charged against him, but the sentences were directed concurrently. There is nothing illegal about it. " In the fifth appeal, the appellant contended that he should have been tried separately for the offence under section 467 I.P,.C. and not for the offence of criminal breach of trust. The respondents urged that there was no illegality in the sentences awarded to the appellant in the other four cases or in not making them run concurrent with the sentences awarded in the other two cases. [883 G] (iii) The appellant could be tried separately for each of the four offences. [891 F]

4023: The respondent was an employee of the appellant Corporation. He had not sought or got the Chairman 's permission laboured under a legal ineligibility as contemplated in section 15(g) of the City of Nagpur Corporation Act, 1948. The appellant who was such an employee and had not sought any or got the Vice President 's permission appointed by the Chairman to preside over the meeting held on May 4, 1968, filed an application before the High Court for setting aside the election of the respondent on the ground that the said Rule 23 of the Corporation Rules framed under section 49 of the Act violated his fundamental right under article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the application holding that it did not stand in the way of the respondent 's election being set aside on the ground of violation of article 14 of the Constitution; and that the impugned rule was not ultra vires the Act. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (i) The impugned rule is not ultra vires of article 14. [803 G] (ii) The impugned Rule does not offend article 14 of Constitution. It is not discriminatory nor is it violative of any fundamental right. [804 F] (iii) The impugned provision in the impugned rule is arbitrary and unreasonable. It is also violative of article 14 because it makes the person ineligible for election at the time when he took part in the election. [805 B C] (iv) The impugned clause in the rule is not severable from the other clauses of the rule. It is severable from those clauses which are severable. [806 A] (v) The impugned Clause is not severability based on the exclusion of certain rights from the general public but is only a partial exclusion of those rights from the particular classes of persons covered by the impugned clause. [807 B]
2301: The respondent Society purchased the land in execution of a decree and at an auction sale held under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Society purchased the leasehold interest in the said land after obtaining the necessary permission from the Government. The Society filed a suit for declaration that the State Government had no authority to acquire the land and that the Society was entitled to an injunction restraining the Government from taking possession of the land. The Trial Court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal and granted a declaration that the Society had title to the land. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Society that the acquisition proceedings were mala fide and in fraud of the Act and therefore null and void and that the society was not entitled to an order of injunction against the Government taking possession of land. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the Society could not be deemed to have been satisfied with the notification under section 6 of the Land Acquisitiol Act, 1894 and that the Government should make a declaration "to that effect". [1193 F] (ii)The High Court was wrong in holding that since the Government was satisfied that the land was required by the Society, it was not necessary to make a declaration under sec. 6 of the Act. The word 'satisfied ' is used in contradistinction to the word 'may '. It means "shall" or "must". The word 'shall ' is generally construed as "shall" because it is intended to convey any of the meanings of "shalls". The word "shall" is sometimes described as "shall". But where the context requires the word "should" to be read it indicates "shall". [1191 G H; 1192 A C]

5825: The respondents were charged with the offence of murder and injuries to two persons. The trial court convicted them under section 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. and sentenced them to death. The High Court, however, acquitted the respondents on the ground that (1) it was not a case of complete dereliction of duty or failure of justice; (2) the judgment of the trial court suffers from a serious infirmity in that he had in a slipshod manner not discussed at all the evidence separately under different heads of the charges framed against each of the accused persons; and (3) the judgment was vitiated by an error of law inasmuch as it did not discuss the evidence separately. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. It is clear from the judgment of acquittal passed by the High Court that it has not considered the evidence separately and has also not discussed the evidence separately on the question of sentence. [873F] 2. The judgment of the High Court does not deal with the evidence separately but only deals with the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. The judgment is silent on the aspect whether the evidence of one witness has been excluded from consideration. [874A] 3. The judgment does not deal specifically with the evidence on which the prosecution has based its case. The judgment merely states that the evidence of three eye witnesses has been excluded. [875B C] 4. The judgment cannot be said to have dealt with the evidence alone. [877D] 5. The judgment has not considered whether the evidence is sufficient to convict the accused or not. [876E] 6. The judgment proceeds on the basis that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction. [878H] 7. The judgment fails to show that the learned Judge has applied his mind to the evidence before him. The judgment, therefore, is vitiated by an erroneous approach. [879G]

418: The respondent was tried by the Magistrate for an offence under section 7 of the East Punjab Essential Services (Maintenance) Act, 1947. The allegation against him was that he had been a sentry in a police party and had disobeyed the lawful orders given by superior officer who had assigned duty to him as such foot constable. The Magistrate acquitted the respondent holding that the order of dismissal from service did not amount to a punishment within the meaning of section 19(1)(b) of the Act. On appeal the Sessions Judge set aside the acquittal but the High Court on a reference made at the instance of the respondent accepted his contention and convicted him. Held, that the order passed by the Magistrate was not one of dismissal simpliciter. The expression "discharge" in section 19(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure means "discharged". The word 'refresher course ' has many meanings and it must take its colour from the context. It may well mean absence of proof or improper exercise of power. In the present case the Magistrate found that the respondent was guilty of disobedience of lawful orders given to him by superior officers. He was therefore rightly discharged.
1886: The Government of India acquired certain land belonging to the appellant company under a notification issued on February 18, 1944. The Government did not deliver possession of the land but purported to take possession of it by executing agreements with the owners. The agreement was terminated by notice dated December 24, 1943, and the appellant took possession of the property. On January 30, 1946, the Government of India requisitioned the land under the Defence of India Rules and the appellant paid Rs. 202/ by way of earnest money. The Government accepted the amount and delivered possession of the premises to the appellant. The question as to whether the contract could be said to have been discharged because of the fact that its performance was rendered unlawful for a period of time or for an indeterminate period of time was left open by this Court in the appeal filed by the appellant. Held, that the contract was not extinguished by reason of the termination of the war and the appellant was entitled to remain in possession of the building. The contract was not a mere one year 's written contract; it was a contract which was made for a period not less than one year. The contract being a composite one involving several obligations, each one of which was enforceable at law, there could be no doubt that the contract became voidable at the option of the Government if the performance of the contract was rendered unlawful by the act of the Government. The contract having been terminated by notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the appellant was not entitled to remain on the land.

4107: The appellant was an evacuee and the house in question was declared as an evacuee property under section 10 of the Evacuee Property Act, 950. He applied to the Assistant Custodian for restoration of the house under sub section (2) of section 16 of the Act. The Central Government ordered that it had revised its order dated 11 11 1960 and restored the house to the appellant. On 6 12 1960 the Central Government ordered, inter alia, that it had reviewed its order dated November 11 1960 and passed a fresh order on 18 3 1957 restoring the house to him. On June 12, 1960 the Central Govern ment ordered that it would be open to the appellant to apply to the Assistant Collector for compensation under section 20A of the Act if he satisfied that there was no justification for the loss sustained by him. The appellant came to know later that on 11 11 1960 the Central Govt. ordered that it should take action under section 20 A of the Act and that the appellant was entitled to compensation only under section 20(1). The appellant filed a suit against the Custodian and the Central Government for a declaration that the order dated 18 3 1957 was illegal and void and for a permanent injunction restraining the Custodian from taking any action pursuant to the said order. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the order of the Central Government dated 11 11 60 was not final and that the order could not be set aside without giving the parties an opportunity of being heard. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order dated 11 12 1960 was merely an administrative order and did not affect the rights of the appellant. [987 E] (ii) The order of the Government dated November 11, 1960 was not final because the Central Government had already decided to restore the house to it. The order of November 11,1960 was merely an executive act of the Central government and did not alter the status quo ante. [988 G] (iii) The order was not final as it was not required to be made by the Central Government. [989 D]
2018: The respondents filed a suit for possession of the land in dispute on the ground that they were the legal heirs of Raj Kaur against Kehar Singh and the Raja of Faridkot. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the suit was barred by time. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The suit was not governed by article 141 of the Limitation Act, 1908 as held by the High Court. Article 142 provides that where a person has been in occupancy of land belonging to another person, he shall be deemed to be a tenant if the land is cultivated by him personally or by any other person on his behalf; and the right to cultivate is also a right which can be exercised under the law relating to agrarian reform. [851 G H] (ii) The respondents ' case was that the lands belonged to them and not to the appellant. The respondents ' contention was that the suit should have been instituted within one year of the date of the decree and not six months from the date of its execution. The respondents did not file any suit after the expiry of six months from June 15, 1944, when the Raja of the Faridkot had already executed a deed of adoption in favour of the respondents. [852 C D] (iii) The respondents could not claim title to the land in question because the order of the Raja was not final and binding on them. [853 E F]
4192: The appellant and his brother were evacuees under a notification issued by the Custodian of Evacuee Property, Uttar Pradesh on December 14, 1955. The Assistant Custodian (Judicial) Deoria declared the appellant and his brothers as evacueees under clauses (i), (ii) & (iii) of section 2(d) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1949. On March 11, 1956, the Assistant Custodian (judicial) Deoria, acting under section 7 of the Act, issued notices to the appellant and the latter, who was then in Pakistan, and their brother Bashir Ahmad, to show cause why orders should not be passed declaring them evacuee and their property as evacuee properties. The notice stated that the information in possession of the Custodian was that they were evacuation persons and their property was being treated as evacuee. The Assistant Collector, Deoria, after hearing the parties, held that the appellant and Bashir Ahmed were evacued from Pakistan and therefore the property was declared evacueed and their property had been treated as evacuee property. The Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal preferred by the appellant and also the revision filed by him. The appellant moved the High Court for quashing the proceedings but the same was rejected. The appellant came to this Court with certificate. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the notice dated November 22, 1956, issued by the Assistant Custodian, Deoria was invalid because it did not contain any particulars about the person or persons who were alleged to have transferred their movable and immovable properties. It was further contended that the notice was issued without giving any particulars about Bashir and his brother. HELD:The notice dated November 29, 1956, was invalid inasmuch as it did not mention the names of the persons who were said to have transferred the properties. [864 C] The notice merely stated that the matter was referred to the Advisory Board. The report of the Advisory Board was only an opinion of the Board and no particulars about the persons who had transferred their properties were given. The report was merely an opinion of an officer of the rank of Deputy Custodian. The report did not disclose any particulars about any person who had transferred the properties to Pakistan. The report merely mentioned that the property was being dealt
4919: The petitioners in the first set of petitions are newspaper companies engaged in the business of publishing and selling newspapers, periodicals, magazines etc. They have been carrying on the same kind of business as a newspaper company. In the Second Schedule to the , under heading 48.01 21, the rate of customs duty leviable is 15% ad valorem. The petitioners in these petitions challenged the levy of additional duty on newsprint which had been levied at a flat rate of 2%. The petitioners contended that there was no need to impose customs duty on newsprints which had enjoyed total exemption from its payment till March 1, 1981, as the foreign exchange position was quite comfortable. It was also contended that there has been a substantial increase in the cost of production by reason of the imposition of the import duty. The petitioners further contended that there had been a substantial reduction in the price of newsprint and the consequent inflationary economic conditions which had led to higher cost of production had made it impossible for the industry to bear the duty any longer. The petitioners also contended that the imposition of auxiliary duty under the Finance Act, 1981 on newspriniting imported into India was unreasonable and arbitrary. The petitioners contended (i) that there was nothing to justify the imposition of customs duty on the newsprint manufactured by them; (ii) that there has not been any violation of the fundamental right guaranteed by Article 19(1)(a); (iii) that there had not been any infringement of any of the fundamental rights guaranteed by clauses (6) and (7) of article 19 of the Constitution; (iv) that there is no violation of any of his fundamental rights guaranteed under articles 14, 19(1) (g), 301 and 304 of the Constitution. The petitioners submitted that there has never been any violation or infringement of any fundamental right guaranteed under either article 19(1 ) (a) or (b). The petitioners contended: (i) There has been a considerable increase in the prices of newsprings and the consequent increase in the price has made it difficult for the industry a class by itself to be able to bear the additional duty. The impugned levy is violative of the equality clause contained in article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it imposes an unreasonable restriction on the freedom
1604: The appellant, who was the son of Chimpirayya, executed a will on January 14, 1895 in respect of his half share in the joint family properties. Subbarao died on May 5, having executed a will dated January 14, 1880 which contained an unequivocal declaration that he had no intention to separate himself from Subba Rao and that the said Subba Rao would take the entire property belonging to him after his death. Subbaratha, the daughter of Chimpira, who was then living with her father in law, filed a suit for partition against the first respondent on the ground that the said Will was invalid as it did not confer any right or interest in the property. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the Will was not proved to have been signed by Chimpiraya, the first respondent, and that the recitals in the Will were sufficient to establish the fact that Chimpirayanad had full knowledge of the said declaration. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether the recitals contained in the Will amounted to a partition is essentially one of intention of the testator to separate himself and the onus to prove such intention lay upon the party challenging the genuineness of the Will. [902 D E] (ii) The question as to whether the recital in the Will itself constituted a partition in status could be raised only at the stage of evidence when the Will was sought to be proved. [903 F] (iii) The question about the validity of the recitals made in the Will does not arise in the instant case because the recitals are not conclusive and do not affect the admissibility of the document in evidence. [904 A B] (iv) The question of partition is a mixed question of law and fact and has to be decided on the basis of the materials produced before the Court. [905 C]
4869: The appellant was the owner of a shop. He filed an application under section 12 read with section 16 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for a declaration that the shop was vacant and he required the same for his personal need. The application was resisted by Jaspal Singh on the ground that he was the heir of Naubat Singh deceased and was in occupation of the disputed shop; that on 4th July 1973 Naubat singh died and the landlord filed an application for a declaration to that effect. The Rent Control and Eviction officer rejected the application holding that the appellant had been living with the deceased Naubatsingh and was also assisting him in doing the business in the disputed premises to the full knowledge of the landlord and so he was entitled to get the benefit of section 14 of the Act. The appeal preferred against this order was dismissed by the Additional District Judge. The revision petition filed before the High Court was transferred to the Additional District judge who held that the appellant was not entitled to get protection of section 14 as he was not the heir on the basis of the will executed by Naubat Singha. The High Court further held that the application for amendment of the plaint was barred by limitation. The High court also held that the tenant was not entitled under section 14 of Act 28 of 1976 to get the protection of section 15 because he was not a person against whom proceedings were pending at the time when the Act came into force i.e. 1st August 1976. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court committed an error in holding that the application was barred by time since the appellant was claiming to be the heir of the original tenant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 14 of the U P Act 28 of 76 is amended by U.P Act 13 of 1972 which provides that a person must satisfy that (i) he was a tenant in occupation of a building with the consent of the landlord immediately before the commencement of this Act and that he was not in occupation of such building after the date of such commencement; and (ii) that he was in occupation thereof at the commencement of the said Act. [895G H
951: The appellants were assessed to income tax and super tax by the Income Tax Officer on their true income. They submitted a return under the Travancore Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1051, claiming that the amount of tax payable on their true agricultural income was Rs. 1,35,736 8 0 and that they were liable to pay that amount subject to credit for the tax already paid, and claimed that they were not liable to pay any further tax. The Commission accepted the report of the Commission and directed that immediate steps be taken to recover under the Income Tax Act from the appellants the tax due according to the findings recorded by the Commission. The appellants contended that the Commission had no authority to assess or reassess the concealed income and that the order passed by it did not authorise the Commis sioner to reopen the assessment. Held, that the Commission was not competent to assess or revise the income of the appellants in respect of the escaped income. The Commission could not, therefore, determine the tax payable by the appellants without making an enquiry as to whether the income was really concealed or not. The Commission had power to assess or compute the income of a person who had failed to comply with the provisions of section 22(2), and if there was any doubt about the correctness of the information given by the assessee, it had the power to make such enquiries as it thought proper and to decide the matter in accordance with law. The Commission was not entitled to go into the question whether the income of any particular assessee was concealed or concealed nor was it entitled to assess or realise any property from any assessee.
3187: The appellants, who were the owners of certain routes in the State of Uttar Pradesh, challenged the validity of schemes for nationalisation of inter State routes under section 68D(2) of the (Act 4 of 1939), approved by the Government of India under section 68C of the Act. The scheme was approved by the Transport Commission and the State Government under section 68E(3) of the Act and the approval was subject to the approval of the Government of Uttar Pradesh. The appellants contended that the scheme was not approved by the State Government as required by section 68F(1)(a) of the and the approval of Government of India was not subject to any condition. The High Court held that the scheme did not require the approval of Parliament as required by article 258 of the Constitution. The High court also held that the approval of State Government was necessary before a scheme could be implemented under section 68F of the Act, and that the scheme had been approved by the Central Government. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the scheme itself was not approved within the meaning of entry 21 of List III of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, and that it was not open to the State Government to implement the scheme without obtaining the approval of Central Government. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme is not an approved scheme within the meaning Of Entry 42 of List III. [903 G] 2. The scheme does not require the prior approval of the Central Government as contemplated by section 68E of the Act for the nationalisation of the route or portion thereof. It requires the approval of that Government. The scheme has been approved by that Government. [904 A B] 3. The scheme cannot be said to have been approved by a State Government. The approval of the State Government is necessary before a Scheme can be implemented under the Act. [905 D E]
2711: The Regional Transport Authority, in a proceeding under section 48 of the , held that it did not consider it necessary to grant permits to individual applicants. The R.T.A. then decided that the proposed route was necessary in public interest and granted the permit to the appellants. The appellants filed writ petitions in the High Court for quashing the order of the Tribunal contending that no appeal against the order of ' the R.T.,A. had been preferred by them as they were not "all interested parties" within the meaning of section 47(3) of the Act. The respondents contended that no appeal lay against the order passed by the R. T.A. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the R.S.T. could not have determined the number of permits which were to be granted to applicants who were not "any interested parties". In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 47(3), if read with section 47(4), makes no difference between cases where applications are invited by the RTA and the R.TA. [247 G] (ii) The R. T,.A. has to decide whether a proposed route should be opened or not. If he decides that an existing route should be closed, he can only refuse to grant a permit on the ground that the proposed portion of the route is likely to overlap with the route on which it is proposed to run. He cannot go into the question whether the proposed route should or should not be opened. [248 B C] (iii) The RTA has to determine the number of routes which should be included for the purpose of granting or refusing a permit. The RTA is required to give its reasons for reaching such decision. It may also call for further information from the applicants. But there is no obligation upon the R.TC. to furnish any data or information. [249 D E]
6655: The appellant company manufactured and cleared from its factory paperboard boxes, cartons, etc. in bulk as well as in packed containers. The excise duty payable on such containers was Rs.1,20,000/ per year. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise, Pune Division passed an order dated January 28, 1982 holding that 'egg trays ' manufactured by the appellant were correctly classifiable under Item 68 of the old Tariff. The Assistant Collec tor of Central Excise Pune Division confirmed the said order. The Collector (Appeals) dismissed the appeal preferred by the appellant. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal of the appellant holding that 'emission on eggs ' is not a 'container ' within the meaning of the proviso to section 11 A(l) of the . In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods manufactured by the assessee were made out of waste paper and they were classifiable as 'articles of paper and paper board '; that the goods were made out either wholly or partly of waste paper or of other materials which could be used for making them. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'containers ' has been used in the Act in a broad sense and includes all types of egg trays whether in assembled or unassembled condition. [326E] 2. It is clear from the definition of 'articles ' in the new Tariff that the word 'otherwise ' means 'in connection with or in relation to the use of those articles '. The word 'includes ' is very comprehensive and denotes enlargements of the original meaning of the word. The word has been advisedly employed to enlarge the scope of the original definition so as to cover all parts of the including within itself all items of goods, all articles and commodities which are intended to become automatically at once fit for consumption. [327F G] 3. The word "excisable" in the new tariff has been used to convey the idea of an article of any substance specified in the First Schedule or the Second Schedule. The word is ordinarily construed as not being in pith and substance only such things as are included in the class or classes of articles
1506: The appellants were charged under section 302/149 I.P.C. for having committed the murder of one Arjan Singh and of another person. The trial court held that the charge under section 302 had not been proved against the accused persons, but that the charge had not been sustained. On appeal to the High Court, the High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellants and sentenced them to death. In appeal to this Court by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the charge of murder under section 302 read with section 34 I.P,.C. had not been duly proved against the appellants and that the charge for murder under section 149 had not been made out. HELD : (i) The charge under section 149 I.P,C. could be established only by direct evidence or by circumstantial evidence. It is well settled that in a criminal case where direct evidence may not be available, the court has to look into factors such as the nature of the offence, the time at which it was committed, its character, that whether it was committed by a particular person or not must be judged by what degree of probability the court has applied the principle and if the answer to the question is in the affirmative, the court will have to hold that the accused alone was responsible for the fatal injury. [864 H 865 A] (ii)The fact that the appellant was carrying a gun with him and was alleged to have fired at the deceased cannot be said to have been proved beyond reasonable doubt. The appellant was carrying 'a licensed gun ' and he used it for the purpose of committing an act of violence. There was no evidence that he used it to inflict any injury on the deceased. The appellant did not use any weapon during the occurrence. He used a gun for the purpose for which he was convicted. [863 C E] (iii)It is not necessary that all conspirators should join for the commission of an offence. The acts of each member of the unlawful assembly must be done only after they are satisfied that their common object is to commit a crime. An overt act, however indirect or During the course of the transaction, would constitute an offence. [866 D]
