7070: The Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission issued a notification inviting applications for the post of munsifs in the State. The appellants, who were candidates for selection to the post of Munsif, applied for it. The selection list was published by the commission on May 28, 1984. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the selection list contending that the selection list had been prepared without following the procedure prescribed by the rules of 1967 and the Government had not approved the names of twenty candidates in view of a number of vacancies and the consequent accumulation of work. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the selection was vitiated as the government had not followed the procedure laid down by the rules for the preparation of the select list. Aggrieved by the decision of the High Court, the appellants have preferred these appeals. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The selection process is regulated by the statutory recruitment Rules framed under Article 309 of the Constitution. Rule 39 of the Rules provides that the selection shall be made by competitive examination conducted by the Commission. The Commission has to prepare a list of candidates in accordance with the standards prescribed by the Government. The list so prepared is forwarded to the Government which may approve the list. The Government may accept the list or may reject it. But the list must contain the names of the candidates in accordancewith the rates prescribed by the Govt. and also specify the manner in which the recommendations are to be made. [1009G H; 10010A] 1.2 The Government cannot alter or temper with the order of merit determined by the Commission but it is certainly open to the government to stop at a particular point where it feels that a particular candidate is not available or is unable to follow the list. In the instant case, the Government had no doubt formed prima facie opinion that the list was defective because of some irregularities committed in the preparation of it. It was only after the Government 's approval that the list became final. The Government could not alter or tempered with the order or the list. [1010B D] 1.3 The Government cannot change its mindset when the list was submitted to it. The Government can always modify or even disapprove the list. If
2362: The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that he was in arrears of rent and permitted increases. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree holding that the tenant had not disputed the municipal taxes and permitted increases and as such not entitled to protection of the Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that (i) the High Court was wrong in holding that the defendant was in arrears and permitted increases; (ii) the conditions under section 12(3)(a) were not present; (iii) the conditions were not satisfied because they were not pleaded or proved; (iv) the amount of Rs. 27 mentioned in the compromise petition was not due from him; (v) the conditions necessary for the applicability of section 12(1) were not placed before the Assistant Judge; and (vi) the conditions did not exist. HELD: (i) Section 12(3) (a) is applicable only where there is dispute about the standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under the Act. [864 E] (ii)Section 12(3), which deals with the mode of recovery of rent, does not apply to a case where the standard rent has been fixed without giving an opportunity to the tenant to show cause against the fixation of standard rent. [865 F G] (iii)The High Court was right in holding that section 12(2) applies to the facts of the case. [866 A B] Shah Bhojraj Kuverji Oil Mills and Ginning Factory vs Subbash Chandra Yograj, , referred to.
7102: The appellant and respondent No. 3 were both appointed to the service on May 26, 1977 on the basis of selection by direct recruitment. Respondent No.3 was a Mazhbi Sikh, which is a Schedule Caste in Punjab. The recruitment to the Service was governed by Punjab Superior Judicial Services Rules, 1963. By Rule 8 A, which was inserted in the rules by notification dated June 14,1977, the instructions issued by the State Government from time to time in relation to reservation of appointments or posts for Scheduled Castes in this regard were made applicable for the purpose of making appointments to the posts in the Service. The orders of the State Government relating to persons belonging to Scheduled Castes in these two groups of cases were also amended by notification dated July 6,1977. In the said letter it was indicated that the vacancies to be reserved for Scheduled Castes had to be offered to Balmikis and Mazhbi Sikhs and since Shri Balwant Rai belonged to a Scheduled Caste other than Balmiki, he was not entitled to any Roster till the quota fixed for Balmikas and Mazhbiy Sikhs was exhausted. The appellant and the respondent No.3 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the seniority list prepared by the State Govern ment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order dated May 5, 1975 was not applicable to the case of the appellant as he was appointed in 1979 and that the Roster was available only upto May 25, 1975. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The order dated May 4, 1975 is not applicable to Balmukhi Singh and others who are appellants in Civil Appeal No. 904 of 1991. [902F] 1.2 The order dated June 14.1977 has been passed by the State of Punjab keeping in view the provisions of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966. The order does not indicate that the vacancy in question has to be offered first to Balmhikis and Mazhabi Sikhs. It merely indicates that the Rosters existing at the time of the framing of the order would be continued. [903A B] 1.3 The order dated July 6.1977 cannot be construed to mean that
3607: The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 2(g) of the , and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ . On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the item did not cover roofing tiles but included articles of pottery covered by item 22 of the schedule to the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the item was not intended to enlarge the meaning of potteries industry in any way; the object being to include articles of potteriate nature in the definition of 'scheduled employment ', the items mentioned were also included in item 22 and therefore the Act was not applicable to the industry of the accused. HELD: (i) The item is not confined to articles of potmovers which are included in item 23. It does not exclude articles of potcars which are used as food or drink. [9 E] (ii) The object of the explanation is only to include articles which are not included in item 24. The object of section 3 is not limited to articles of food which are included therein. The object is to include articles other than those specified in items 24 and 25. Therefore, the item cannot be extended to articles which are included within the definition of "scheduled employment" in section 2(j). [10 A B] (iii) The object being to add "any article" in the definition, the items included must be excluded from its purview. [11 D E] (iv) The object is not to include articles made of potatoes which are not generally known as potatoes. The word "potteries" has been defined in section 2 (1) (d) to mean any trade, business, manufacture or calling of employers. The word is wide enough to include all possible articles of potconalt including potters. [12 E F] (v) The object was to include articles manufactured of potable commodities such as potash, pottery etc. [13 C] (vi) The object would have been different if the objects were not included in the definition. But the definition of the word "scheme" is exhaustive as regards articles of potaments. [14 E F]
8: The appellant was the son of a Hindu, who died on 25th April 1905. He was adopted by his wife in 1905 and after his death he filed a suit for recovery of possession of certain properties which were given to Gnanambal, the widow of the testator 's wife, on the allegation that under the will he was entitled to get these properties after the death of the testator. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it and held that the adoption of Gnanambali by the widow was not valid. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Under the terms of the will, the widow was entitled to adopt a son of her husband, if there was no disposition of the remaining interest after the death Of the life tenant. But the widow was bound to adopt a daughter before her death, if she so chose. [902 D E] (ii)The word "difference" in section 2(14) of the , means "difest in desire". The word "divorce" is used in the widur d sense of extinction or destitution. It does not mean any kind of compulsion resulting from the existence of a state of mind or an existing state of things; it means something more than mere compulsion resulting form of compulsion from the act of all the parties concerned. [903 F H] (iii)In the case of adoption made by a Hindu female, the adoption has to be in accordance with the custom and ushering in force in the community in which the property is situated. If the adoption is by a Hindu male alone, then the adoption cannot be effected except by following the provisions of the Act. [904 A B]

4946: The appellant, a trade union representing employees in the Chambal Hydel Irrigation Scheme under the Department of Chambal Project of Government of Madhya Pradesh in Gwalior Division, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the State Government refusing to refer the dispute for adjudication. The State Government refused to refer the matter on the ground that it was not necessary or appropriate to make a reference. The High Court quashed the order of refusal and directed the Government to consider the question whether a reference was necessary or not. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The State Government had by refusing to refer a dispute to the Tribunal, giving the reasons for its decision, acted arbitrarily and without any evidence whatsoever in that behalf. [639 C] (2) The State is a party to every litigation and every person who has a grievance against the State Government should be informed by the State Government so that there may be an effective adjudication of the dispute. The State cannot act arbitrarily at its whims and fancies. It must act fairly and justly not only to the sufferer before the public, but also to the third party. If the State fails to take proper action against the erring official, the responsibility of such action would be very much higher than what it would have been expected from the guilty party. [640 D F]
5318: The respondent assessee, a non resident company, was assessed to income tax as representative assessee of ten non resident companies. In the assessment year 1962 63, the Income Tax Officer held that the nonresident companies had business connection with the Indian Company and therefore the Indian Company was entitled to be treated as an agent of the said non resident companies under section 163 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. 40: The appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge for offences under sections 147, 148 and 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted the appellants but the High Court acquitted them holding that there was no evidence to show that the first accused had ever protested to the existence of the dispute or that he had ever threatened to kill the complainant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) It is not possible to apportion the liability between the parties in an offence like murder. The existence of a dispute as to the right of which the fight must have taken place cannot be made out. [969 D] (ii) The High Court erred in thinking that the case was one of self defence. The fact that the dispute arose out of a sudden quarrel would not necessarily lead to the conclusion that it was only the first appellant who was responsible for the occurrence. The fact of premeditation does not affect the question whether the incident took place or the dispute arose. [970 H; 971 A] (iii) The High Courts ' interference with the order of acquittal is called for only when they find that the view taken by the trial court is unreasonable or perverse. [972 B C]

125: The first defendant, a limited company, was the owner of a flat in Bombay. He let it out to the second defendant on a monthly rent of Rs. 370 per month. The second defendant sublet the flat to the first defendant at a monthly rent which was Rs. 370. The first defendant was in occupation of the flat as a tenant under the first defendant. The second defend ant contended that the suit was not maintainable because the first defendant had no right to sue for compensation from the second defendant. The first defend ant pleaded that the suit as against him was not one between a landlord and a tenant within the meaning of section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and that the suit should be dismissed. Held, that the first defendant was not a person aggrieved by the claim made by the second defendant and he could not maintain the suit. The first respondent was not a licensee or a tenant within section 28 of that Act. The first appellant was not a tenant of the second defendant but was a tenant of a tenant who had sublet the premises to the first respondent. The first appel lant was not a servant of the second respondent. The second respondent was not entitled to maintain the suit as a licensee or tenant. The first Respondent was not a lessee of the second appellant. The first Respond ent was not a landlord within the meaning section 28 of Act 1 of 1947. The first respond ent was not the tenant of the first respondent and the suit was barred by section 28 of this Act.

201: The petitioners were displaced persons from Pakistan who migrated to India after the partition of 1947. They were allotted specific areas of land under the statement of conditions, contained in Notifications Nos. 489 1/S and 4892 IS, dated the 8th July, 1949, on quasi permanent basis in lieu of lands left by them in Pakistan. In 1952 they decided to allot evacuee lands for the current Kharif and Rabi of 1947 48. In July, 1951, the petitioners moved the East Punjab Government that they should be allotted first grade lands. On the 14th October, 1953, the Deputy Custodian General dismissed the revision petition of the petitioners. The petitioners filed a writ petition before this Court under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the order of the Deputy Custodian. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (1) the order of cancellation of allotment had been made without notice to the petitioners as required by section 16(2)(b) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, and (ii) the order violated their fundamental right of property guaranteed under article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. Held, that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief. The order of cancellation did not infringe any fundamental right of the petitioners nor did it infringe any other fundamental right of theirs. The order merely cancelled the allotments made to the petitioners and directed that possession of the lands allotted to them would remain with the petitioners. It was not necessary that the petitioners must have been in actual cultivating possession of the land allotted to them at the time when the order cancelling the allotments was passed.
59: The petitioner, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of aluminium products. In 1951, the Central Bank of India Ltd., which was incorporated under the . acquired its registered office at Bombay and the State of Bihar acquired its registered offices there. On January 26, 1950, the Central Government made an order under section 3(1) of the , directing that all properties of the Bank shall vest in the Central Government free from all encumbrances. The petitioner challenged the legality of this order on the ground that it infringed his fundamental rights under article 19 (1) (f) and article 31(1). Held, that the impugned order violated his fundamental right under article 19(1)(f) and Article 31(1), as the impugned order did not impose any condition for the payment of compensation for taking away or abolishin g property but only imposed a condition for the acquisition of property by the Central Government. The impugned order did no more than to remove the fetter placed upon the right of the petitioner to carry on his business in the goods manufactured by him. The impugned orders were therefore protected from attack under article 32 of the Constitution. The impugned action could not be justified under article 31(2) as it had been taken without the authority of law. The impugned Act did not offend against article 14 of the Constitution and was not void under article 13. The impugned act did not contravene articles 19(1) (g) and 31(1) and was saved by article 31(5) from the operation of article 19(6). The impugned Act was not protected by article 31 (2) as the impugned Act did no more protection than what was protected by article 19(5). The impugned act was not one of acquisition of property for the purpose of the Union but was one of acquisition for the Union. The impugned acts did not amount to acquisition of property within the meaning of article 31(4) and were protected from attack by article 31. The impugned Acts were not protected from attack on the ground of legislative incompetence. The impugned laws were not protected by articles 31(2), 31A(1) or 31(2).

49: The appellant firm was a manufacturer of cloth. It entered into contracts with the respondent firm for supply of cloth and supplied to it, but before the contract could be completed, the respondent firm filed a suit for damages for breach of the contract on the ground that the appellant had committed an act which was beyond its control and therefore the appellant 's claim must fail. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to recover damages from the respondent firm because the contract did not create any obligation or liability between the parties; that the appellant could not recover damages under section 56 of the . In appeal by special leave the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit. Held, that the appellant firm was not entitled under the doctrine of frustration to recover damages for breach in the absence of an agreement to the contrary. The contract was a contract for the performance of a contract for work and labour and the appellant was liable to pay damages if the work done was not in accordance with the specifications. The appellant was not bound by the contract and the respondent firm was not bound merely by the contract but also by the terms thereof. The appellant could not claim damages for breach arising out of the breach of contract. The appellant firm could not claim any damages against the respondent firm in respect of the breach in the circumstances of this case. The appellant had not been able to prove that there was any legal obligation upon the respondent firm to deliver the goods contracted for to the appellant. The appellant 's plea that the performance of the contract had been frustrated by circumstances beyond their control was not established.

2736: The appellants were the adopted son of one Kothandaraman, who died in 1943. According to the plaintiffs, after his adoption, Tahsil Naidu was entitled to a half share in the joint family property as successor in interest of one Kothenarmannammal and her husband. The main question that arose for decision was whether the adoption of the appellants was valid. Held, that the adoption of a person by another person is not valid unless it is proved that he had at the time of the adoption given his consent that the person adopting had been properly informed of him. The fact that the consent was obtained on the ground that the person was not competent to give the consent does not make the adoption illegal or void. The fact of giving the consent would be irrelevant if there was no authority from the person who gave the consent. The fact which makes a consent illegal does not make it illegal simply because the consent has been given by some other person. The fact must be established by evidence that the consent had been given under the influence of the person who had given the consent.
1201: The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of possession of the village on the basis of a lease granted by the Nizam to his ancestor. The appellants contended that the village had been granted as bilmakta with a fixed sum which was payable in perpetuity for any land granted by the Ruler or the jagirdar to any person and therefore the respondent was entitled to remain in possession of the said village even after the death of the grantor. Held, that the case of the respondent was that the village was granted as bhoga and not as bilamakat but as bazar and not as a bilamkunnarum tree. The case of the appellant was that the grant was not permanent and could only enure for the lifetime of the grantee and therefore the respondents were not entitled to remain on the village. The grant was not a permanent one and the grant did not create any interest in the property. The grant in the present case was not a bilmakhtha or bazar but a bazar. The grant did not confer on the grantee any title to the land nor did it create any interest therein. The grant merely conferred the right of a permanent nature of cultivation over the land and did not create an interest in the land itself. The grant could be terminated by notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the respondents were entitled to recover possession of the land from the appellants.

5965: The respondent assessee had purchased in the relevant previous year 2500 shares of Bharat Starch & Chemicals Ltd. and sold them on 31st March, 1959. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the possibility of a prosecution being launched was not an irrelevant consideration; (ii) the possibility was not a bar to the order of preventive detention; (iii) the possibility that the prosecution would be launched was an irrelevant consideration because the prosecution was in all probability dropped as the appellant might have been able to establish that his possession of the goods was not unlawful; and (iv) the order of detention was bad for non compliance with the requirement of the law. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 3 of the is not unconstitutional and invalid for the reason that it does not provide for any procedure at all in regard to the consideration of the existence of circumstances which may reasonably lead to the conclusion that the detaining authority has no such power. [476F] 1.2 The satisfaction of the detaining authority must reflect on the basis of cogent materials and must be based on some objective criteria. If there are no grounds for the subjective satisfaction of the Detaining Authority then it is not possible to say that the detenue has been prejudiced in his defence at the trial. [477G H] 2. The fact that the detenu 's property were seized by the police could not be a ground for the Detaining authority to come to the conclusion about his complicity or involvement in criminal offences. [478A B] 3. The order of detention cannot be sustained. [479C] 4. The order is illegal and invalid. [480B]
4920: The appellant was a tenant of the land in question. He filed an application under section 20 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 for ejectment of the respondent from the said land on the ground that he required it for personal cultivation. The Assistant Collector dismissed the application holding that sec. 7(1) of the Act did not provide for termination of tenancy and that the tenancy could be terminated only by taking possession of the land reserved by the landowner for his personal cultivation. On appeal, the Commissioner held that sec. 8(2) of theAct provided for two grounds for termination of tenancies : (i) that the land comprising the tenancy has been reserved by the land owner for his personal cultiva tion; and (ii) that the landowner owned the standard acres of less land and the land falls within his permissible limit. In revision, the Financial Commissioner upheld the order of the Commissioner. In the appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The words 'subject to the provisions of sec. 7 ' are being read by us as 'notwithstanding the provisions of section 7 but that may not be a correct way of looking at what is meant by the word 'reserved '. [864 C] (ii) The proper way of looking into the scheme of secs. 7, 7A and 8 is to hold that while sec. 7 enumerates the grounds on which the termination of tenancy is sought, sec. 8 provides for additional grounds on which tenancies subsituted after the commencement of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Second Amendment) Act, 1956 may be terminated. [865 D E] (iii) The propert y of looking at sec. 8 is to take care of the situation arising out of the provisions of the Act relating to the termination of tenan cy rights. [866 F G]
6588: The respondents were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Sonepat for the murder of one Partap Singh and causing injuries to others. The trial court convicted them under section 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. and sections 323,325 read with section 34 I.P,.C. and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life and ordered to pay a sum of Rs.500 each under section 148, I.P .C. They were also convicted under section 325 and sentenced to R.I. for six months under section 323, I. P. C. and one year under section 325, I.p.S. respectively. The High Court by its judgment dated 30.11.1982 acquitted the respondents of the major charge under section 302, I.PC. on the ground that there was no prior enmity between the parties. The State preferred an appeal against the acquittal of the respondents. The High COurt by its judgment in appeal set aside the acquittal order of the respondents and recorded their conviction under section 304 Part I, I. p.C. on the basis that in view of the statement made by 665 Paras Ram at the time when the investigating officer made the inquest report a somewhat different version was given. The High court further held that the sentence already undergone by the accused should be reduced from R.I., for one year to R.T.A. for three years. The State appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts ' approach is not correct. It is clear from the evidence that the deceased and the eye witnesses were close relatives. There was no previous enmity between the two sides. The altercation arose out of a very insignificant matter. The prosecution has failed to prove the motive for the crime. [676F G] 2. The High courts ' approach is wrong because it would have been better if the deceased had stated before the police that he had seen the assailants giving blows to the deceased. The evidence of the doctor who conducted the postmortem examination could not have been taken into consideration as the doctor did not give any opinion regarding the cause of death. The doctor was not examined. The High Com mission had merely recorded his own findings. He had not even mentioned
4620: The petitioner, a member of the Indian Revenue Service, was convicted for an offence under section 304B I.P.C. and sentenced to three years ' rigorous imprisonment by the Sessions Court. He filed an appeal in this Court against his conviction and sentence. His wife, Smt. Amarjit Kaur, had applied to this Court for relief in the matter of the death of her daughter. She also made a similar application to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that no case for grant of special leave had been made out. In the Special Leave Petition it was contended that the High Court should not have entertained the petition as there was no allegation of any dowry demand or harassment having been meted out to her. Dismissing the Special Leave petition, ^ HELD: (1) It is not possible to accept the contention of the petitioner that he has been falsely implicated in the case because he did not make any complaint to anyone. [117 A] (2) There is nothing in the evidence on record which would justify the finding that the petitioner was guilty of the offences charged. [117 B C] (3) The petitioner was a member of an organisation called the "Rajya Sabha". The marriage between the petitioner and the deceased daughter took place about 30 years ago. The police officers who were present at the time of marriage with the deceased daughter, however, could not investigate the case. They had also to look after the day to day work of the Police Station. The Sub Inspector of Police visited the hospital and was told by the doctor that the deceased daughter had been subjected to torture and she died within 24 hours of the examination. The Sub inspector was not examined before the trial court. The SubInspector was not examined. [117 D E]
3175: The Jammu and Kashmir Universities Act, 1969 was enacted to provide for the establishment of a University for the development of the education in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. Section 2(b) defines "University" as including a college or an institution deemed to be a university under section 3. Section 13 provides that every person employed by any such college shall on the date he becomes a teacher, be entitled to have his pay fixed at the maximum of the scale applicable to the post against which he is appointed, less any allowances granted to him during the period of his service. Section 14 provides that all employees of the University of Jammu and the University of Kashmir shall become the employees of the respective Universities on and from the commencement of this Act. Section 15 empowers the Vice Chancellor to make appointments to temporary posts created or approved by the University Council. Section 16 empowers the Vice chancellor to make appointments of teachers in the University of which he is the Chairman. Section 17 confers power upon the Vice Chancellor for making appointments to temporary vacancies or other posts until provision has been made for their appointment by the competent authority. Section 18 provides that no person shall be appointed by the University unless he has been confirmed as a full member of the teaching staff of the University. Section 19 provides that the Vice Chancellor may, with the approval of the Syndicate, appoint a Professor or Assistant Professor or any other person as a teacher of the University for a period not exceeding six months. Section 20 provides that the Proctor shall be responsible for the discipline of the University and its properties and shall be responsible to the Vice Chancellor, for the maintenance of discipline among the students and for ensuring that the provisions of the Ordinance and the Regulations are duly observed. Section 21 provides that the powers of the Vice Chancellor shall be exercisable by an officer not below the rank of a Joint Secretary to the Government. Section 22 provides that the provisions contained in the Statutes, Ordinances and Regulations shall be deemed to be, and always to have been, for all purposes of the University, and they shall continue to apply to the teaching and other work done by the students of the University subject to the provisions of those Statutes. Section 23 provides that the statutes, ordinances and regulations shall be submitted to the Chancellor who shall either modify them as may be necessary or refer it to the Senate for consideration
6448: The petitioner in the two petitions filed under Article 32 of the Constitution are the purchasers of certain immovable property sold by the Income Tax Officer, Delhi Circle, under the Income Tax Act, 1961. They purchased the property on 12.4.1988 and applied for a certificate of sale on 14.4.88. On 14.4 1988, a certificate of purchase was issued by the T.R.O. to the petitioners. The petitioners purchased the property in question on 12.5.88 after the date of the auction sale. The petitioners sought refund of stamp duty paid on the certificate of sale. The original of this certificate of sale was liable for stamp duty and a further duty of Rs. 4.50 was also chargeable on the copy of the sale certificate to be forwarded to the Sub Registrar within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the whole or any part of the immovable property comprised in the certificate is situate. The petitioners contended that the certificate should have been endorsed to the Sub Registrars but it was actually sent to them on 12. 5.88. The High Court dismissed the writ petition at the stage of admission. Dismissing the special leave petition, HELD: 1.1 The expression revenue officer ' in section 84 (4) of the means the Collector of Stamps and the Sub Registrar who has registered the certificate of transfer. [189E] 1.2 In the instant case, the Sub Registrar and the Collector did not accede to this request apparently on the ground that this could not be done unless the certificate of purchase is endorsed to the subregistrar. The certificate of sale sent to the petitioners by the T R O was sent to them by the T Reo Department on 12.12.87. The T R O had no authority to do so as the registration officer was not competent to register the certificate of the transfer. [190F G] 1.3 The certificate of purchase sent by the T r O to the petitioners was sent to the Sub Regis trar of Registration for registration on 12.10.89. The Sub Regis tered Officer had no authority whatsoever to send the certificate of regis tration to the Sub Registry on 12.11.89. [191H; 192A B] 2.1 The petitioners purchased property
1915: The respondents, who were the sons of Lingayya, claimed maintenance from the appellants under Hindu law. The trial court decreed the respondents ' claim for maintenance and consequential reliefs. On appeal, the High Court gave them leave to amend the plaint by making suitable averments for the award of maintenance. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the respondents were not entitled to any maintenance during their lifetime under the Hindu law as it stood prior to the commencement of the Act, because (a) the first respondent was not a Dasi and the second, third and fourth respondents were not Dasiputras of Lingayat; (b) the husband of the first appellant was not a person competent to contract maintenance; (c) the husband was not a trustee for the wife; (d) the husband had no right to maintenance; (e) the first appellant being a Brahmin adulteress, he was not competent to contract the maintenance; and (f) the respondents were entitled to maintenance out of the estate of Lingaya. HELD: (1) The provisions of the Hindu law are applicable only to the estates of Hindus dying after the commencement of Act, and not to the estates which have been acquired before the Act came into force. [864 C] (2)The definition of "Sudra" in section 2(g) of the Act is wide enough to include a Sudra. The expression "Divorce" has been defined in section 2 (h) of the , to mean any sum declared by the Muslim Law to be Hiba or other binding grant or marriage. The definition is wide enough so as to cover a Sudra also. [865 D E]
6061: The petitioners are Ex servicemen and Ex civilian. They were serving in the Assam Rifles as Subedars, Dandas or any other armed forces of the Union. They had been allotted land, grant of title deeds and facilities for movement by air to and from Mohanbari, freedom fighter, freedom to develop the allotted areas, grant of advance by way of loans, provision of marketing facil ities for disposal of surplus produce, guaranteed supply of essential commodities and provision of the basic required of life for the purpose of encouraging the all round economic development of the area. The petitioners contended that the scheme was not a package deal but a package scheme intended to benefit all those who were similarly situated as the petitioners and they could not be discriminated against. Disposing of the writ petition, this Court HELD: 1.1 The scheme is not a package scheme meant to benefit all persons who may be similarly situated. It is a package deal with the benefits available to the persons belonging to the same class. [578C] 1.2 The scheme has been made applicable to all persons belonging to different categories depending on their ranks in the Scheme. The petitioners have been allotted land and grant of title deed and facilities for transportation of surplus produce. The scheme is meant to help the persons belonging the same class of persons. [577D E] 1.3 The scheme is aimed at providing a package deal to all persons who are similarly situated. The scheme cannot be said to be a package deal. The scheme has not been designed to benefit all the persons who might be similarly situated.[577F G] 1.4 The scheme is intended to benefit only those persons who are identically situated. The petitioners are not entitled to the relief claimed. [576G] 2.1 The petitioners are entitled to the benefits of the scheme. [579A] 2.2 The Central Government has already constituted a committee to examine the problem and make its report. The report of the Committee shall be placed before the Parliament. [570B] 2.3 The Central Government will consider the report of the committee and take appropriate action within four months. [575H; 576A]
795: The appellant was the manager of a temple in Tirunelveli District. He made an application to the District Court under section 3 of the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, against the respondents for declaring that the temple was not a public one and declaring that the respondents were entitled to maintain it. The District Judge held that the temple had been established by the appellant for religious and charitable purposes and that there was no need for the respondents to join the deity because of an averment by the respondents that the temple itself was not a private one. On appeal by special leave: Held, (i) that the suit was barred by limitation as the respondents had not filed any application for a declaration that the temple as a public one. (ii)The suit was barred on the ground that the deity was not a family or private one. (iii)It could not be said that the deity had no right whatever in the properties of the temple. (iv)The suit must be dismissed as barred by limitation.
2383: The appellants were dealers in coal and were liable to sales tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 15 of 1948. They had sent their goods to their depots outside the Province of Uttar Pradesh for example, to Calcutta in the State of West Bengal before any contract of sale in respect of the goods was made. The Sales Tax Officer assessed them to sales tax on the basis that they were not liable to pay sales tax as they did not actually exist in their stock in trade at the time when the contracts for sale were made. The appellants filed revisions before the revising authority under section 10 of the Act. The revision petitions having been dismissed they moved the High Court by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the out of State sales would be taxable (1) if the goods were in existence in the Province of U.P., at the time of the contract of sale, and (2) if the property in the goods passed in pursuance of the contract for sale after the goods had left the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the sales being in the course of inter State trade or commerce could not be taxed unless the goods were manufactured or produced within the Province of that State. HELD : (i) Under section 99 of the Government of India Act, 1935, the Provincial Legislature was authorised to make laws for the Province subject to such exceptions and modifications as the legislature of the Province might by law prescribe. Section 11 of the Act provided for the making of rules for the guidance of officers and authorities applying to the Province. Rule 2 of the Rules framed under section 10(3) of the Act prescribed that every dealer whose total turnover exceeded one crore rupees shall be liable to pay tax on his taxable turnover. Rule 3 laid down that the selling dealer shall issue a bill or cash memorandum setting forth the fact that he has purchased the goods mentioned therein and that the bill or cash memo should contain a statement of all the goods sold. Rule 4 required the selling dealer to state whether he intended to purchase the goods from the selling dealer. Rule 5 required the selling agent to submit to the assessing authority a return of the goods purchased and to produce evidence in support thereof. Rule 6 required the selling agents to furnish returns of the goods so purchased
183: The appellant was arrested in pursuance of an extradition warrant issued by the Regional Com missioner of the United State of Rajasthan who, on his arrest, made a demand for the sum of Rs. 3 lakhs which he had paid to the appellant from the Nawab 's service in the United States of Rajasthan. The appellant filed an application under sections 491 and 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for release of the appellant on the ground that the sum of money was paid to him by the Nawab of India after the 15th August, 1947, when the Tonk State ceased to exist. The High Court dismissed the application but granted a certificate under article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution. Held: (i) The Extradition Treaty between the Republic of India and the Tonks Agreement executed on the 8th August, 1869, did not continue in force in the United State and the appellant could be proceeded against for any offence committed prior thereto. (ii)The treaty entered into between the British Government and the Tonga l Encyclopedia Britannica, referred to in section 7 of the Extradition Act, was continued in force by the "Stand still Agreement" entered into on the 8 th August, 1947. (iii)It is only when the treaty subsists that it can be extended to the territories of the United States.
2299: The respondents, who were the owners of certain land in a village in the State of Himachal Pradesh, applied for permission to sell the trees standing on their land. The Compensation Officer held that as the applicant was a cultivating tenant over the land he was entitled to acquire right, title and interest of the said land owner on payment of Rs. 62.56 as compensation which should be deposited. He allowed the application and granted proprietary rights in the land to the deceased Moti Ram. The appellant 's appeal before the Commissioner and the Judicial Commissioner affirmed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The word "land" has been used in section 2(5) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887, in a generic sense and includes all lands which are irrigated or capable of being irrigated from similar features. The word "lands" is not defined in the Act. The definition of "land" given by the Act is wide enough to include not only land but also trees on such land. [117 A C] (ii)The word "land", as used in section 11 of the Act, means land which is not occupied as the site of any building in a town or village and is occupied or has been let for agricultural purposes or for purposes subservient to agriculture. The word 'land ' is defined in section 2 (3) of the Act to mean "any land which is used or capable ofbeing used for agricultural purposes. and 'is defined to mean "a land which is irrigated or capable at tion of being irrigated by human efforts or the use of water which is likely to be so overcome that can be called "land". [117 D E; 118 B]
253: The respondents claimed exemption from assessment in respect of sales effected by them on the ground that such sales took place "in the course of the export of the goods out of the territory of India" within the meaning of article 1115 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The Sales Tax Authorities rejected their claim and assessed them under section 3 of the Travancore Cochin General Sales Tax Act, 1125 (Act IV of 1125). On appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, the High Court held that the sales were completed before the goods were shipped and could not therefore be considered to have taken place in the course of export and that the sales tax was payable accordingly. Held, that the sales made by the respondents were completed before they were exported and could not be considered to take place in the ' course of export because the export was complete when the goods arrived at the port of destination. The sales tax was also payable on the turnover of sales effected after the goods had crossed the customs barrier or had moved out of the country. The sales of the respondents did not amount to a sale within the meaning Of article 1116 (1) of the constitution and the sales were not completed before the property in the goods passed in the State of Travancore Cochin. The sales Tax authorities were therefore justified in imposing the sales tax upon the respondents. Held further, that the High Court was right in holding that the sales in question were completed before goods were shieeded and could not, therefore, be considered to be in the course ' of export. Held also, that the Sales Tax Authorities were justified in refusing to assess the respondents on the ground of the existence of export trade. Held also that the sales of the respondent were completed before their goods were shiug ed and could not he treated as having taken place in 'the course of export. The sales were completed in the course and the export was completed before the shipment. The sales did not occasion the export. The goods were delivered for consumption in the State where they were delivered in the course, of import. The sales merely occasioned the export. They were not sales in the course. of export.
2436: The appellant was the principal debtor of a bank. He executed a bond in favour of the respondent for Rs. 11,723.56 nP. On June 15, 1951, the respondent borrowed from the appellant a sum of Rs. 11.723.37 nP. and interest thereon. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent on July 1, 1951, claiming a decree for the amount due. The trial court decreed the suit against both the respondents but the High Court, in appeal, set aside the decree holding that the respondent had not discharged the liability of the principal debtor in spite of demand. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The surety became liable to pay the entire amount. The surety became entitled to enforce his dues in the manner provided by section IO of the Contract Act. [625 D] (ii) The surety has no right to restrain execution of the decree against him until he has exhausted his remedies against the principal. The surety is bound to discover at his peril all the properties of the principal and sell them. If he cannot, then proceed against the principal, he lost his remedy against the principal and he may then recover the amount from the principal. [626 F G] (iii) The surety was not entitled to any more than to the benefit of sec. 140 of the Indian Contract Act. He could only be proceeded against under sec. IO of that Act. [605 C]
2678: The appellant was the Chief Municipal Officer of the Municipal Council, Raipur. He filed a complaint before the Magistrate and the Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Raipur, who issued summons to the accused, namely, the Municipal Council and the Chief Municipal Office. The accused appeared by counsel and filed preliminary objections. The Magistrate passed an order dismissing the complaint under section 203 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The accused moved the High Court under section 439 Cr. P.C., for quashing the order of dismissal but the High Court dismissed the application holding that no revision lay under section 439, Cr. P,.C. against the order of the Magistrate. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The word "includes" in section 2(g), means "shall be deemed to include also a person 's motor transport undertaking". [917 B] (ii)The words "private carrier" have been given a specific meaning in the , and it is difficult to limit this specific meaning on any reasonable basis. It is difficult to differentiate between private carriage vehicles and private carriage vehicles. [918 D E] (iii)Section 2(g) of the excludes from its purview a motor transport undertaking. [919 C]
4311: The Central Secretariat Service (Amendment) Rules, 1979 were framed by the Union Government in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 read with section 24 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985. Rule 12 of the said rules provides that the vacancies reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes shall be filled up by promotion from amongst candidates belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, respectively. The petitioners who belong to the Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe categories applied for selection to Grade I posts under the Central Secretariat Service Rules. They were included in the field of selection for the purpose of drawing up the select list for 1977 for promotion to Grade I post. After an interview by the Selection Committee, ninety one unreserved vacancies were filled from the first 90th one unreserved vacancy was filled from the second 90th one candidate from the Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes, remaining unfilled because no candidate belonging to those categories was found suitable for including in the field. Accordingly, the President promulgated the Central Secretariat Services (Amendment)Rules, 1979 whereby sub rule (2a) was inserted below sub rule (1). The petitioners challenged the validity of the amendment on the ground that it violated their fundamental right under article 16(1) of the Constitution as they had not been considered in the light of the Office Memorandum dated 20th July 1974 issued by the Department of Personnel & Administrative Reforms. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Office Memorandum dated October 20, 1979 is not ultra vires the Constitution. It merely clarifies the position that the operation of the office memorandum dated April 20, 1979 does not preclude the Government from making a provision for reservation of vacancies in favour of members of the Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes in the event of non availability of suitable candidates belonging to these communities. [1189G H] 2. The Office Memoranda do not have the force of law. They are mere executive instructions. They do not create any rights in the officers and the rights cannot be enforced against the officers in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. [1190A B] 3. The Office memoranda do neither create nor extinguish any rights. They merely clarify the position that there would be no bar to the consideration of the claims of Scheduled Castes and scheduled tribes for promotion if they fall within
3195: The appellants were manufacturers of matches manufactured by them. They had been subjected to excise duty at the same onerus rate as has been applied to larger producers, wilfully indifferent to awhile, to a historically well recognised classification between the smaller and the larger group of match manufacturers. The impugned notification provided that the excise duty payable on matches in any class of factories shall be at the rate of 20 nP. per gross of matches each upto 100 million matches, and that the non mechanised sector comprising different small matches, depending upon their capacity, in addition to large matches, shall be allowed to be cleared at the rate Of Rs. 3.75 per gross of boxes 5O matches each, upto 75 million matches. The appellants challenged before the High Court the validity of the impugned notification on the ground that it discriminated against them vis a vis the other manufacturers who were similarly situated and discriminated against. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned notification was not discriminatory but only a device to avoid discrimination. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court, ^ HELD: (1) The impugned notification is not discriminatory nor does it offend article 14 of the Constitution. [419F] (2) The impugned Notification is intended to prevent evasion of excise duty. It is designed to prevent evasion or avoidance of payment of excise duty without attracting the provisions of section 3 of the Act. The object of the impugned Notification is to prevent evasion and prevent evasion of Excise Duty. [420G] (3) The impugned exemption notification is not an invitation to the public to accept an offer to do so. It is intended to further the policy of the State towards securing the principles of excise duty or additional revenue which one of its major objects is to promote the development of industries for the promotion of alleviation of the goods produced. [421A B] (4) The impugned provision is not discriminatory but is intended to encourage the small matches who have developed manufacturing and marketing muscles to compete with the power using big matches. [422B C] (5) The impugned levy is not discriminatory. [423D E]
725: The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for declaration that she was the owner of certain lands in the estate of her deceased husband and for possession thereof. The defence taken was that the respondent had come into possession of the properties left by her brother in presence of the reversionary heirs, as the heir of her father and brother according to the Zamindara Custom prevalent in the District of Amritsar, and that the respondent 's mother was not competent to make any such claim. The trial court held that the respondent was entitled to succeed to the lands but the High Court on appeal reversed this decision and decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the respondent had failed to establish the custom pleaded by him; (ii) the respondent having been excluded from claiming title under the general custom of the Punjab, his case must be considered as confined to the respondent; (iii) the respondent was not entitled to the properties under the general customs of the Punjab in preference to the respondent because he was the sister of the last male holder of the estate; and (iv) the respondent could not have claimed the properties under section 4(1)(a) of the Punjab Preferential right of pre emption which was not available to the collaterals. HELD: (i) The respondent had failed both to prove the special custom of the tribe or family entitling her to succeed to ancestral property. [1099 A] (ii)The respondent had failed also to establish the existence of a custom of the family of her late husband. [1095 D] (iii)It is well established that the custom of the community of the sanctity of the Got (Santhal Pargana of Kheri) prevails among the members of the tribe in the matter of succession to property. [1107 B]
5671: The respondent No. 3 was charged with having committed an offence punishable under section 111 read with section 135 of the Customs Act, 1969. He was convicted and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 1 lakh. The respondent No 2 was acquitted by the trial court but the Sessions Judge confirmed his acquittal. On appeal, the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to establish the ingredients required to be established in respect of the offence under the Gold (Control) Act, 1968. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 403(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 provides that no finding or sentence passed by a Magistrate shall be called into question on the ground that it is not possible to take the view or that, the decision of the Magistrate thereon can directly affect the decision of any other person given under any law relating to offences being tried summarily. [904E] 1.2 In the instant case, the basic ingredient required to constitute the offence of theft under the Customs Act is the theft of goods. The essential ingredient therefore is dishonest misappropriation of the goods. The respondents were charged with having commited the offence of criminal breach of trust under the Gold Control Act. The same facts are required to be proved in respect of an offence under the Customs act. [905F G] 2. Section 403 of the Cr P.C. is applicable only when there is a reasonable possibility of repetition of the acts which will give rise to one of them as an alternative to the commission thereof. The prosecution has not been able to prove that the respondents had dishonestly disposed of the gold in favour of any third party. [906A B]
2637: The respondent filed a complaint under section 20 of the , against the appellant Corporation alleging that the appellant had committed offences under sections 4(1)(a) and 537 of the Indian Penal Code. The Magistrate dismissed the complaint on the ground that it was not made by a competent person. The High Court upheld the order of the Magistrate. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 537 of , which provides for the taking of cognizance of criminal cases is in pari materia with section 2(vii) of the Criminal Procedure Code. Under section 537 the Commissioner may institute legal proceedings as regards any matter which may be referred to him or which he has reason to believe to be applicable to the case before the Court and may either himself take the action, if necessary, or refer the matter to the Municipal Commissioner for investigation and report. [902 F G] (ii)Section 537 of Cr. P.C., 1898, makes it obligatory on the Commissioner to authorise the person authorised to exercise the powers of the Corporation in the matter of institution of legal proceedings. It does not make the Commissioner an officer of the Corporation empowered to initiate legal proceedings. The Commissioner can delegate his functions to the Vice Chairman or any municipal officer. [903 A B] (iii)The Commissioner cannot file a complaint under the Act without the sanction of the Corporation. The Corporation is the authority competent to file the complaint. The Corporation has no power to file the same. [904 D E]
3983: The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. They filed a civil suit against the respondents for partition and possession of their lands on the ground that they had become full owner by operation of law. The trial court decreed the suit, but the first appellate court reversed it holding that the decree was not binding on the respondents. The High Court dismissed the second appeal filed by the appellants. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the respondents ' case was covered by section 14(1) of the Act and that the sale by her in favour of the respondent was null and void. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) Section 14(1), which is applicable to the facts of the instant case, does not recognise any "pre existing" right of Bai Vajia in the property in dispute. [864F] (ii) The expression "possessed by" has been used in the context of the Act in order to give full effect to the intention of the legislature. [865G] (iii) The expression 'possession ' has been defined in section 2(4) of the , to mean the possession of the person in possession of either spouse or of any other person with whom he or she had entered into possession or who would have had, in his or her possession, if this Act had not been passed. [866A B] (iv) The expression, "possessed" in section 14(I)(b) means "actually in the possession of any other party" in order to be "acquitted". [867B]
707: The appellant was declared elected to the State Assembly. His election was challenged by the first respondent on the ground that he had been disqualified under section 7(1)(c) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, for being chosen as and for being a member of the Legislative Assembly of the State of Madras. The Election Tribunal held that the nomination paper of the first respondent had been improperly rejected and dismissed the application. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the decision of the Election Tribunal must be set aside and the election petition restored to file in accordance with law. The question whether a candidate is disqualified under section 625 of the Act has to be determined not by degree but by the nature of the right claimed by him or by the relationship of the person who claims to be the holder of the office, but to establish his claim to the office on the basis of the disqualification prescribed by section 101 of the Act. Hari Vishnu Kamath vs Syed Ahmad Ishaque, (1955) I.L.R. 38 All. 534, approved.
1706: The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Bihar. They claimed compensation for the lands under acquisition at a uniform rate for the period from 1 4 67 to 30 2 67. The Land Acquisition Officer made an award on 30 2 67 and fixed the compensation payable for the lands at Rs. 10,000 per acre for survey No. 339/1 to 3 and Rs. 10.000 per acre to the remaining lands. The appellants did not accept the award of the Land Acquisition Officer and made applications in writing to him within the time allowed by law for referring the matter for determination of the court. The appellants contended that the reference was incompetent as no amount of compensation had been awarded by the Land Acquisition officer and no objection raised by the State Government that in the absence of any reference on the question of quantum of compensation by the Land Acquisi tion officer, the Court had no jurisdiction to consider that matter at all. The High Court rejected these contentions and held that it was open to the appellants to raise this contention before the Reference Court but ultimately it decided to go into the merits of the case and remanded the case to the Subordinate Judge for making a fresh reference. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (Per Bhagwati & Vivian Bose JJ.) The High Court was wrong in holding that the appellants had waived their right to challenge the award of compensation by filing applications after the lapse of nearly two years. [675F] The appellants were not entitled to any notice of the award of payment of compensation. [666A] The appellants had not challenged the award of Rs. 10 lakhs per acre for the land acquired. The award of Rs, 10 lakhs per acres was made on 30 2 68. The appellants had accepted the award without protest and had not filed any application for review or modification of the award. The appellants could not be permitted to take advantage of its own mistake. [667B C]
4714: The appellant Corporation was created under the State Act of 1950. Section 2(oo) defines retrenchment to mean termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include (a) voluntary retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf; or (b) termination of the service on the ground of continued ill health. The respondent employees were appointed in the appellant Corporation on probation for two years and such probation can be extended. Thereupon an industrial dispute was raised which was referred to the Labour Court for adjudication under section 10 of the . The Labour Court held that termination of services of the employees while on probation amounted to retrenchment and for non compliance with the provisions of section 25F of the , the termination was bad. The High Court upheld the decision of the Labour Court. In appeal before this Court it was contended that the order terminating the services of the employee was illegal because the termination was in violation of the provisions of Section 25F of The Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of the services of a permanent employee is not retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo). [864E] 2. The definition of retrenchment in section 2(o) is wide enough to cover cases where the employee is retrenched and the termination is found to be invalid. The definition is wide enough so as to include cases where the employer himself terminates the services of his employee without complying with the requirements of section 25 F of the . [865H 866A] 3. The word 'retrenchment ' has been defined in section 2 (oo) to mean the termination by the employers of the service by notice to quit or for one month 's notice period either on the report of the Manager or on failure to comply with the formalities prescribed by section 25F. [867B] 4. The term 'reinstatement ' has been used in the wider sense of providing relief to the employee from the termination of his service. [868C] 5. The word `termination ' has been interpreted by this Court to mean `reinstatement of the employee '

Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. [839E F] 2. In view of the fact that the maximum period of detention mentioned in section 10 will run from the date on which the order of detentiOn is communicated to the detenu till the expiry of the period of detention, the respondent cannot successfully contend that the period of one or two years as mentioned in section '10 will run from 7th May, 1979, and even if the period of two years, as mentioned in Section '10 will running from the date the actual detention is over, the respondent would get the benefit of the invalidity of the order of the High court. [840F G] 3. The order of detention against the respondent was made on 7th May 1979 and this appeal was being heard on 15th September, 1981, which was beyond two years. If the submission of learned counsel be accepted, two unitended results follow; (i) if a person whose case is pending before the Customs Officer, admitting that he is a member of his crew, he gets the benefit of invalidation of the order which he should not. 6019: The appellants instituted a suit in respect of a homestead land which was part of the said coal mine. The company re strained the lessee from taking any further lease of the land and the lessee continued to hold the land till the date of vesting. The company filed a written statement denying the claim of the appellants. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the disputed land formed part of the North Bhuggatdih Colliery, which had vested in the Central Government under section 3 of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973. The High Court affirmed the decree. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the disputed laud was not a mine as defined in the Mines Act, 1952, but was a mine as understood in the dictionary meaning of the word 'sand '; that the intermediary interest in the land were not extinguished with the vesting of the estate in the Central Govern ment, and that the intermediary interests in the land did not vest in the Central Govt. and that the suit lands were not mines comprised in the mines and that the intermediaries were entitled to retain possession of the lands. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The suit property is a mine within the meaning of the Mines Act. The intermediary interest in a mine is not extinguished with vesting of the property in the Central Gov ernment. [903 G] 2.1 The suit land is an area where the mines are situated. It is not a mine within section 2(g) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957. The mines are not mines comprised therein. The intermediary interests in these mines are not extinguished with such vesting. [904 A B] 2.2 The suit land forms part of the coal mine. It is a mine where the mine is situate. The intermediary rights in the mine are not extinguished except with the consent of the Central Government. The lease of the appellants having come to an end consequent upon the issuance of notification under section 3, the plaintiffs have no title to be declared and the decree of the trial court is liable to be set aside. [905 D E]

5898: The respondent, an Executive Engineer in the State of Punjab, was working as a Junior Engineer in the Industrial Supply Section of the Directorate of Industries. On the basis of a complaint lodged by one Shri R.S. Dhingra, the Director of Vigilance, Punjab, a First Information Report was lodged against him under section 5(1)(2) read with section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 120B IPC. The said First Information Report having been quashed by the High Court, the prosecution against the respondent was initiated on the basis of the same. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the aforesaid order of the High Court contending that Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules had been misinterpreted by the High court in holding that the said rule placed an embargo on initiating judicial proceedings for prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years of the cause of action or the event referred to in the said rule and the High Court committed an error of law in taking the view that the said Rule placed an embarket only in respect of cases where the Government Servant is prosecuted after the expiry of the period of four years. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the prosecution against him. The appellant contended before this Court that Rule 2:2 of the Rules has been misinterprised by the High Courts in holding that in the case of a criminal proceeding on the date on which the complaint or report of the police officer on which the Magistrate takes cognizance is made, the time of 4 years has to be counted from the date on and from which cognizance of the offence can be taken by the Magistrate. It was further submitted that the High Court has misconstrued the provisions of Rule 2: 2 of the Punjab Rules and has wrongly held that the said Rules are applicable to the facts of the case. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that the High court was right in holding that Rule 2 of the Rules is not applicable to the case of the respondent because he was not prosecuted within the period of 4 years of his retirement. 3259: The appellants were licensees under section 10 of the Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961. They were found to be selling gur and shakkar in their own shops within the notified market area without submitting accounts and without payment of fees. They were asked to show cause why legal action should not he taken against them for violation of rules 29(3) and 31(1) of the Rules. Since they did not submit accounts and did not pay the fee, they were asked to explain by the Market Committee why legal action shall not be taken against them as well as the levy under the Act. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy on the ground that they were liable to pay market fee on the basis of best judgment assessment. The High Court allowed the petition quashing the order of assessment as arbitrary and violative of the principles of natural justice. It also quashed the demand notice issued by the Administrator of the Market Committee for payment of market fee. The appellants in civil appeal No. 299 of 1972 had also filed a writ application in the High court questioning the levy under Act. The High court allowed the petition and held that the appellants were liable to payment of market fees. The appellants have preferred these appeals by special leave against the decision of the High Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (i) The appellants are licensees under section 1O of the Act. They were charged with the duty of rendering services which they failed to do. They were called upon to show cause against the imposition of the said duty. The appellants submitted their explanation. The Administrator of the Committee after some correspondence levied on one of the appellants, M/s Prem Chand Ram Lal, appellants in Civil Appeal No. 120 of 1972, a fee of Rs. 5014/ as market fee on their basis of best judgments assessment. The appellants were asked to pay the same. The appellants challenged the levy on two grounds, namely, (a) the appellants were not liable to pay the market fee on account of the fact that they did not render any service to the Market Committee and (b) the levy was not justified. [311H; 312A] (ii) The appellants were not guilty of any breach of the rules. They were not charged with any criminal offence

3624: The appellant, a manufacturer of metric tons of manganese dioxide, was served with a notice under section 131(3) of the , for institution of a suit for recovery of refund. On 10th February 1975, the appellant received a consignment of ten metric tons. The Assistant Collector confirmed the assessment order and also directed refund of duty. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality of the demand made by the Assistant Collector. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the power of suo motu revision contained in section 131(5) of the Act is subject to the provisions contained in section 132 (3) and 131 (5) of 'the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: Section 28 of the Act provides that where the Central Government is of opinion that any duty or customs has not been levied or has been shortlevied, it shall give a notice to show cause against it within the time limit specified therein and also directs the refund of such duty or tax collected except in cases covered by clauses (a), (b) and (c) of sub section (1). [987 E] 988 Section 131(5), as it stood at the relevant time, provided that where the duty or customs had not been levied ad valorem on any goods, the authority levying the same may, if he thinks fit, amend, vary, alter or modify the amount of duty chargeable on account of such goods. The proviso to the said clause states that the period of six months mentioned therein should be computed from the date of the levy. [985 F G] In the instant case, the appellant did not claim refund of the excess duty paid by him but only claimed refund of the duty paid by mistake. The appellant could have claimed refund of duty paid by means of an application before the appropriate authority for revision of the order of refund. [986 B C]

5665: The respondent, a contractor, entered into two agreements with the appellants for the execution of certain works. The last one was on 30th May, 1971 and the final bills were submitted in July 1972. On 29th May, 1972, the respondent accepted the four final bills and gave no claim declaration in respect of the four contracts. The appellants filed an application under Sections 8 & 20 of the Act for appointment of an Arbitrator. The respondent refused to refer the dispute to arbitration. The appellants then filed an application before the Civil Judge for appointment of the Arbitrator. The Civil Judge allowed the application and appointed an arbitrator. The appellants challenged the appointment of the arbitrator by filing a petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the Civil Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the application as the respondent had not been able to show that the agreement between the parties was void or voidable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Article 181 of the Limitation Act, 1908 would apply to any petition or application filed under any Act to a Civil Court. [860G] 2.1 The expression "any petition" in Article 181 means a plaint or a written statement, etc. The word "appeal" is used in the widest connotation. It does not mean an appeal. [861A B] 2.2 The expression "appeals" has been used in the wider sense of appellate proceedings and not in the narrower sense of all further proceedings including those taken in civil courts. [862C] 3. The expression "arbitral award" is defined in section 2(c) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 to mean any decision which the court may choose to give. [863D E] 4. The expression 'arbitrator ' in the Act includes an arbitrator. [864F G] 5. The expression is not restricted to judicial orders made in exercise of criminal jurisdiction. It includes all matters which are expressly directed to be superior. [865E F] 6. The expression means only when there is a right to something in addition; it means right to take steps in a suit and make necessary directions for its implementation. [866B]

In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that without the particulars of supply and service of the specified list of documents, the ground could not be said to have been vague and the High Court erred in holding that the detenu had not been informed about his right to make an effective representation against the order of his detention. [960 G] (a) The expression "actually" in the context of the Act means "actually done". [961 F H] (b) The fact that the detenu has not been informed that he has a right to make a representation against the detention order cannot be regarded as furnishing a ground for preventive detention. 3768: The appellant, a Hindu female, was married to the respondent in 1949. She died in 1960. In April, 1961, she filed a suit for maintenance and obtained a decree on June 30, 1962. 992: The appellant was a shopkeeper and was carrying on his business in the shop. On appeal the High Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to one month 's pay. [141 E G] 6. The word _special reasons means those exceptional reasons which make the decision of the court justified under the law. The words "special reasons " are of widest amplitude so as to cover exceptional cases even though they may be justifiable grounds. [141 F] 7. The word .special reasons ' in section 354 Cr.
