1543: The assessees were the shareholders of a private limited company. They held shares in a private company and were assessed to income tax under section 16(2) (i)(c) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessees contended that the dividend received by them was not dividend within the meaning of section 2(1) (d) of the Act as it was paid out of capital and such payment was not taxable. Held:(i) The dividend could be taxed only when it is paid to a shareholder and it was not necessary for the assessee to prove that it was paid to a person other than the shareholder himself. The words "paid" and "deposited" in section 2(i)(c), and the words "paid", "depositor" and "account holder" are used interchangeably. The word "deposits" in section 16(3) (ii) means "depositing or paying". The word "pay" in section 17(2) means "to receive on behalf of the company, to make payment on its own account, to pay money to another." The word "payment" in section 18(3) means "the payment made to a person receiving the money, or to someone who has put the same; to receive payment on behalf of or against the principal, and does not include any payment made to the payee by way of a loan or an agreement with regard to the payment of money. The word 'pay ' in section 18 (3) means the payment made to another person in consideration of some act or thing specially authorised by the company or other body corporate, and the word 'payee ' in section 17 (2) means the person to whom the money is paid or transferred.
4401: The appellant was the tenant of a shop in a building in which the respondent was residing. He filed a petition under the Rent Act against the respondent for eviction on the ground that he required the premises bona fide for his personal occupation. The Rent Controller dismissed the petition holding that the landlord had not made out any case for eviction and directed the eviction of the appellant. The respondent filed an appeal before the District Judge who dismissed the same. The High Court also held that the appellant had given an untrue version of the incident since the Judge had not given any direction for furnishing the complete address of the respondent before him. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant did not dispute in the High Court that he hurled a shoe at the Judge which hit him on the shoulder. The Judge, however, took the view that the appellant 's version was like this and that the appellant gave an untrue statement of the truth. [813F] 2. In the circumstances of the case, it is difficult to hold that the appellant was making false allegations against the Judge. The appellant was not only unwilling but was trying to secure a decree against the respondent. It would be travesty of justice if the Judge proceeds with the matter without giving a proper opportunity to the appellant to defend himself or to explain the conduct of the respondent. [814A B]

1251: The appellants were in unauthorised possession of a house. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality of the order of the Deputy Custodian on the ground that the Deputy Custodian gave no notice or opportunity to them to meet the case and that the Custodian had no jurisdiction in the matter in view of the provisions of the . The High Court held that the Deputy Commissioner had no power to give notice to the appellants under section 18(1) of the Act, and that the Deputy Collector had no jurisdiction to evict the appellants. Held, that the Deputy commissioner had no jurisdiction under section 18 (1) of Act 18 of 1949 to evict the appellant without giving him an opportunity to explain his case and that he was entitled to be heard in defence. 2172: The appellants filed a suit for preemption in respect of certain agricultural land. The respondents claimed that they were the collaterals and co sharers of the land in question, but the appellants had no share in the land. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal by the appellants, the High Court held that the appellants were not entitled to preempt the land which was allotted to them in lieu of their land which was the subject matter of sale. They had no right to pre empt the land which would be subject to preemption in the same way as the original holding or tenancy. [868 C D]

6927: The respondent assessee, a non resident company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 67 under section 12(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act 1922. The assessee filed returns on the basis of which it claimed privilege in respect of certain documents. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of privilege by his order dated March 31, 1963. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the said order. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the documents were not relevant for the purpose of determining the question whether the privilege claimed by the assessee was available to the assessee or not. The High Court also held that the assessee had no locus standi as the documents were filed after April 1, 1962 but before April 1, 1964 in respect of assessment years 1962 63 and 1963 64. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Revenue it was contended: (1) That the High Court erred in holding that the documents in question were not relevant because they were filed after the coming into force of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922; (2) That the Tribunal erred in holding the documents were inadmissible in evidence; (3) That the assessee had failed to establish that the documents contained any intellectual property value. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) Section 138(b) of the Income Tax Act provides that where an application is made to the Commissioner in the prescribed form for any information relating to any assessee in respect of any assessment made under the Act or the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on or after the 1st day of April, 1960, the Commissioner shall furnish or cause to be furnished to such assessee or other person as may be specified by him, all such information within a period of three months from the end of the month in which the information is so furnished. [558F G] (b) Sub section (1) of section 138 provides that where a person makes an application to the Commissioner, in the prescribed Form for any information, relating to any asses sees, the Commissioner may require the production of the document concerned. 3545: The appellants were office bearers of the Civil Employees Unions in the various Centers of Defence Establishments. They filed a writ petition in the High Court to impugn the authority of the Commandants (Respondents and 3 herein) in declaring the Union represented by the appellants as unlawful association. The main ground taken was that the impugned action was violative of their fundamental right to form associations or unions conferred by article 19(1)(c) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the right of the appellants to form associations under article 19(i)(c) had been lawfully taken away. It also held that the impugned notifications were ultra vires the and were struck by articles 19(1) (c) and 33 of the Constitution, and that the impugned notification was invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned Act was not protected by article 19 (2) of the constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Article 19(1), (c) & 33 of the constitution are subject to Part III of the Constitution which provides for protection of rights of persons employed in any establishment. [773F] 2. The impugned Act is not protected by Article 19(2). The impugned Act does not infringe any of the Fundamental Rights of the appellants. [774H; 775A] 3. The impugned notification imposing restrictions on the members of the Armed Forces covered by section 2(b) of the Act is not ultra vires the powers of the Central Government. [775B] 4. The impugned Notification imposes restrictions on the fundamental rights of the appellants under article 19 (1) ( c ) of the Constitution and is struck by article 33 of the Con stitution. [776C] 5. The impugned Notifications are not ultra vires article 19(2) of Constitution. [777D E] 6. The impugned notifications are valid. [778E]
3435: The appellant was a Hindu undivided family of which the respondent was the Karta. In the assessment year 1954 55, the Income Tax officer included certain items of jewellery and ornaments in the total income of the appellant as being his personal effects under section 2(4A) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the expression "personal effects" meant such items of movable property as were necessary adjuncts to an individual 's own personality and the nature of sale being voluntary or otherwise was irrelevant for the purpose of section 12B of the Act, but since the articles were used for the purpose for which they were intended, they could not be considered to be household utensils within the meaning of section 2(1)(vi) of the Act. The High Court agreed with the view taken by the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: (i) The expression "personnel" is not defined in the Act. It has been used in the widest connotation and it includes all kinds of movable property including jewellery, clothes and utensils. [277 E] (ii) The gold caskets were not household utensils as they were used for special occasions but were only household articles which were normally, ordinarily and commonly so used. The use of the word "personal" in the context of the Act cannot be equated with the term "property". [278 F G] James Anderson vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay City II, , James Andonnn vs Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Bombay, I.L.R. [1965] Bom. 1062, James Andontworld vs Commissioner of Incometax, Madras, I.T.R. , James & Orthopaedic Surgeon vs Commissioner of lncome tax, Bombay City I.L., referred to.
6813: The petitioner 's wife died on 13.8.1986, prior to the amendment of Section 304 B in the Indian Penal Code by Act 43 of 1986 w.e.f. 19.11.1986. The petitioner filed a criminal complaint against Respondent Nos 2 to 5 who are the husband, his parents and sister which was trans ferred to the Court of Judicial Magistrate First Class at Dhari and registered as Criminal Case No. 382 of 1988 for an offence under section 498 A read with section 34 I.P.C. The petitioner ' s wife got some vague information about their daughter Chhaya and went to Bagasara, the same day but were unable to meet or see their daughter who had died. The petitioner alleged that their daughter 's death was unnatural resulting from torture by her husband and his relatives. The petitioner also alleged that his relatives were demanding dowry from her and her parents. The petitioner contended that the death of his daughter was unnatural because she was subjected to harassment by her husband, his relatives and his relatives for dowry. The High Court dismissed the application holding that section 304 B did not apply, will not preclude the peti tioner from contending that any other more stringent provision is attracted on the accusa tions made. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the amendment being prospec tive was inapplicable to a death which occurred on 13.08.1986 prior to the date of the amendment. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The amendment does not take away the right of the accused to claim compensation under section 357 Cr. P.C. It only provides for payment of compensation to the victim of the accident or family of the deceased. [943F] 1.2 The amendment does no more than introduce a new right to compensation in respect of the death of the victim. The right to compensation is implicit in the right to consid er the claim for compensation under section 300 Cr. P C. The right of the victim to claim compensation is a statutory right and the Court cannot direct payment of compensation without giving an opportunity to the prosecution. [944A B] 1.3 The law permits the victim to be heard before he is asked to pay compensation.
1100: The appellant was the Mahant of a Hindu undivided family, in the District of Bhagalpur. He took over the management of the Court of Wards and under the order of the Subordinate Judge he handed over charge of the Court Receiver to the appellant on January 8, 1950. On January 15, 1950, the appellant submitted a return of income of the estate to the Agricultural Income tax Officer, Monghyr, for the Fasli year 1355 corresponding to September 16, 1948, to September 15, 1949. Appeals against the order of assessment preferred to the Commissioner of Agricultural Income tax and the Board of Agricultural Income Tax were unsuccessful. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appellant was not liable to be assessed to pay agricultural income tax. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held:(i) Section 3 of the Bihar Agricultural Income tax Act, 1944, is not a charging section; it only provides machinery for recovery of tax and does not confer any right upon the assessee. (ii)The income received by the appellant from the Receiver was the income of the appellant. The receiver was not entitled to treat the appellant as an assessee and recover tax. The receiver could not be deemed to be an assessee within the meaning of section 2(m) of the Act. (iii)Section 13 merely provides a machinery for recovery, and is not a charge. It only provides a machinery to recover tax. (iv)It is not sufficient to show that the income was derived from the property of the receiver but other facts will make the receiver liable.
7101: The appellant was charged with offences punishable under sections 120B read with Sections 420 (Cheating), 468 (Forgery) and 471 using as genuine a forged document. He was also charged with offences under section 120 B read with Sections 467,468 ((Forty) and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that conspiracy had taken place outside India and therefore the sanction under section 188 Cr. P.C. for prosecuting him was not necessary. 2027: The workmen of the appellant company were retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation. It does not mean that the employer can fix different retirement age for different classes of workmen. [530 F G] (3) The age for retirement of the clerical and subordinate Staff in the appellant company is fixed at 58 years. 2613: The first respondent, a registered society, was carrying on the business of banking in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Tribunal by its award held that the reference of the dispute to the Tribunal was invalid because such disputes were required to be referred for decision to the Registrar of the Co operative Society under section 61. The Tribunal also rejected the plea of the Bank that the reference was incompetent as no question of jurisdiction arose out of the said reference. The Bank thereupon filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the Tribunal 's award. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The jurisdiction of the Industrial Tribunal to adjudicate upon the industrial dispute referred to it under section 10(1)(d) of the is not barred by section 61 of Act 7 of 1964. [214 G] (ii) The jurisdiction conferred on the Tribunal under section 10 is a judicial one and is not subject to any conditions which the nature and extent of the jurisdiction may dictate. It is open to the Tribunal to decide the dispute itself or refer it to another tribunal if it finds that there are no grounds for making the reference. If the Tribunal decides the matter without deciding the preliminary issue as regards the competence of the reference, the Tribunal would be acting without jurisdiction. [215 B C] (iii) The jurisdiction to make a reference to the Industrial Tribunal is a judicial function and is not limited by the terms of the reference. The jurisdiction to deal with a particular dispute is a judicial power. [216 D E]

445: The appellant was a tenant of the respondent in respect of a flat. The respondent filed an application under section 9 read with Schedule A of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950 for fixation of standard rent in respect of the flat. The Rent Controller fixed the standard rent at Rs. 1,000 per mensem and directed the tenant to deposit the arrears of rent within one month from the date of the order. The tenant preferred an appeal to the Appellate Authority which allowed the appeal on the ground that the provisions of section 9 of the Act applied to the three promises which formed the subject matter of three separate proceedings in the courts below. The landlord challenged the order of the appellate authority by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution but the same was dismissed. The High Court held that the provisions Of section 9 were not applicable to the three premises in question because the premises were outside the scope of the Act; that there had been a great increase in the cost of maintenance, as also of repairs and replacements of electric and other installations, that there had, been a considerable enhancement of the charge for electricity supplied by the Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation Ltd., and Government duty on the same; and that the fact that the Act did not make specific provision for increasing the rent with reference to the charges aforesaid would also point to the conclusion that the Act was not intended to the applied to the tenancies in question because these were outside the purview of the Act. Held:(i) Section 9 of the West Benaal is not applicable to a case where the premises are situated within the limits of the City Civil Judge 's court. The Act does not make specific provisions for increasing the standard rent of the premises. The Act applies to all the premises irrespective of whether they are situated within or without the limits of a city civil court. The expression "any building" in section 9 of Act means any building or part of a building or any hut or part of any structure or any part thereof. The Act is not intended to apply to buildings situated within the city limits. It is not meant to be so. The Act has no application to buildings situate within the limits limits of the city civil court, and it cannot be said that the Act applies only to buildings situated in the city limits
844: The appellant was the Health Officer of the Municipality. He filed a complaint before the Magistrate of Howrah alleging that the Sanitary Inspector had no authority to sanction the prosecution of the appellant and his servant, and that he delegated his powers under section 537 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923, to the Health Officer. The Magistrate held that the power delegated to the Health officer by the order dated April 7, 1951, was not revoked but only extended to the Chairman of the Municipality as a result of delegation by the Chairman by the order, Exhibit D. The Chairman was further directed to take action against the appellant for offences under sections 488/407 read with section 488 of the Calcutta Corporation Act, even though he was not the Chairman of that Corporation. The appellant moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order dated 4th July, 1951, on the ground that the order dated 7th December, 1951, amounted to delegation of the power of the Commissioners under section 538 of the Calcutta Muni cipality Act, 1917, and therefore, the Commissioners could not have validly authorised the Chairman to delegate his powers under that section to any other person. The High Court dismissed the petition. Held, that the order of the Chairman dated 7th Decem ber, 1951, did not amount to delegation of his functions to the Health Officers of the Municipality and was not in the nature of an administrative act. The order merely authorised the Health Officer to exercise the powers of Commissioner under section 539 of the Calcutta Munici pal Act, 19 17, and the order did not amount either to delegation or abdication of those powers. The order did not affect the jurisdiction of the Chairman to authorise him to delegate his functions to any other officer. The order was not therefore invalid on the ground of delegation of the powers of the Commissioners to another officer.
2519: The petitioners were the Chief Minister of West Bengal and the Chief Minister, in his capacity as a Minister of the State Government, was impleaded as respondent No. 1. The petitioners contended that the speech was likely to prejudice the public against the State Government and that it was likely to have the effect of misrepresenting a piece of illegal legislation before the Court. It was further contended that the order was mala fide and was not warranted by any facts or circumstances. Held: (i) The object of the Order is to prevent widespread agitation in connection with the Order and it is not necessary that every one must say what he means. The object of an order may be temporary but it cannot be said that it does not come within the mischief of section 2(a)(2) of the Act. The object is to prevent obstructions which might impede the free flow of inter course of trade and commerce. The object itself would be defeated if the Order is held to be invalid on the ground that it was passed without the authority of law. The order could not be struck down on the ground of mala fides. The order was not therefore bad for want of jurisdiction. (ii)The expression "public interest" has no fixed definition and it cannot be defined according to what a court of justice will find its fullest use in a particular case. The question whether a particular act is public interest or the like is essentially a question of fact. In the present case, the petitioners had not only the right to speak but also the duty to act in a manner that will improve their dignity and prestige. They had the right to publish and circulate the speeches and to take part in the proceedings of the Court. The Court had the power to strike out or make a new contract or amend or continue any existing contract. The Court could strike down the contracts if it appeared to it reasonably probable that the Government would not have acted in accordance with the provisions of the law.

96: The appellant was charged with murder and the prosecution case was that he had administered potassium cyanide poison to a woman in her house, that he had no concern with it, and that he had committed offences under sections 302/34 and 201 Indian Penal Code. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : (i) The High Court erred in law in not examining Palvinder Kaur at great length because of the fact that the alleged confession of the appellant was an exculpatory statement. 333: The appellants were partners of a firm known as Harnam Singh Jagat Singh. The defence was that when India was partitioned on 15 8 1947 the appellants froze all evacuee assets and later compelled the respondent to hand them over to the Custodian of Evacuee Property in Pakistan. 2946: The appellant was a Head Mistress of an aided school. The Manager appealed to the Director of Public Instruction. The appeal was allowed by the District Educational officer. The appellant then filed a suit against the order of the District Educational Offi cer. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it holding that the rules contained in Part II headed "Rules for grant of recognition and aid to elementary schools" framed under the Act were merely executive directions having no statutory force and therefore could not be enforced. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The rules contained in part Il headed "Rules regulating the conditions subject to which schools may be admitted to recognition or aid". The rules are made under the Act and they are not inconsistent with the Act. The rules are only administrative instructions and do not have statutory force. They are only administrative directions and cannot override the provisions of the Act. [10 A B] (2) The rules in Part 11 are executive orders and they can be enforced only if they are consistent with the Act and the rules. If the rules are silent on any particular point, the Government would be entitled to take appropriate action. But, if there is any doubt, the matter has to be referred to the Government whose decision shall be final. [11 C D] (3) The rules are not ultra vires of the Government. They are merely executive directions. The rules do not confer any right on any person which entitlement depends upon the terms of the rules. They are meant to be effective in their breach and constitute a class within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution. The rules, however, do not confer an enforceable right on the individual. In the special leave petition it was contended that the case against the appellant had not been proved and the State appeal against him had not been admitted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The prosecution case was based upon circumstantial evidence. The circumstances relied upon by the High Court were (i) the agreement between the appellant and the Government of India to extort money from the Government of Rajasthan; (ii) the fact that the appellant had received Rs. 7,000 as illegal gratification from Puran Chand in connection with his official duties; (iii) the fact of the appellant having taken the stand that part of the said sum had been kept by him with himself; and (iv) the fact he had sent Rs. 7000 to the Government of Haryana for being paid to the appellant. [575F G] 2. The evidence clearly established that the appellant was a member of an unlawful assembly and had entered into an agreement to extort bribe from the Government. He was charged under section 120 B IPC read with sections 109 and 120B I.P.C. and was convicted. The conviction and sentence are set aside. [566A C] 3. The appellant was a public servant at the time of the offence and was in service. He was dismissed from service after departmental inquiry. The order of dismissal was set aside. The appellant is entitled to be reinstated in service. [567D E]
3668: The appellant was one of the sons of a Hindu Undi vided family. In course of the proceedings for assessment of income tax for the year 1955 56, against the Hindu Undivided Family, an application under section 25A of the Income Tax Act, 1922 was made claiming partition w.e.f. in intestacy of the family. The appellant was also one of the other members of the family, and was impleaded as respondent No. 1. The Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat II, respondent No. I, passed orders on January 28, 1960 holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief from partition and that the income tax authorities were directed to record partition and to proceed with the assessments on the basis of the partition decree. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated January 28, 196o. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. The question for consideration was whether the appellant was entitled to claim partition from the joint family property or from the members of the joint family. HELD: (i) The appellant was not a member of the joint Hindu family. He was not a partner in the firm 's business. The partnership was dissolved and he became a partner with the firm. The appellant had no share in the profits of the firm. He was therefore not liable to be assessed as a partner of the firm '. [121 F] (ii)The order of the Income tax Officer granting partial partition is not final but it can be challenged only under section 24A of the Act. The order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner is appealable under section 24AA(3). [122 D E] (iii)In the present case, the appellant was a member of a Hindu undivided family which was dissolved and the order of the income tax officer granting partial partition was without jurisdiction. [123 C]
2272: The respondent club was granted a licence by the Government of Maharashtra for running a race course. The licence was renewed from time to time and ultimately it paid a sum of Rs. 22 lacs as licence fee. The respondent filed an appeal before the Small Causes Court under section 217 of the Bombay City Municipal Act, 1948 challenging the assessment on the ground that the amount claimed was excessive. The Small Causes Court allowed the appeal holding that the amount of licence fee claimed was excessive and directed the assessing authority to determine the net rateable value after allowing deductions made by the Corporation and the appellant. In revision the High Court held that considering the unique nature of the use of the premises by the club, the proper method for determination of the annual rent was the profits basis method but upheld the appellant 's objection as regards the disallowance of certain items of expenditure. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the proper method was the profits, basis or not. [143 G] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that looking at the various aspects of the matter, the proper methods for determining the annual rent would be the depreciation of the premises in the position of the licensee and not the rent which the landlord might reasonably expect to obtain from those who run his business. [144 C D] (iii) The High court was also right in holding the reasonableness of the method adopted by the Corporation. [145 E] (iv) The High courts were right in not interfering with the quantum of the amount of the licence fee assessed. [145 F] (v) The High 922 Court was wrong in disallowing the claim for deduction of certain items. The High Court had taken into consideration the fact that the licence fee was a lump sum payment and the amount of profit earned therefrom could not be included in the gross receipts. [145 H 146 A] (vi) The High 'Court was wrong in holding that since the licence fee is a lump sum, the same should be deducted from the gross receipts instead of deducting therefrom the gross receipts in the manner prescribed by section 154(2). [145 B C]
364: The petitioners, who were the owners of certain lands in Touzi No. 28 of the Collectorate of Hazaribagh, instituted a title suit against the State Government and the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 (Bihar Act 1 of 1951) for a declaration that the said lands had vested in the State under the provisions of the Act. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the lands did not vest in the State on the publication of the notification under section 3(1) of the Act and therefore the lands did neither vest nor meet the liability of the State under section 4(a). HELD:The lands did not come within the definition of "estate" as defined in the Act. [990 G] The Act does not define the expression 'estate '. It is an inclusive definition and includes buildings on such land. The Act does give power to the State Government to declare by a notification that the estate or any part thereof shall be deemed to have passed to and become vested in the state free from all encumbrances. The Act gives power to the Government to acquire the estate or part thereof by agreement with persons having rights therein. Section 4(a) provides that the State Government may acquire the estate of a person after giving notice to the persons interested and publishing them in the manner prescribed by the rules made under the Act. Section 4 (b) provides that if the estate has been declared to be vested in the Government under the Act, the vesting order shall cease to have effect. [992 D E; 993 A C] The Act contemplates acquisition of the estate of the person whose estate has been notified by the State Government under section 3 (1) of Act. The Act makes no provision for the transfer of the estate to the State. The Act only vests the estate in the State when the notification is published under section 3. The Act also does not contemplate acquisition of the estates by agreement. [993 B C] The word 'vest ' in the context must mean 'to remain ' in the estate for the purpose of its management. The Act uses the expressions 'vesting ' and 'acquired property '. The Act is a piece of legislation with respect
2670: The assessee company purchased the shares of a private limited company and paid the price thereof to the company. The company was assessed to income tax under section 12 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee contended that as the arrear dividends pertained to the years 1945 to 1954 had not claimed the dividend declared by it during the accounting period amounted to Rs. 43,925/ , the said sum should be treated as dividend and should therefore be assessed under section 12 Of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee acquired the shares on which the arrear dividends were received in the course of its share dealing business and that the sum of Rs. 43.925/ so received by the assessee represented business income arising under section 10 of the Act. On reference the High Court held that the amount could not be regarded as "dividend" as the assessee was not the registered shareholder in the years for which the arrear dividend was declared. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether the amount could be regarded as dividend or not is essentially one of fact. It is well settled that if a person acquires any interest in an article or stock in trade or carries on business with some third party, he cannot be considered as a registered shareholder of the company. [864 C] (ii)The mere fact that the assessee has a beneficial interest in the shares does not make the shares a real property within the meaning of section 12 of Act. The shares are not goods within the meaning Of section 2(g) of the Act and they are not goods. [865 D E] (iii)It is not correct to say that the assessee is not a registered shareholder. The shares may be in the nature of stock in trade but they are not 'goods ' within the meaning section 2(e) of the Income tax Act. [866 F G] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai & Co., Bom bay, Bombay, ; and Commissioner of Income Tax, Gujarat vs Ahmedbhai umarbhai & Company, Ahmedabad, , referred to.
5086: The appellants, who were the tenants of certain lands in the Malabar district of the State of Kerala, claimed a deduction of Rs.33,747.09 from their agricultural income on the ground that it was payable towards interest on a loan of Rs.4,00,000 taken by them from M/s. Kottayam Planters Ltd., and that the amount was credited to the revenue accounts of the assessees. The assessing authority brought the amount to tax. The High Court held that it was not agricultural income. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The assessee did not have any agricultural operations at all. They had been carrying on business as cultivators or owners of estates. They had paid interest on a sum borrowed for the purpose of meeting the interest which they derived from the land. The interest was received in respect of the land acquired by them. [165H; 161A] (ii) The remission cannot be considered as amounting to the receipt of agricultural income. It is not an item of income. It has nothing to do with the activities of the assessees, and that it does not arise from the agricultural operations carried on by them.[164C] (iii) The remission could not be considered as an item of agricultural income within the meaning of section 3 of the Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1950. [164D E]
6032: The respondents, who were the owners of certain evacuee property in Pakistan, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the legality and validity of the order dated 5.2.1973 passed by the Custodian General (second appellant) under section 8(1)(a) of the Evacuee (Administration of Properties) Act, 1950, declaring that the sale was invalid since the property was evacuee property and belonged to one Shah Mahmood who had migrated to Pakistan during the disturbances of 1947 and continued to live there as an evacuee. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that when the High Court decided to go into the question whether Section 8 of the Act has outlived its purpose and hence the concerned officers of the State need not entertain any applications made in future under Section 8 regarding the house, the Custodian may dispose of the same in accordance with law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 8 of Act 30 of 1950 is a piece of beneficial legislation intended to protect the interests of persons residing in the State of evacuee property. [470F] 2. Section 8 provides for a summary remedy for the disposal of evacuee property which has been notified as evacuee property. Section 8(1) provides for a right of appeal against the decision of the Custodian. Section 14 provides for a second appeal against the order of the Custodian General. [471G H] 3. Section 8 also will have to be retained and made use of by genuinely interested parties. If the Custodian considers the application under Section 8 about the title of the person claiming to be the property, he must make an enquiry and decide whether such property is evacuee property or not. If he decides that the property is evacuee Property, he should make an order accordingly. If he comes to the conclusion that the property cannot be traced, he should pass a certificate to the effect that the property has been declared to be evacuee property. If he finds that the property can be traced without being traced, then he should make a report to the Custodian General pointing out therein the fact of the matter and requesting him to take necessary action. [473A B] 4. Section 8 does not provide for any fresh application
1432: The appellants were tried by the Sessions judge for offences under section 302 read with section 149 and section 201 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night between the 26th and 27th July, 1957, the appellants collected in front of the house of Kali Charan appellant, collected in front and took away the dead body of his brother from the village and that when Kali Charan Singh asked him to go home he did not do so and handed over the gull and the bandolier of cartridges to Dharam Singh who had a pistol in his hand. The appellants were convicted under section 302/149 and section 201/109 read with section 109 of the Indian penal Code and sentenced to various terms of imprisonment. The High Court confirmed the convictions but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by special leave it was contended that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not corroborated by the medical evidence and that the High Court erred in holding that the eye witnesses had seen the occurrence and their evidence must be accepted. Held: (per Das, C. J., Ayyangar, Mudholkar and Aiyan, JJ.) that the evidence regarding the presence of the appellants at the time of the murder was corroborated by the F.I.R. which indicated that the appellants had taken part in the assault. The evidence of the doctor who conducted the postmortem examination showed that there was no external injury and that the death was due to shock and haemorrhage as a result of the injuries. The evidence relating to the recovery of the gun used for committing the offence was not sufficient to establish that the appellants were responsible for the murder.
3853: The appellant was convicted and sentenced by the High Court under section 302 I.P.C. to death for having committed murder of one Hari Singh, his brother Hari Singh and another. The evidence against him consisted of the testimony of two eye witnesses, P.W. 2 and P.W 13. The first information report was written by Bharat Singh on the dictation of Hari Singh. The second information was recorded by Bharat Singh at about 4 a.m. on the dictated information given by Hari Singh. After investigation the police submitted a charge sheet against the appellant. The trial court accepted the prosecution case and convicted the appellant under section 302 read with section 34 I.P,.C. and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal the High Court acquitted the appellant holding that the evidence against him had not been corroborated by the medical evidence. In this Court the appellant contended that the evidence of the eye witness was not corroborated by the other evidence. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) The evidence of the doctor who conducted the postmortem examination was not sufficient to prove the nature of the injury caused by the fire arm. [108 E] (ii) The evidence in the case was not sufficient for conviction. The doctor found only one injury on the head of the deceased. The doctor could have easily ascertained as to which of the two injuries were fatal. The doctor did not say that the injury No. 1 was sufficient in the ordinary course to cause death. The doctor had stated that the injury Nos. 1 and 2 were possible if a lantern was burning. The doctor was not examined. The doctor has not stated that the lantern or the torch was burning. He has merely stated that the fire arms were used. [109 A C] (iii) There is no reason why the evidence of an injured witness should be discarded unless he is corroborated in material particulars by independent evidence. It would be hazardous to come to a conclusion of guilt in a case based upon circumstantial evidence unless the evidence is consistent with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and inconsistent with his innocence.[110 B] (iv) The circumstances relied upon by the High court are not sufficient to sustain the conviction of the appellant. [111 D]

Section 55 of the Act provides that every 'ulthurai servant ' whether hereditary or nonhereditary shall be appointed according to rules to be framed by the Commissioner. Rule 12 provided that every 'uruhty servant ' whether nonhereditari or non hereditary shall obtain a certificate of fitness from the head of an institution to perform the functions of the office or performance the service after having due regard to the claims of members of the family, power to make rules providing for the qualifications to be possessed by the officers and servants for appointment to non hereditary offices in religious institutions, the qualifications to he possessed by hereditary workers for succession to office and the conditions of service of all such officers and servants. Under this rule making power the State Government made the Madras Hindu Religious and charitable Endowments (Amendment ) Act, 1970 which introduced section 55A into the Act providing for the appointment Of office holders and servant in religious institutions by applying the rule of hereditary appointments. By section 116 of the Amending Act, 1970 the State Legislature enacted the Tamil Nadu Hindu Public Trusts Act, 1950. Rule 12 laid down the procedure for appointment of office holder and servants. Rule 13 provided that every member of the public shall be entitled to appoint a fit person to perform the services of the office holder or servant in the religious institution. Rule 14 provided that every office holder or other employee of the temple shall be paid remuneration at the rate fixed by the Commissioner from time to time. Rule 15 provided that every person appointed as office holder
5205: The petitioners in the writ petitions were employed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh Public Works Department. They filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the constitutional validity of clause (3) of Article 371 D of the Constitution on the ground that it was ultra vires the proviso to Clause (5) of Article 372 of the Constitution and also on the ground of violation of Articles 14, 16 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned clause was violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution inasmuch as it conferred arbitrary powers upon the State Government to revise its order by passing a general order which would have effect only if the order had been passed by the State Government or the Governor. Dismissing the writ petitions, HELD: 1. The power of judicial review is not intended to be an appellate authority. But the existence of the power to decide and pass orders is not a condition precedent for the exercise of that power but its exercise is required to be determined in accordance with law. [888C] 2. The Administrative Tribunal constituted under the Act has jurisdiction to deal with service matters specified in the order of the State Government and it cannot be said that the State Government has no power to pass any order affecting the conditions of service of persons employed in the ministeri al services of the State. [889E F] 3. The Administrative Tribunals are competent to hear cases within their territorial limits and pass appropriate orders. [890F G]
5302: The respondent plaintiff filed a suit for declaration that the sale deed executed by the widowed mother of the respondent was invalid and was not binding upon him and for recovery of possession thereof. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that the alienation was not something which a man of ordinary prudence would have effected had the properties been owned by him and thus held it not binding on the respondent. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellants, it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that the alienation made by the widow was not something that a man of normal prudence would make if there were no averments of facts necessary for attracting section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act or section 4 of the Kerala Compensation for Tenants Improvements Act, 1958. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. Section 2(d) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 defines 'land ' as any land which is used for agricultural purposes. The definition of 'land ' given in section 2(g) of the Act is wide enough to include buildings also. [904C] 2. Section 2 (h), which provides for the definition of 'Land ', shows that the definition of land includes buildings also. The definition is wide enough so as to cover buildings which are constructed on land other than agriculture. [905F G] 3. The High Court has rightly pointed out that the High court has taken note of the fact that the property involved in the case was situated in the State of Kerala and that the property was situated in Kerala State. It is true that the property in question was situated in State of Kerala but the High Court has considered the matter from another angle viz., that the property is situated in State other than Kerala State. The High court has found that the property had been purchased by the widow of the respondent in the year 1952 and she had become the absolute owner of the property in the year 1956. The High COurt has further held that the respondent was entitled to recover possession of the property from the appellants. [906H; 907A B]
5814: The petitioners in the Writ Petition are the P & T Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Employees ' Welfare Assocation (Regd.) Delhi and the Federation of All India Scheduled Castes & Scheduled Tribes Employees P & T Department, New Delhi. They were working as P.S.Cs. in the Central Administrative Tribunal. The Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the policy contained in the letter dated 23.12.1983 was not applicable to the P.Ss. like the petitioners. The petitioners filed an appeal before this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. Disposing of the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The policy contained in letter dated 23rd December 1983 is not applicable to P.S., which is a Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe employee. [628F] 2.1 The P & T Personnel Department of the Government of India had issued a letter dated 23th December 1983 wherein it was stated that the benefit of reservation would be available to those employees belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes who were promoted earlier but later promoted along with others. The said letters also contain instructions regarding reservations for SC/ ST/BC etc. to be applied while making promotions. The said instructions were reiterated by the Ministry in its letter dated 25th July 1985. [629B C] 3. The P &T Personnel Department of Government of India has issued a letter bearing No. 11012/7/85 Estt. (A) dated 23rd October 1986 stating that the benefit given to the employees belonging to Scheduled Castes and Schedule Tribes will be withdrawn from the date of issue of the letter. The said order was based upon the assurance given by the Government of Delhi in the year 1985 that the benefit would be extended to all the employees belonging the Scheduled Castes & the Scheduled Tribes. 4741: The petitioners, who were members of a State Legislature party in the State of Maharashtra, challenged the constitutional validity of the Maharashtra Legislature (Delegation of Powers) Act, 1971 (Maharashtra Act No. XXVII of 1971), which was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its legislative power under Entry 40 of List I of the VIIth Schedule to the Constitution and the order made by the Government of India imposing ban on the sale or distribution of lottery tickets of other States. The petitioners contended that the expression "Betting and gambling" includes and has always been understood to have included the conduct of lotteries. It was further contended that the Government of a State organised a lottery without the entrustment of executive power as contemplated by Article 258 or in disregard or defiance of any condition that may have been imposed while entrusting executive power as envisaged by Article 257 of the Constitution. The petitioners also alleged that the Government had never intended to make any law regulating the conduct of the lottery nor had it ever intended to prohibit the sale of the tickets of other State Lottery tickets. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "betting andgambling" means the conduct of a lottery. [445C] 2. The expression 'betting or gambling ' is not defined in the Constitution. It does not mean merely a right to take part in an activity prohibited by law. It means that there should be no interference with the free flow of trade, commerce or intercourse. The expression is used to denote the conduct of all kinds of lottery including those which are not interconnected but which are conducted by the organisers of a lottery called the State Lotteries. The State Lothance is one such thing. The State Government can regulate the conduct of such lottery only if the State Government so directs. [441D E] 3. The expression in Entry 40 of the Union List of the VII Schedule to the Consti tution is wide enough to include the conduct of lottery. The expression means that there must be a law prohibiting the sale or the distribution of any form of lottery. There is no doubt that the expression includes the conduct of many forms of lottery including the conduct of
6018: The respondent joined service as technical assistant with the Gujarat State Electricity Board. While he was posted at Surat, he was transferred to Ukai subdivision under the order of the Superintending Engineer dated 29th March, 1974. Pursuant to the order of transfer he was relieved from his duties at Surat on 30th March,1974 to enable him to join at Ukai Subdivision under the orders of the Superintending Engi neer. He made representation for cancellation of his transfer order on the ground that his mother aged years was ailing and it would cause great inconvenience to him if he was required to join at the place where he had been transferred. The respondent also filed a civil suit challenging the validity of the order of his discharge from service by means of a writ petition before the High Court. The learned Single Judge held that the order of discharge was issued in violation of the basic principles of natural justice and set aside the same. The Division Bench allowed the appeal preferred by the appellants but it held that the respondent 's claim for back wages was not tenable because he had already been paid salary in terms of interim order of the Court. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the respondent having been discharged from service pursuant to the order passed by the Superintending Engineer, the respondent could not be said to have been visited with any evil consequences; that the order discharging the respondent from service was illegal and void ab initio as no opportunity was afforded to him before discharging him; and that the respondent was entitled to full salary and allowances. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. It is now well settled that when an order of dismissal is challenged as invalid or illegal, the principle of natural justice is to be treated in abeyance till the final decision of the case. If the authority passes an order of discharge in breach of the rules of natural justice, such order will be liable to be annulled being struck down as invalidityarising from article 14 of the Constitution. [362E F] 2. In the instant case, the respondent has been given adequate opportunity to defend himself. The question whether he should be re instated from service or not does not arise as there is nothing to show that the respondent has ever been discriminated against in the matter of re instate
4976: The petitioner, a retired Judge of the Rajasthan High Court was appointed as a District and Sessions Judge on July 1 , 1974. He continued to be in service till July 31 , 1977 when he was elevated as a Judge of the High Court. His total period of service as a Judicial Officer , though counted from the date of his appointment as a District & Sessions Judge, he was 29 years , 9 months and one day while his service as a Judge ,of the High Court was a period of 9 years and 21 days. In the High Courts pension payable to such Judges was calculated at Rs. 11,820 per annum under clause (a) of Para 2 of the First Schedule read with the Rajasthan Rules and to that figure was added the additional pension of Rs. 700 per annum under Clause (b) of Para II of the Schedule to the High Courts Judges ' (Conditions of Service) Act, 1958. The petitioner filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the fixation of his pension by the State Government. The petitioner contended that the amount of pension should be arrived at on the basis of the last pay drawn by him as a District Judge and not on the basis that he would have been eligible for the benefit of selection grade if he had been appointed a High Court Judge. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The amount of pension is to be arrived at, on the basis Of the last pay, drawn by him , as a District judge, which has to be taken into account for the purpose of calculating his pension. [612F] 2. The expression "basic salary" means basic pay including stagnation increments, if any, but does not include special pay. The expression is used to indicate a special pay. It is not possible to construe the word "basic" as "salary". The amount of the pension is to he arrived at on that basis. Under para 2 of the Second Schedule read with Rule 2 of the Rajasthan Rules, the retiring Judges entire service as a District Judges were entitled to a pension of Rs, 15,320 per annum only. Under clause (b) thereof, the pay which they would have drawn in the selection grade if they had been appointed as a High Court Judges, had he been appointed a District
3344: The appellant, a new entrant in the State of Tamil Nadu, applied for stage carriage permits. The Respondent No. 1, the State Transport Authority, invited applications from eligible applicants for one stage carriage permit. The appellant was not satisfied with the marks awarded to him and filed an appeal before the State Transport Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the appeal as devoid of merit. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The rule itself emphasises what is obvious, that the paramount consideration of the interest of the public, as enshrined in section 47(1), must given full weight while awarding permits. That means to say that the various factors set out in Rule 155 A are subject to Section 47(1). There is no doubt that the interest of travelling public is highlighted while evaluating the relevant worth of the various claimants. There is another thing particularly when the appellant has been awarded a contract for a short route. [813D E] (2) The appellant being admittedly a new entrants, was entitled to preference. [814F] (3) In the instant case, the appellant being a new ententer, was entitled, having regard to the public interest in the matter of passenger transport service, to more than 50 per cent of the total number of applicants who had applied for the stage carriage permits, and the fact that the appellant had secured higher marks than the respondent No. 1. [815B C]
2809: The Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959 was amended by the Maharashtra Legislature with retrospective operation. By section 2 of the amending Act the definition of "goods" was amended and in cl. (13) after the words "and commodities" the following shall be, and shall be deemed always to have been, added, namely: 'and all materials, commodities and articles". The expression "goods" included at all relevant times standing timber agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale. The appellant who was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Rules, 1959, was assessed to sales tax for the years 1967 68 and 1968 69 on the ground that the timber agreed to he sold had been cut and removed before the sale or under its contract of sale without any agreement to sell the timber. The High Court dismissed the petition filed by the State holding that the timber was not "goods" within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act and that the appellant could not be taxed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the expression "goods", in Entry 48 in List 11 of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was in pari materia with the expression "taxable turnover" in Entry 54 in List II of the Government Of India Act, 955, must be given a restricted meaning and should be confined only to transactions of sale of goods as defined in the Act and not to transactions of contracts of sale of such goods. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (i) The expression "tax able value" is used in two different senses, namely, (1) the value of goods and (2) the value ad valorem. [955 C] (ii) The expression 'taxable turnover ' has a wide connotation and includes all materials, articles and articles including all materials whether manufactured from goods or other articles produced in the course of manufacture or not. [956 D E] (iii) The expression has a wider connotation than 'turnover '. [957 F] (iv) The expression means what it says and does not limit its scope to something which would be the subject matter of a contract. It is the substance of the transaction which determines its character. [958 G] (v)
2835: The appellant company was carrying on business in shares and other commodities. In proceedings for assessment of income for the year 1952 53, the Income tax Officer computed the income of the company from its business at Rs. 3,39,899 and declined to take into account the loss suffered by it in the share transactions. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business activities of the company were not the "same business" within the meaning of section 24(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 as then in force. Accordingly, the Tribunal upheld the claim of the appellant company and directed that the loss be set off under section 24(1) of the Act. The High Court answered the question against the appellant company. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the High Court erred in holding that the two lines of business constituted one business and the other one business. The two lines of activity is distinct and separate from each other. The existence of a common management, common business organisation, common administration, common fund and a common place of business is furnished in this case by the existence of common management, Common Service Organisation, common administration. ,of course, the decisive test for determining whether the two lines are the same business is the nature of the two functions. But the existence of a joint management, common administration and a common office is not conclusive. The two line of business is different and the distinction between them is made clear by the use of the words "is concerned with" in section 24(3).
4235: The appellant tenant was in occupation of two plots of land. The respondent agreed to pay and discharge all taxes and outgoings imposed on the two plots of the land. On the expiration of the term of 15 years or sooner termination of the lease, the respondent agreed to deliver back the possession of the lands alongwith structures thereon. The appellant 's case was that he had erected a building on the land and had been paying rent to the respondent. The respondent contended that the appellant was not liable to be ejected under section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rent Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the appellate court held that it had no jurisdiction to give a decree for ejectment in respect of the two buildings constructed on the land. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In this Court the question for consideration was whether the respondent was entitled to the protection of section 12(1) (a) of the Act. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 12(1)(a) of Bombay Rent Act applies only where the tenancy is created by a registered instrument. [1019 G] 2. The expression "rent" has not been defined in the Act. The word "rent" is of general import and does not include a mortgage. A lease may be express or implied. It need not necessarily be expressed or implied. The word 'rent ' means the amount of money which a tenant is liable to pay to the landlord. The word has been used in the context of a lease where there are two inconsistent expressions, one requiring different meanings. The word is generally used in relation to a lease where the terms are identical with those of a lease in which there are separate words. The word may also mean different things in the same document. The word must be understood in its ordinary sense meaning the term which is being used in the sense in which people conversant with the subject matter with which the document dealing would like to deal would. [1099 H 1099A] 3. The word rent is of a very wide connotation. It may be paid either in cash or kind or both. The word `rent ' is of a wider connotation than the word `landlord ' because the word `tenant ' is of widest
4259: The petitioner was convicted under section 376 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for seven years. He filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed the same on the ground that there was no corroboration of the testimony of the prosecutrix, that there was absence of injuries on her person and so the conviction was unsustainable. In the special leave petition it was contended that there was lack of corroboration of the statement of the prosecutrix and that the court 's verdict was based on mere surmises and conjectures. Dismissing the special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The law as it stands today is that there is no rule of law or practice to support a conviction in rape cases unless there are very strong reasons to do so. [404F] 2. The law requires corroboration of the evidence of the prosecutrix by direct ocular evidence, and not by a photographic test, or by medical examination. [405A B] 3. The law does not require that the victim should be subjected to any attempt at some act or the other that there must be any contemporaneous record to show that such acts or conduct had been accomplished. It may be permissible to have such instances proved where the victim of sexual assault has been threatened with violence or has been rendered helpless by one of the accused persons against her whom she lodged report with the police. [403C D] 4. The law prescribes various kinds of safeguards to protect the rights of the victims of rape. The court has to take into consideration all relevant factors including the desirability of ensuring that the protection afforded by the statute is given an effective deterrent to prevent the commission of the crime. [402B C] Pratap Misra & Ors. vs State of Orissa & Anr., ; , referred to.
6345: The appellants, who were duly elected Directors of the respondent No. 1, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the requisition notice dated 5.9.89 for giving fresh notice to the elected members and the expert co opted member, contending that under the scheme of the Act read with the Rules and the bye laws of the Society the members of the Board of Direc tors are entitled to sit and vote at the meeting when the Committee considers the vote of no confidence against the Chairman of the Committee, and that the said right is not available to the nominees of the Financial Institutions and the expert Co opted member. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the members of respondent No.1 had got a limited right to vote at a meeting to elect Chairman or Vice Chairman, as the case may be, and that they were entitled to sit at the meeting. [491G H; 492A] 1.3 The expression "Committee members"

5524: The Public Service Commission issued a notification on July 17, 1973 determining inter se seniority of all the candidates appointed on the basis of 1970 examination in accordance with their position in the list submitted by the Commission under Rule 19 of the Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission 's Examination Rules, 1951. 1089: The appellants were under an agreement with the Textile Mills Co. Ltd., Madras, appointed managing agents for 20 years of the Textile Mills Company and the Agency Company on July 11, 1945. 2093: The appellant company terminated its services of the respondents workmen on July 17, 1967. The respondents workmen challenged the termination order before the Labour Court by filing a number of demands. The Labour Court held that the retrenchment was unjustified and illegal and directed reinstatement with full wages from the date of the award. The appellant contended that the action of the management in retrenching the workmen amounted to an unfair labour practice. The Labour court accepted the contention of the workmen and held that departure from the rule "first come last go" could not be made because some junior members of the staff were retained since the company had recorded in the resolution its reasons for departing from the rule as "first come, first go". The Labour Court further held that the number of employees required to carry on the work after the imposition of a ban against the business of the appellant could not exceed the number retained by the appellant. The Labour Appellate Tribunal confirmed this finding. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant company. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the action taken by the management was mala fide and that the action was arbitrary and without any justification. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) The action of the appellant was arbitrary and capricious. The appellant was justified in retrench ing the respondents workmen. [764 C] (ii) The Labour Court has to see whether there is any violation of the rules of natural justice or the decision of the management is vitiated by non application of mind. [765 D E]

It would be unconstitu tional in view of the constitutional bar to levy tax on sales in the course off inter state trade. 5543: The appellant joined the service of the Narang Bank of India Ltd. as a clerk cum typist on July 12, 1973 and was confirmed in his service on October 1, 1974. The appellant filed an appeal before this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution against the award of the Industrial Tribunal. His appointment was purely temporary and subject to the approval of the competent authority. He was paid out of the funds of the bank at the rate of Rs.400 per month. The appellant had no right to be absorbed in the service or to be posted at a place where there is no post of clerk cum typists. 2744: The respondents were appointed as Professors of Surgery and the appointment was made on a purely temporary basis till further orders. They challenged the validity of the proviso to sub rule (4) of Rule 30 of the Rajasthan Medical Service (Collegiate Branch) Rules, 1962 by filing writ petitions in the High Court which were allowed. The High Court held that the proviso to Sub rule (4), which empowered the State Government to make only a temporary ' or officiating appointment ', could not override the provisions of Ordinance No. 65 and that the appointments of Dr. Rishi dated July 28, 1963 as Principal of the College was not challenged either in the High court or before this Court. The High COurt also found that the proviso had been added to Rule 30(4) with retrospective effect during the pendency of the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the proviso was not ultra vires of the rule making power under the University Act, but was merely an enabling provision empowering the State Government for withdrawing affiliation of colleges if the conditions laid down therein were fulfilled. Dismissing the appeals, HELD : (1) The proviso to sub r.(4) of r. 30 of the Rules framed under the University of Rajputana Act of 1946 is not ultra vires the rule making powers of the State Government. [563 F] (2) The proviso has no application where the question raised principally centres round the validity and effect of the proviso. It is only when the main provision of the proviso is declared invalid that the consequential provision would cease to have any meaning and effect. [562 C]
3779: Section 5 of the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948 provides that a dealer liable to pay tax under the Act shall be liable to pay the same on his total gross turnover. The appellant who was carrying on business in the State of Punjab as a call keeper and also as a call earner carried on a profession, trade or calling within the State of Haryana, filed returns for the assessment years 1959 60 and 1960 61. The assessing authority determined the taxable turn over at Rs. 1,10,560/ . The appellant 's contention before the assessing authority was that the sum of Rs. 1.10,540/ which he had paid towards the tax for the relevant year exceeded the taxable turn up of Rs. 2,000/ which he was required to pay. The assessing authori ty rejected this contention and computed the aggregate amount of the tax to be levied. The appellant ' s further contention was that the said sum was not liable to be taxed as the whole of the income was not assessable. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the order of the assessing authority. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal holding that the sum paid by way of tax was not taxable. The High Court held that section 3 of the Act did not apply to the facts of the case because it was not shown how the sum paid was taxable. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The question whether a particular item falls within the class of cases where the Act does not provide for taxation is essentially a question of fact. [864 C] (2) The High Court has clearly erred in interpreting section 3 in such a way as to make section 2(b), read with section 5 of the Act, useless in determining the tax in accordance with the grada tion laid down in the schedule 2 of the Act.[865 D E]
4798: The appellants were the owners of certain lands in Pakistan. They filed a suit against the Union of India and the Defence Secretary, Government of India, for recovery of possession of the lands on the ground that the notice exhibit A 8 was not valid under section 80 Code of Civil Procedure. The defence raised was that the notice was not properly served upon the plaintiffs as they had no knowledge of the suit being filed. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the notice could not be said to be insufficient because it did not give the names of the parties who were the owners in the locality but only the names of two of the plaintiffs. On appeal the High Court held that the notice did not fulfil the requirements of section 80 Code and the suit was maintainable. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The notice must substantially fulfil its work of intimating the parties concerned generally of the nature of the suit intended to be filed and if it does so, it would be sufficient compliance with section 80 of the Code. [235 G] (ii)The notice is a complete and unambiguous warning that it has been given by the defendants to the plaintiff and the latter has no objection to any such direction being given. It is also a notice which gives the plaintiff an opportunity to state his case. [236 B] (iii)It is clear from the language of section 80 that it is mandatory that the notice should contain the name of the person or persons giving the notice. If the notice contains the name of one or more persons, it cannot be said that the notice is invalid merely because it is given by two out of three. [237 C] (iv)In the present case, the notice must substantially fulfill the requirement of section 80. The notice must not substantially fulfil the work of intimation of the suit to the owners of the land. [238 D] (v)Section 80 provides that where there are more than one plaintiffs and all the plaintiffs are the same, then the notice shall be deemed to have been duly served on all the plaintiffs. But the proviso requires that the omission of the number of plaintiffs shall not cause any prejudice to the defendant. [239 E F]
532: The respondent was a Sub Inspector of Police in the State of Bihar. He was dismissed from service by an order passed on December 20, 1948, and his appeal against that order having been rejected by the Deputy Inspector General of Police on June 7, 1949, he filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said orders as being violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the dismissal order had not become final until the Inspector General of Po lice gave its decision on April 22, 1950, and that as the last mentioned order had been passed after the Constitution had come into force, it had no jurisdiction to deal with the order of dismissal which had been passed at a time when the Constitution had not come into force. Held, that the High Court had no power under article 226 of the Constitution to issue such a writ to quash the order of the dismissal passed by the District Superintendent of Police on December 20. The order of dismissal passed by him had not become conclusive as to whether the respondent was or was not guilty of misconduct within the meaning of article 311(2) of the Constitution and the High Court could pass appropriate orders regarding the validity of the order of dismiss al lowance.
2083: The Mysore Public Service Commission (Functions) Rules, 1957, were made under article 309 of the Constitution. Rule 4(2) provided that "the functions and duties of the Public Service Commission shall be as set forth in the rules of recruitment of such service specially made in that behalf". The Mysore State Civil Services (General Recruitment) Rules, 579 Held, that the Mysore State Civil Service (General Recruitment), Rules 1957, framed under article 309, of the Constitution, were not rules made under article 3O3 of the Constitution and therefore could not be enforced. The Mysore State Government had no power to make the Rules under article 309 beyond the period of one year from the commencement of the Constitution which was long before the Constitution came into force. The Mysore General Services (General Recruits) Rules, 1958, were not statutory rules but were merely administrative arrangements made in exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to article 309 of ' the Constitution. The Mysore Public Services (General recruitment) Rules,1957, were not made under article 320 of the Constitution; it was only made under article 313 of the Constitution that the rules might provide for recruitment to the posts of Deputy Engineers and above. The Mysore Government had no authority to make the rules under article 309 after the expiry of the period of two years specified in article 3O4 of the Constitution as required by article 320(3).

[1097F] 4. Section 53 B provides that where there are two or more Hindus, the provisions of section 53A shall apply to them. [1098G] 5. Section 53 C provides that where one of the
6788: The appellant imported the goods detected defects and the foreign supplier accepted the defective goods and damages and agreed for payment of compensation. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim on the ground that the damage was discovered after the goods were out of customs control. The Letters Patent Appeal preferred against the said decision was also rejected by the Division Bench of the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. The appellant is entitled to the same rate of interest as provided under Section 28 of the Act.
