4749: The petitioner was a Judge of the Madhya Pradesh High Court. He retired from service on 31.1.1983. On February 2, 1983 he wrote to the Registrar of the Madhya pradesh High Court that he was entitled to payment of cash equivalent of leave salary in respect of the period of earned leave at his credit on the date of retirement as provided in Rule 20B of the All India Services (Leave) Rules 1955. The Accountant General of Madhya Pradesh authorised the petitioner to draw cash equivalent of the unutilised leave due on 855 full allowances as defined in sections 3 and 9 (1) of the Act. The petitioner informed the Registrar of Madhya Pradesh High COurt that he was drawing the amount as indicated in the communication without prejudice to his right to claim Rs. 24,000 to which sum under the law he was entitled. The AccountantGeneral of Madhya Pradesh on March 25, 1983 intimated the petitioner that he was paid an excess sum of Rs. 2,220 by his communication dated July 17, 1982. The petitioner represented against the said circular letter but the same was rejected. The petitioner filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the validity of the circular letter. The petitioner contended that the said circular letters were violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It was further contended that the provisions of section 5(3) of the Indian , as amended by the Madhya Pradesh Act No. 18 of 1984 would apply to the case of the petitioner also. The petitioner relied on the provisions of the Act to justify the circular letter of February 18, 1983. The petitioner also prayed for refund of the excess amount paid to him. Allowing the petition, HELD: 1. The Act does not make provision for payment of the retirement benefit contemplated under rule 20B of All India Services Pension Rules, 1954. [857F] 2. The expression 'actual pay ' has been used in Rule 20 B of the All india Services Pension Rules 1955. Rule 20B makes it obligatory for the Government servant retiring on superannuation or otherwise to give notice of retirem ent to the authority concerned before the same is accepted. The expression "gratuity" has been defined in Rule 2(b) to mean gratuity except when the payment of gratuity is governed by the Payment of Gratuity

3110: The appellant 's land was acquired by the Government for construction of a residential colony. The Land Acquisition Officer fixed the market value of the land at Rs. 90,000/ per acre. 1550: The appellant was the owner of a car. She died in April 1953. In the year 1953, she made an application to the Insurance Company for insurance of her car. The Insurance Company sanctioned a loan of Rs. 1,000/ to her husband. The car met with an accident on May 2, 1953 and was damaged. The car was insured against a policy issued by the Bharat Fire and General Insurance Co., Ltd., and the policy was due to expire sometime in April, 1953. The car at that time was insured against policy issued by Bharat Fire and Gift Co., Ltd. The car had been delivered to the appellant 's husband by the Insurance Company. The car developed a complete de save and except the period when it was stopped from the Insurance Company 's office. The car left a state of its own accord. The car did not have any insurance coverage. The car thereafter went off the road and was completely burnt down. The car again fell into a deep gorge. The car then became totally damaged. The appellant applied to the Insurance company for insurance of the car but the Insurance Company refused to act upon the application. The appellant filed a complaint before the Magistrate who convicted her under sections 464 and 468 I.P.C. and sentenced her to imprisonment till the rising of the Court and to payment of fine. The High Court confirmed the acquittal under section 419 I.P,. Code. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The concept of fraud is well known. It has been evolved as an equitable doctrine, based on a however low or confused in the following two Articles of Association. The first article provides that where one party acts dishonestly, and the other party does not part with his actus reusly, and the second article provides that the person deceived may also be guilty of fraudulent concealment. [598 D] (ii)The word "fraudulently" means "wrongful, deliberate, motivated by ill motive, active participation in aiding, or abetting, the doing of a criminal act in the execution of which he is charged". [599 F H] (iii)Fraudulently means a fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy
273: The respondent, a national of Pakistan, was allowed cash credit limit of rupees three lakhs by the Mailsi branch of the Central Bank of India Ltd. on the 23rd June, 1947, shortly before the partition of British India. On the 23rd July, 1947, he filed a complaint against the respondent under sections 380 and 454 Indian Penal Code and also under section 412 of the Code before the District Magistrate of Gurgaon. The trial magistrate rejected this complaint and dismissed it on the ground that the respondent had not been able to prove his plea of citizenship by evidence. He held that the respondent could not be said to have acquired Pakistan nationality by merely staying in there from 15th August, 1947, till 10th November, 1947, when he did not return to Pakistan. He further held that the offence of obtaining a loan from the Government of India for the purchase of a motor car was committed only after he returned to Pakistan and not before. The High Court, in appeal, accepted the contention of the respondent and convicted him under section 424 Of the Code. Held, that the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of the exception (1) of section 489 of the Code as he had not been proved to have voluntarily resigned from the service of the Dominion of India before the 15th August 1947, and was therefore not 'a citizen of India within the meaning of article 5(2)(b) of the Constitution.
387: The appellants were charged with offences under sections 435 and 436 of the Indian Penal Code. They pleaded not guilty to those charges but the Assistant Sessions Judge disagreed with the jury on the ground that the jury had not taken a proper judicial mind. He held that the charge was defective as he did not invite the High Court as required by section 307(3) Of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, in regard to the charge to the jury being defective. The High Court also rejected the reference made by the Assistant Sessions judge to the High Court stating in the letter of reference that on the evidence recorded before him the appellants had been in possession of the Palani and the Punjaul but were dispossessed of the same some time prior to the passing of the decree in the title suit on December 16, 1950, and were therefore justified in taking steps for recovery of possession thereof from the appellants. The High COurt further held that the reference was in the circumstances of the case not competent and it set aside the convictions and sentences passed upon the appellants. Held, that the reference must be allowed and the reference made to the High court invalidating the verdict of the Assistant SessionsJudge. The High Courts had no power to interfere with the trial courts ' decision when they found that there was no sufficient evidence to support the verdict. The High court could not substitute its own judgment for the one reached by the Trial Court. The High courts had no jurisdiction to reverse an order of acquittal merely because the trial court had itself held that another view of the evidence was possible.
6683: The appellant was prosecuted for offences punishable under the provisions of the . After examination of the prosecution witnesses and recording of the statements of the accused under Section 342 of the old Code of Criminal Procedure (corresponding to Section 342 of Cr. P.C.) the Trial Magistrate allowed the complainant to examine the three witnesses as prayed by it, notwithstanding that the case was pending before the Trial Court for considerable length of time. The defence counsel did not ask for any appeal against the judgment of the High Court allowing the two other revision applications, but only sought permission from the trial court to examine the 3 witnesses as prayed for by it. The trial Magistrate allowed the application and directed the prosecution to produce the three witnesses within a period of 15 days. On an application made by the defence counsel, the High Court allowed the second revision petition filed by the respondent and quashed the order of the trial Magistrate. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has gravely erred in allowing the second revision petitions filed by the State. [716E] 2. In the instant case, the prosecution had been permitted to examine the witnesses as prayed. The prosecution should have at least examined the three witnesses. The prosecution ought to have given an opportunity to the defence to cross examine the witnesses. It is not open to the prosecution to fill up the lacuna in the prosecution case. [717F G] 3. The High Courts are right in holding that the prosecution should be permitted to adduce evidence in support of its case. [776G] 4. The High courts are also right in permitting the prosecution to examine the defence witnesses. [718A B] 5. The High court was wrong in allowing the revision applications. [719D
1878: The appellant company was engaged in the business of running a Dual Auto Mill and the two Dual Autos. The workmen were dismissed after a domestic enquiry commenced on February 4, 1967 which was carried on exparte because these workmen did not choose to be present. The dismissal order was passed by the management on February 25, 1967. The appellant challenged the dismissal order before the Labour Court under section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Labour Court held that the enquiry was not proper and some of the witnesses were re examined before the Tribunal whose verdict was against the Company and hence this appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The dismissal order is not a speaking one. It does not contain any reasons. [864F] (ii) The evidence of the Union and the witnesses examined by the management has been considered by this Court in Kalindi & Ors. vs Tata Locomotive & Chemicals Ltd., [1979] 3 S.C.R. 942. In that case the Union had filed an application for permission to produce certain documents. The Labour court refused to permit production of those documents. The High Court allowed the application. The company went in revision to the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The company contended that the enquiry held was not proper as many workmen were employed to look after the two mills. The Labour Appellate Tribunal rejected the revision application holding that the enquiry conducted was not proper. The company appealed to this Court. HELD: The Labour Appellate Tribu nal erred in allowing the revision application. [865H; 866A] (iii) The finding of the Labour Appellate TribunaL that the enquiry is not proper is based on no evidence. The finding is perverse. [867B] (iv) The finding that the enquiry has not been properly held is also perverse. [886G]
6474: The appellant, a resident of the Eastern India, was born and brought up in the Indian Union. He was born and registered as a citizen of India on 1st January, 1950. In the year 1948 he made an announcement that it had been decided by the then British Government that the Province of Bengal and the West Bengal shall be partitioned. On 30th June, 1947, the Governor General made an announce mation that it had come into force with effect from 1st January 1949. On 30.6.1947, the Governor of West Bengal promulgated an Ordinance called the West Bengal Nationalisation of Land and Building Ordinance, which was later replaced by the West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955 (West Bengal Act No. VI of 1956). By section 3(1) of the said Ordinance, the Governor 's intention to establish new States was expressed by the words "in the Western India to Pakistan" which meant that the territory of India originally comprised in the East Bengal State but now forming part of the State of West Bengal. The West Bengal Nationalization of Land and Bigha has been defined in section 2(2) of the Ordinance as "the territories specified in the Schedule to this Act". The appellant challenged the constitutional validity of the said ordinance and the Ordinance on the ground that it violated his fundamental rights under articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Ordinance did not infringe any of the fundamental rights of the appellant. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned ordinance and the subsequent action taken thereunder were ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature and that the impugned Act was beyond the legislative competence of the State legislature. It was further contended that the impugned Ordinance and the subsequent proceedings taken thereunder were invalid because they contravened the provisions of article 31(2) Of the Constitution. It was also contended that the Act was void being violative of article 13(3)(a) of the Constitution inasmuch as it was inconsistent with the provisions of Part III of the Constitution and was therefore void. The contention of the respondent was that the impugned legislation was not one to which article 31(4) applied and that the Act violated the guarantee given to the citizens under articles 14
3303: The appellant was the owner of certain lands in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the ceiling on land ownership under section 2(2) of the U.P. Act No. 1 of 1952, which provided that "the ceiling shall be computed (a) in the case of a land owner who held or had held land as tenant, at the rate of 10% of his 'sarrender value" and (b) in any other case, at the prescribed percentage of the 'rate of land revenue '. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the land inherited by the appellant and later transferred to his sons and wife were not hit by section 10A of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the land owned by the appellant was not liable to ceiling; that the land was inherited by him and later transferred by him to his sons, and that the provisions of section 10A did not apply to him because he was not an agriculturist. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Act is a social welfare legislation intended to protect the interests of tenants and agricultural labourers. The Act has been enacted for the purpose of providing for the acquisition of land in excess of the ceiling area and for matters connected therewith. [631F] (ii) Section 2(4) of the Act provides that the ceiling on the area of land owned by a person is to be computed in accordance with the following sub sections. Sub section (5) provides that where a person holds land as a tenant, he shall be deemed to have purchased such land if such land is situated in more than one patwar circle. [632B C] (iii) The Act does not provide for the determination of the ceiling on holding of land by a person as a tenant. The Act only prescribes the procedure for determining the ceiling area. The Act does nothing more than prescribe the manner of computation of the ceiling. [630C E] (iv) The Act contemplates that the surplus area should be determined after making such enquiries as may be necessary and after hearing objections from the persons interested. The Act also requires the Collector to make a report to the Government stating therein the total extent of land which each
3630: The appellants are dealers in hides and skins. They purchased raw hides and tanned skins locally as well as in the course of inter State trade and commerce. The matter relating to the assessment year 1968 69 was referred to the Sales Tax Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the purchase price of raw hides or skins was not exigible to tax under the State Act. The appellants challenged the validity of items 7(a) and 7(b) of the Second Schedule to the State Act before the High Court which upheld the validity of item 7(a). The appellants contended that the item did not cover the purchase price at the point of 3 last chase in the State. The appellants contended (i) that the item could not be said to fall within Entry 7(a), (b) and (c) because there was no levy of tax under the state law, (ii) that the rate of tax on purchase of raw hide and skins was higher than the rate of purchase of raw skins; and (iii) that the sales tax authorities were not justified in imposing sales tax on the sale price of raw skulls. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The sales tax authorities had the power to assess the dealer for the purpose of levying tax on the purchase value of raw hood and skins purchased by him. [764 C] (2) The rate of tax is fixed on the sale of raw materials used in the manufacture of goods. The rate of sales tax is also on the sale proceeds of the raw materials used. [765 D E] (3) The rate has been fixed on the basis of the sales tax levied on the sale value of the raw material. [766 F G]
6931: The State Government published a draft scheme under section 68 C of the approved a draft scheme. The respondents filed a writ petition challenging the self same scheme contending that the non exemption of the routes i.e. The High Court upheld the contention and held that their exclusion is discriminatory. The Govt. was directed to consider their case and to pass appropriate orders to accord exemption from the scheme. In pursuance of the direction, the State Government considered the matter and passed an order holding that the exclusion is discriminatory and directed the grant of permits to the private operators. The appellants challenged the order of the Govt. in this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The scheme which was framed on the basis of the directions issued by the State Government was not open to any objection or representation at all. It was open to the State to frame a scheme for an area or route or part thereof and necessarily has the effect of excluding the existing or potential private operators from the field to render transport service in that partially prohibited area etc. while retaining similar private operators in other areas, route or partthereof. [864F G] 1.2 The scheme having been framed in exercise of the power under sub section 2 of section 68D of the approved the State Government had no authority to exclude the existing or frozen stage carriage services altogether. The exclusion completely or partially is permissible under the statute itself and is writ large. [865H; 866A] 1.3 The exclusion is permissible under section 68C of the Act. The exclusion is effective and operative from the date it is brought into force. The exclusion cannot be made applicable to the existing operators. The exclusion does not apply to existing operators. [867B] 1.4 The exclusion is not arbitrary but is based on a rational differentia having a rational relationship with the object of the legislation. The exclusion must be reasonable and should not be arbitrary. [868G] 2. The exclusion consists of two steps viz., (i) the existing permit holder may ply his vehicle on one part of the route and (ii) the like introduction of the new route will bring about the exclusion of the existing permit holders on both sides of the route. The exclusion operates only during the
3971: The appellants were importers of certain goods. They had imported some goods from abroad and paid the customs duty on the basis that they were their own goods. The Customs authorities, however, rejected the bills of lading and other documents of title on the ground that the amended sections 14 and 15 of the , applied to them as the rate of duty was not the same as that applicable to the goods in question. The appellants filed applications for refund of the amount paid by them under protest. The Central Government dismissed the applications. In appeals to this Court it was contended that (i) the amendment did not apply to cases where the goods were removed from the warehouse after July 7, 1966, but only where the bill of entry had been presented before that date; (ii) the amendment applied only to cases where a bill of entry has been presented before the date of removal of goods from the warehouse; and (iii) the amendment made applicable only to cases which were cleared from the warehouse when the bill of lading was presented. HELD: (i) The amendment applied only where the Bill of Entry is presented before the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed for the presentation of the bill of Entry. [864 E] (ii)The amendment applied only if there is no bill of entry or if there are no documents evidencing the payment of duty. It does not apply to a case where the bill is presented before that day. [865 F G] (iii)In the present case, the amendment applied not only to cases in which the bill of entries had already been presented before 7th July, 1966 but also to cases where such a bill of entries was presented before that time. [866 A B] (iv)It is not correct to say that the amendment applies only to cases arising out of a bill of Entry which is presented before 7.7.1966. [867 D]
555: The appellant was a Civil and Additional District and Sessions Judge in the former State of Bikaner. He was transferred to Ganganagar on July 31, 1950. On December 9, 1949, he received an order from the new Rajasthan Government that his increment became due and payable on April 23, 1950. He made a representation to the Government of Rajasthan against this order but it was rejected. He then filed a writ petition for mandamus under article 226 of the Constitution praying for a direction that his pay should be fixed at a stage equal to the existing salary of a Civil and Extra Assistant Commissioner. The High Court held that the post of Civil and Extra assistant commissioner fell within the purview of article 81(1) of the Covenant and therefore the appellant could not claim the benefit of article 81 (3). Held, that the order of transfer did not amount to a reduction in rank nor did it affect the appellant 's right to continue as Civil and Extra officerage officers until they were duly appointed to the judicial service of the new State of Rajasthan. The order of transfer merely required the appellant to perform certain duties which he must do till he is confirmed as Civil and extra assistant commissioner. The appellant had no right to the post of civil and additional assistant commissioner.

He tendered his resignation on 21.1.1986 and joined the service of the Bank on 7.2.86. On 7.2, 1986 he received a letter from the bank informing him that his resignation had been accepted with immediate effect by the competent au thority with immediate effect. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the purported acceptance of his resignation and for a direction to the bank to treat him as in service of the appellant. A Single Judge of the High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent 's resignation could not be treated as effective only on the 30th June, 1986 when it was accepted by the competent authori ty. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal preferred by the bank. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The regulation 20 provides for a notice to the employer only in order to protect the employ ee. It does not provide that the resignation would have become effective only on 30. 615 June, 1986. The respondent having accepted the resignation w.e.f. 7.2., 1986, he became entitled to all benefits while being in service. [616F G] 2. The respondent wrote a letter to the bank by which he purported to withdraw the resignation letter dated 21st January, 1986. In the letter he purported to give up his claim to pension. The bank did not take any action against him till he sent a reply to the letter. The respondent was not justified in withdrawing the resignation letter at the instance of the bank. [617B C] 3. The respondent is not entitled to the benefit of Regulation 20 because he has resigned from the service of bank on 7. 2. 1986. The resignation cannot be said to have become effective merely on the expiry of three months from the date of its acceptance by the competent autho rity. The respondent 's letter of resignation was accepted by competent authority on 7.8.85. The respondent never intended to resign from the service. He was, therefore
4879: The appellants were teachers in the service of the State of Punjab. They claimed revised scales of pay on the ground that they had taken graduate degrees and, therefore, were entitled to the benefit of grade provided they have 1st and 2nd Division Master 's Degree. The circular letter dated July 29, 1967 was issued by the Government of India providing for a revised scale of pay for teachers in Government schools with effect from November 1, 1966. Paragraph 3 of the Circular letter stated that "the number of posts in Lecturer 's grade will be i.e. 742 posts for the existing school Lecturers and 2nd division master 's Degree". The appellants challenged the validity of the said paragraph as violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court upheld the validity of paragraph 3 of the circular letter holding that it was applicable only to teachers in Government Schools and not to teachers working in private institutions. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The case is covered by the judgment of this Court in Kirpal Singh Bhatia vs Union of India [1975] Supp. S.C.R. 634. [741F] (2) The State Government has no authority or power to make any order which would entitle the teachers to the benefit or revision of pay scales on the ground of their having acquired higher qualifications in the course of their service. [740A B] (3) The circular letter of the Government of Indian Ministry of Education and Culture dated February 19, 1979 does not offend Article 14 of the Constitution and is not ultra vires the Constitution. [739B]
3182: The respondent landlord let out the premises in dispute to the appellant on a rent of Rs. 125/ per month. On 1 9 1962 the respondent applied under section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 for evicting the appellant on the ground that she was a woman and that she was charging a fabulous amount as rent from her sub tenant Sohan Singh. The Rent Controller held that the appellant was the legally wedded wife of Sohan Singh and that she had been receiving the rent as sub tenant from her sub tenants. The Rent Control Tribunal confirmed this finding. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that two substantial questions of law were involved in the appeal one relating to the status of the appellant as wife and the other whether on the facts found the ground of sub letting had been established. It was further submitted that the High Court erred in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) The High Court has dealt with the case as if this is a matrimonial proceeding in which the status of appellant as wife was under direct challenge. And that was what the High Court meant by saying that even if it be assumed that the appellant being the wife of Sohail Mollah was the wife of the respondent, she, who was entitled to possession of the shop premises as a tenant, must be presumed to have sub let the same to Sohan Singh to carry on his business, In the present case, the High Court was of the view that even if the appellant was wife of Sohhail Mondal, she, having been receiving the rents as sub tenant, must he presumed to have so received the rent as a tenant. [526 F] (ii) The High court was right in holding that even if there was no question of law, much less substantial question of law or fact, the High court was in error in interfering with such finding. [527 B C]
5094: The appellant assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax as a registered firm. In the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1966 67, it claimed that the amount of Rs.1,85,043 and Rs.1.82,742 received by him from his father in his individual capacity should be deducted towards the assets of the joint family. The Wealth Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the said amount had not been received by the assessee as his personal property. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that under the Hindu Law when a son inherited separate and self acquired property of his father, it assumed the character of joint Hindu Family property in his hands qua the members of his own family. It therefore held that the sum of Rs. 1,85,034 received by the appellant as his personal income was not liable to be deducted as his personal asset. The High Court also held that under section 8 of the , the income from assets inherited by a son from his father from whom he had separated by partition could not be deductible in computing the business profits of the assessee 's joint Hindu family. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, the Court ^ HELD: 1. Under the Hindu Law whenever a son inherits separate and selfacquired property of his parents, it assumption is that it will devolve first upon the heirs being relatives specified in class I of the Schedule. [262G H] 2.1 When a son inheritable separate and self acquire property of his parent, it assumption has to be made in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The scheme of the Act is that the income from the assets inherited from the father by the father by way of self acquired property must be taken to have been received by him as his personal capital. But the fact that the income is received by the father as his personal revenue does not make any difference. The income from the asset inherited by the father from which he had separated cannot be said to be the income of the joint Hindu family because the definition of "accrue" in section 2(4) of the Act includes an "income" which may have accrued or arisen to the person receiving
2567: The appellant company was in financial difficulties in 1954 and was unable to meet its obligations. The Government of U.P. sanctioned the proposal submitted by the Collector, Deoria, to sell the holdings and the property for realising Rs. 8,38,176 13 0. The sale proclamation was issued on October 4, 1955, for recovery of the total amount due. The Company moved an application before the Commissioner under r. 285 1 of the U.P Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1951, praying that the sale be set aside. The Commissioner rejected the application. On appeal the High Court held that the sale was not vitiated by any irregularity or mistake in publishing or conducting the sale. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 2861(2) of the U P. Zamindari Abolition and land Reforms Act provides that all arrears of land revenue cannot be recovered by any process other than the processes mentioned therein. The words "any" in the section are wide enough to include all proceedings which may be taken for realising arrears of land Revenue. [470 D] (ii) The word "recovery" in section 2861(1) means the realisation of land revenue as a tax. The word "tax" is used in the widest possible terms according to its natural meaning. It does not mean a tax levied with retrospective effect. The word 'revenue ' has been defined in the General Clauses Act to mean revenue derived or derivable from any tax imposed by the appropriate authority. The word is used in a wider sense to include all steps, costs and expenses incurred or actually incurred in the execution of the duties of a tax including all payments made in connection therewith. The word has been used in the narrow sense of receiving money by deposit of money, though it does not mean money actually received. [471 E F; 472 A B] (iii) The word 'income ' in section 28 61(2) means income accruing or arising in favour of a person. The word must receive a liberal construction so as to advance the object of the Act. [473 C]
5438: The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant tenant on the ground of sub tenancy. The Trial Court passed a decree for eviction and the same was confirmed by the High Court in appeal. In the Second Appeal, the High Court held that the present petitioner was not a sub tenant but he was bound by the decree passed against him because in the suit he was not a party. Hence this revision petition. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the present Petitioner was not a tenant and as such he was bound under the decree passed by the Trial Court. [904C] 2. Section 2(4) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 is an agreement for management of business of the tenant. There was no parting of possession of the premises. The landlord had knowledge of the document and as such could not be said to have consented to the bargain. [905D] 3. The High court was right in coming to the conclusion that there was no consent of the landlord to the bargains. [906A] 4. The High COurt has rightly held that the respondent landlord had consented to sub tenancy. [907B] 5. The High Courts judgment is set aside and the order of eviction passed against the respondent landlord is restored. [908G]
6267: The appellant landlord filed an application under section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 for the eviction of the tenant/respondent on the ground that he required the suit premises bona fide for his personal occupation. The Rent Controller dismissed the application holding that the permission granted by the Rent Controller under section 21 was invalid so that the tenant could not be evicted on expiry of three years from the date of the permission. The appeal preferred against the order was dismissed by the Rent Control Tribunal and the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the scope of the enquiry contemplated under section 21 is limited only to examining the existence of jurisdictional facts which permit grant of permission to create tenancy for limited period of 3 years. On behalf of the respondent it was urged that the scope is limited only when the tenant is in possession of the remaining building which comprises of sufficient accommodation to meet the bona fide need of the landlord 's family; and that the premises were constructed in 1972 and the second floor of the building was never occupied by the landlord being let out to other tenants from time to time. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The scope of the inquiry contemplated under section 2(g) of the Act is restricted to examining only the existence of the jurisdictional facts which permits grant of permission for creation of a tenancy for limited periods of 3 years and no more. [439C] 1.2 The scope of enquiry under section 21 has been narrowed down by the Supreme Court in the case of M.A. Khader vs B.R. Naidu & Ors., ; In the instant case, the landlord 'S son of the tenant was aged only about 19 or 20 years on the date of filing of the application for eviction. He had already retired from service. His wife is also a member of the family. The landlord 's further appeal to the Rent Control Tribu nal and then to the Delhi High Court failed. The landlord is in possession and the tenant is a major son of the landlord. The landlord has two sons who are aged only about 20 or 20 years. The landlord does not require the suit premises for a limited period of three years. The requirement of the landlord is bona fide. [440E F] 1
6924: The respondent was manufacturing and selling industrial alcohol under a licence granted by the District Magistrate, Banaskantha. On an application made by the respondent, the State Government directed that the manufacture, import export, transport, storage, sale, purchase use, collection or cultivation of any intoxitant, denatured spirituous preparation, hemp, Mowra flowers or molasses shall be under the supervision of the Prohibition and Excise or Police Staff as it may deem proper to appoint, and that the cost of such staff shall be paid to the State Government by the person manufacturing, importing, exporting, transporting, storing, selling, purchasing, using collecting or cultivating the intoxicant, denatured spiritous preparations hemp, hemp Mowra Flower or molasses. The respondent challenged the levy of excise duty on the ground that the levy was not authorised by law. The High Court held that since the entire judgment of the High Court proceeded on privilege theory it could not be said that the levy which was really a fee did not fall within Entry 51 or Entry 33 of the concurrent list. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the levy being in the nature of excise duty it was not covered by Entry 33 of List II of VIIth Schedule. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power to levy tax or duty on industrial alcohol is distinct from the power to levy fees. There are two different situations in which a fee can be levied. The first is provided for control of production, supply and distribution of an essential commodity like intoxicating liquor etc. [857F G] Synthetics & Chemicals Ltd. & Ors. vs State of U.P. & Ors., ; , referred to. 2.1 The second is provided for regulation of the manufacture, possession, transport, purchase and sale of an essential article like intoxicating liquor, etc. [ 858A B] Syn thetics & Chemicals 's case followed. Synthetic & Chemical 's case dealt with the issue whether excise duty was payable at a particular point of time when the distillery was situated. The question was one of construction of a statute. [859C D] Syncore (J) case considered.
2993: The appellant company was incorporated on October 11, 1941. It carried on the business of banking and had investments in shares and securities. In 1956, the said managing agency was renewed for a period of five years in view of the provisions of the . The Income tax Officer found that as during the year 1941, the said Managing Agency constituted a capital asset and the assessee company was entitled to the benefit of section 23 A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. On appeal by the assessee company, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that as the assessee company did not carry on any business or operation in the nature of banking business, it must be considered an "investment company" an expression not found in the Act. The Tribunal referred two questions to the High Court which were answered against the assessee company. The High Court answered both the questions in the negative and in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court erred in holding that the assessee company is an "insurer" within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Act. [650 D] (ii) The definition of "income" in section 2(4A) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 includes interest paid by a company on moneys borrowed from the Government or the Reserve Bank of India or any other bank. The definition of income under section 2(7) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 does not include interest paid by an assessee on moneys borrowed for the purpose of carrying on his business. [649 C E] (iii) The assessee company was not an "Investment Company" within the first part of the second Explanation to section 23A of the Income tax Act. The assessee company could not be regarded as an "insurers" within the second part of the said Explanation. [648 F G]
4400: The appellant, a registered dealer under the Gujarat Sales Tax Act, 1969 was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling electricity. In May, 1970 he purchased raw materials from a Registered dealer who in turn sold them to a licensed dealer who used to purchase raw materials for the manufacture of taxable goods which would be sold by him in the State of Gujarat. He also obtained a certificate in Form No. 19 as provided under section 13(1)(B) of the Act read with Rule 24(4) of the Gujarat Sales tax Rules, 1970 stating that the raw materials purchased against declaration in Form No 19 were sold to Gujarat State Electricity Board against declarations in Form prescribed in Entry 5 of the Government Notification issued under section 49 of the Gujarat sales tax Act, 1969. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid notification and rule 24(4), inter alia, contending that the said notification and rule was ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not liable to pay purchase tax on the ground that certain electric goods manufactured out of raw materials etc. purchased against declaration made in Form No: 19 were sold contrary to the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The appellant is not entitled to claim exemption from payment of purchase tax on goods purchased by him. [864F] 2.1 The scheme of the Gujarat Act shows that the Act contemplates the levy of general sales tax on goods which are not included in Schedule I at least once inside the State in the series of sales and purchases even though they may have been converted into manufactured goods and that is why Form No.19 requires the purchaser to state that the goods will be used by him as raw or processing materials or as stores in the manufacture of tax free goods. [865G H; 866A] 3. Section 16 of the Act provides that every dealer shall furnish a return in such form containing such particulars as may be prescribed showing his turnover during the year to the assessing authority in such manner and within such time as may be specified. The appellant was carrying on the business of manufacturing electricity. He was assessed to purchase tax under section 16
4960: The respondent was a sub tenant of the appellant firm. He had been inducted as a sub tenant by the appellant in the suit shed on a monthly rent of Rs. 500. The appellant terminated the licence and filed a suit for mandatory injunction directing him to vacate the premises. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal and decreed the suit. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended that the respondent became a licensee of the appellant after the expiry of the period he terminated the licence, filed the suit for mandatory injuction. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent had become a licensee of a different kind from the appellant firm, the appellant could not be denied relief merely because he had parted with possession of the property to the respondent. [183F] 1.2 The respondent had purchased the entire property including the suit shed from its original owner by that sale deed. Even if there was some delay, the appellant should not be driven to file another round of suit with all the attendant delay, trouble and expense. [184B C] 1.3 The respondent had acquired title to the property under the lease by the original owner. The appellant had no right to evict the respondent. The respondent had already obtained a decree against the appellant for the eviction of the appellant. The respondent has not suffered any damages or mesne profits. [185D E] 1.4 The respondent had sold the entire property to the appellant by a registered sale deed dated 27th August, 1979. The appellant was only one of its partners. The respondent was only one 'of its partners. Therefore, the respondent was not entitled to recover possession of the suit shed. [186E F] 2. The respondent is entitled to protection under section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act. [187H] 3. The respondent cannot be denied the benefit of section 116 of Indian Evidence Act on the ground that he had parrotly executed the sale deed. The respondent 's case must fail. [188A B]
1255: The appellant was the owner of a forest in Bihar. He had granted the right to cut and remove bamboos and certain other timber to be found in a specified area of the forest village. The forest authorities took proceedings under section 15 of the Bihar Private Forests Act, 1946, for the restoration of possession of the forest to the appellant. The appellant contended that the notification issued by the Governor under section 14 and the other provisions of Chapter III of the Act were invalid as they contravened articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution. Held, that the notification dated March 30, 1949, issued under section 14 of the Bihar and Orissa Public Forests (Validation) Act, 1948, which came into force on April 1, 1950, could not be challenged as invalid on the ground that it was issued under section 2 of the Bihar Act 12 of 1949. The notification did not purport to be under section 14 or any other section of the Act. It merely purported to be under sections 3 and 4 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, and was therefore valid. The notification was not one made under section 14 but one under section 3 of the Act, and the notification was not a valid one.
5139: The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1960 and had two textile mills, namely, the Textile Mills (Taking over of Management) Act, 1972 and the Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1974. The textile mills were taken over by the Government under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Special Provisions) Act, 1976 on the appointed day. The management of the two mills was taken over by a Court under the provisions of the Act. The appellant challenged the taking over of the management by the Court before the High Court which held that the mills were not sick textile undertakings. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the mills did not fall within the definition of "sick textile undertaking" as defined in section 2(d) of the Act and therefore the take over could not be taken over. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The textile mill was taken over under the SICA on the appointed date. The Court found that the mills had been closed for a period of more than three months immediately before the appointed day and the closure of which was prejudicial to the textile industry. The Court also found that the management of the mills had remained closed for a long time. [942F] 2. The textile industry was taken over on the appointed. The Court held that the textile mills were not entitled to any compensation. [943C] 3. The textile undertaking was taken over only in the year 1977. The Court further found that the workers were paid their dues by the Company. [941D] 4. The textile units were taken over on April 1, 1977. The Company was directed to pay the arrears of wages to the workers. [940E] 5. The workers were entitled to receive from the Company. The workers would be entitled to receive the same amount of wages as they would have received if they had continued to work in the mills. [939B] 6. The workers shall be paid their full wages except where there is no other legal obligation to do so. [944C]
5268: The respondent was appointed as a temporary officer in the Force on 20.6.1976 and was confirmed with effect from 1.7.1977. On 20.9.1985 he was allowed to continue in the promotional post till he attained the age of superannuation. The Division bench also upheld the direction and dismissed the appeal. 383 In the appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellants, it was contended that since the respondent has been given a regular appointment in the Force w.e.f. the date the amended rule came into force, he is entitled to count his service from the date he joined the Force and he is entitled for all benefits including pensionary benefits. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent was entitled to absorption in the Forces. [388H] 1.2 The respondent was not eligible to claim absorption as he did not complete three years ' continuous service. The amendment of the rules was necessitated because of the fact that the respondent had put in more than 20 y
6438: The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) and 3(1) (iii) of the COFEPOSA Act, 1974. He was informed that if he desires to make a representation to the Advisory Board, he may address it to the Chairman, Advisory Board and that he could also make a representation addressed to the detaining authority or the Central Government. The grounds of detention were served on him on 24th September, 1988. On 21st May, 1988 the Customs Officials searched the appellant 's person and recovered certain gold ingots from his possession. The appellant made a representation dated 27th September,1988 to the detaining author ity, Home Secretary to Government of Kerala being satisfied that there was sufficient cause for the detention of the appellant. The representation was rejected by the State Government on 1st October, 1988 and the Central Government rejected the same on 2nd November, 1988. In the grounds of detention it is stated that the Collector of Customs furnished proposals for the detention on 24th March, 1988 and detention order was passed on 21st May 1988 and the appellant was detained on 6th August, 1988. The appellant challenged the detention order in this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The right conferred on the detenu under clause (a) of sub section (2) of Section 9 of the Act is not an empty formality but an indelible precious right which can be availed of by a person who has been prevented from carrying out the provisions of the statute before he is actually detained. [813E F] 1.2 The right provided under clause (b) of sub sec. (2) is of vital importance because it is necessary to curb malpractices and provide a deterrent against those guilty whom the law provides. It is imperative to ensure that the safeguards provided under clauses (4), (5) and (6) are observed in their proper form. Any unexplained delay in this regard will be a breach of law and therefore, violative of clause (4). Therefore, the continued deten tion must be held to have been vitiated as the requisite period of time for complying with the requirements of clause (7) of Article 22 of the Constitution had expired. [811H; 812A B
4364: The appellant company terminated the services of the respondents workmen in pursuance of a notice of termination. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the termination order on the ground that the termination was illegal as it was not retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(OO) of the . The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : Dismissing the appeal: (i) The expression 'retrenchment ' is used in the sense in which a contract of employment is understood by industrial adjudication in India and it has been construed in the narrow sense of conveying its meaning from the Latin maxim "Duith law Nemo" 989 by Crawford, Spooner, and Jones vs Ludh Budh Singh, [1940] F.C.R. 110. The expression 'turn over ' means the total length of service put in by the workman during the last 12 years. It does not mean the actual date of termination of service. It means the date of termination or the actual date when the workman reaches the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf. [890 G H; 891 A B] Hariprasad Shivshankar Shukla vs A. In order to provide for the situations which the Supreme Court held are not covered by the definition of ' retrenched employee ' in section 2(0OO) Of the , the Parliament added section 25F providing for the payment of compensation to the workmen in case of transfer of undertakings and in case of closure of undertakings respectively. The said provision is in pari materia with section 2(oo)(bb) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The expression "control", therefore, includes both administrative and supervisory control. [881 D E] Hariprakash Narain Srivastava vs U.P. State Road Transport Corporation, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C. R. 548, followed.
159: The appellants were convicted by the Sub Divisional Magistrate under sections 297 and 500 Indian Penal Code. The High Court set aside their convictions and sentences on the ground that they had not been given a proper notice of their intention to file a complaint under section 190, Criminal Procedure Code, and that they had been deprived of an opportunity to meet them at the time of the alleged commission of the offence. Held, that the High Court was in error in holding that the offences charged were one under sections 296, 500, 501, 502, 506, 501 and 511 of the Indian Penal Code and that the magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offences under those sections. The offences mentioned in the complaint were punishable with imprisonment for 6 months or more and the magistrate had taken cognizance of them after giving the requisite notice under section 195(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The offence under section 500, I.P.C., is punishable with imprisonment of 2 years or more and not with imprisonment for 3 years. The offence of defamation is committed when it appears that the same has been voluntarily made in writing or by means of a document signed by the accused and which purports to be his handwritings and documents. It is not necessary that there should have been consent or connivance between the person complaining. The consent or connivance must be in discharge of the official duty. The offence committed by the accused must be within the cognizance of the court which can take cognizance.
2605: The appellant was a factory employing about 4,000 workmen. It had four different applications under section 33C(2) of the , before the Labour Court, Hubli. The second application (LCH) No. 101 of 1965 was filed by one workman alone on 19th April, 1965 claiming a sum of Rs. 8,910/72P in respect of his over time work and compensation for work done on weekly off days. The third application (LWA No. 101/1965 was filed by the workmen alone on 19.4.1965 claiming a sum o.f Rs. 8.910/70 P in respect of their over time work, compensation for work of done on weekly of off days. All these applications were consolidated and heard together. The Labour Court held that all the workmen were entitled to overtime work as claimed by them and directed payment of the amounts found due. The appellant challenged the decision of the Labour Court by four writ petitions under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed all the writ petitions. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the jurisdiction of the Labour court under the general law was barred by the fact that the same relief could have been claimed by the workmen by filing applications under section 20(1) of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. Section 20(1), which is a self contained provision made for relief in such cases, provides that no claim for wages or salary or allowances shall be entertained except with the previous sanction of the appropriate Government. [864F] 2. Section 20 (1) of Act 14 of 1947 is not intended to exclude the operation of any other statute. The scheme of the Act shows that the legislature has taken care to make special provisions for certain categories of workmen who may be entitled to overtime payment at the rate specified in the Schedule. The object of the Act is to provide for a speedy remedy to those employees who are entitled to overtime payments at the rates specified in the schedule. The Act does not contemplate the grant of any exemption from the operation of the Act, but only provides for a summary procedure for the determination of the amount of wages payable to the employees. [865H; 866A B]
5889: The appellant was granted permission for starting B.Ed. (Bio) Course in the first respondent University. The Government granted permission to various private bodies and individuals for starting Botany, Zoology, Persian, Zoologen, Politics etc., but did not issue any notification in two dailies with wide circulation in the State of Andhra Pradesh. In the beginning of September 1984, the Government headed by the Director of School Education issued notifications in two daiies having wide circulation in Andhra Pradesh. The appellant challenged the cancellation of its approval on the ground that it contravened the conditions of grant of permission. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the parties did not comply with the conditions of the grant of permission; all those writ petitions were disposed of by common order dated March 7, 1986. The High court held that the cancellation was as arbitrary as the grant of ' permission '; the appellant had no power to cancel the permission already granted; the appellant could only apply for affiliation after complying with the conditions prescribed by the Government; the appellant was entitled to continue the college; the appellant should have been given an opportunity to make a representation against the cancellation; the Government was competent to cancel the approval; the appellant 's college was running without recognition from the Central Government; the Government had no power under the Act to grant permission; the Government itself had granted permission to the appellant; the Government could not delegate the power to the University; the Government being the creature of the statute, it could not delegate it. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant was not entitled to run the college. [895F] 2.1 The appellant was entitled for affiliation. The appellant has failed to establish that the conditions of granting permission are not complied with. [896G] 3.1 The Government is the final authority to decide whether or not the conditions are consistent with the provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The Government may reject the application for reasons to be recorded in writing. [897H] 3.2 The Government cannot delegate the power of granting affiliation to the University. The University can also withdraw the affiliation if the conditions are not fulfilled. [

In the present case, the appellant had two other assailants with him who were awarded life imprisonment. It is apparent that there was no motive for the appellant to kill the innocent child who died, a circumstance which has influenced the courts below in awarding the capital sentence. [714B C] 3. The fact that no opportunity was given under section 235(2) Cr. P.C. to adduce instead of going through the exercise of sending the case back to the trial court, the question of sentencing would not arise. [715E F] 4. 4605: The appellant, a double M.A., and holding a Doctorate in the subject applied for the post of Principal of Shrinath Intermediate College, Garhmalpur, Sahulie, Distt. Saharanpur. On April 27, 1981. He wrote to the Manager of the College requesting for an appointment order stating that the Committee of Management of the College vide its Resolution No. 3 dated April 19, 1981 appointed him as Principal on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay alongwith DA admissible under the rules. The appellant thereupon filed a Writ Petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Resolution No.3. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The selection committee constituted under section 17F of the Act has to make a selection in accordance with the procedure prescribed therein. [787G] 2.1 The power to appoint includes the power to suspend or dismiss the teacher. The power of termination of service by way of punishment carries with it the power to terminate such employment by paying one month ' salary in lieu of notice. The power under section 16 F (2) is intended to achieve that purpose. The power conferred upon the State Government under section 16 G (2) to terminate the service of the incumbent is not confined only to dismissal or removal from service but also to reduction in rank, which may be imposed on the incumbent after following the procedure laid down therein. [798B C; 788C E] 2.2 The word "removal" used in section 16 F of the Act must receive a liberal construction so as to advance the object of the Act and serve as a guidance for the exercise of the statutory

On that very day, the management sought approval from the Industrial Tribunal under section 33(2)(b) of the Act of the action taken and towards meeting the requirement of the provision paid to the workman before hand a sum of Rs.607.90 as wages for one month, before hand a certain amount as wages for the one month, Before the Industrial Tribunal the respondent raised an objection contending that the domestic enquiry held against him was illegal and invalid inasmuch as he was denied a reasonable opportunity to defend himself. 5478: The appellant was a Principal of an Intermediate College. She was suspended by the Vice Chancellor of the University on January 27, 1986 and after her dismissal from service, she filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of suspension as arbitrary and illegal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of dismissal passed against her was not sustainable because (i) the order of the Vice Chancellor suspending her was passed by the Vice Chairman of the Board of Management without there being any provision for appeal against such an order; (ii) the order was passed by a person who was not the Chairman of the Committee of Management but was acting as the Chairman of such Committee; (iii) the order dated March 7, 1987 was passed by an officer subordinate to the Vice Chancellor; (iv) the order passed by the Chairman of a committee of management was not competent authority to pass the same; (v) the order impugned was passed by one of the members of the Committee, who was not competent to pass the order of punishment; (vi) the order did not disclose any application of mind by the Vice-Chancellor; (vii) the order had been passed by the Manager of the institution without there being a proper enquiry held; (viii) the order also did not disclose whether any enquiry was held before passing the said order; and (ix) the order made by the Vice chancellor was mala fide. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order of the Chairman of an authority which is higher than the Vice Chancellor cannot be sustained. [363F] 1.2 The order of suspension passed by the Principal of an intermediate college was passed by him without there being anything to show that he was authorised by the Managing Committee to suspend the Principal. The order was passed in collusion with the Authorised Controller. The order of dismissal was passed by another person who was neither the Chairman nor the Vice Chancellor. [364A B] 1.3 An order of dismissal can be passed only when the power of review is expressly conferred on the authority. The order could be passed by the authority who is superior to the Vice Chairman. [365B C] 2. The order passed by a subordinate authority must be supported
2126: The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of certain properties. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the properties in suit were not public religious endowments as defined by section 2(12) of the Act, and therefore, did not constitute 'public religious endowment ' within the meaning of the Act. HELD: (i) The Commissioner had no power under section 6 of the Act to levy contribution on the properties in dispute. [439 E] (ii) The Commissioner could not assess any property in dispute or recover any contribution from the properties in question. 3656: The appellant was appointed as a teacher in the Municipal Corporation of Delhi. He was dismissed from service by the Deputy Commissioner (Education) on the ground that he had misbehaved with his son, and an enquiry was held against him under the rules. The Disciplinary Authority having accepted the report of the Enquiry Officer, the appellant filed a writ petition challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Disciplinary Authority had neither recorded its findings with respect to the charge drawn up against the appellant nor given its reasons for coming to such conclusion. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The order of dismissal passed against the appellant must be set aside. [813F] 2. The order is not only illegal but also mala fide. It is not necessary that every quasi judicial authority should record its reasons for its decision. [814A] 3. In the instant case, the order of the Disciplinary Authority does not indicate either the conclusions of the dismissing authority or the findings recorded by the enquiring officer. Nor has it indicated either the tentative view of the disciplinary authority or the finding recorded by the inquiring officer. The impugned order of the Appellate Authority and the order of 'the Tribunal are quashed. [815B C]
4018: The appellants were owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. They filed a suit for declaration that the notification under section 4 was illegal and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the respondents from proceeding with the acquisition of the lands in their possession. During the pendency of this suit, the then Government of Bombay after considering the report submitted under section 5A, made a declaration under section 6 as per the notification dated 14th August 1953 declaring that final plots 41, 43 were required for the purpose of State Transport. The respondents amended their plaint adding a relief for quashing the notification under sections 4 and 6. The trial court dismissed the suit but the first appellate court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the second appeal. In the special leave petition to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Government had no power to issue a notification under section 6; (ii) the Government could not issue a notification in respect of a final plot 41 which was sought to be acquired after the expiry of two years from the date of the notification; (iii) the Government acted mala fide in issuing the notification under s.6 without any authority or power in that behalf; (iv) the Government did not have power to issue the notification under 6; and (v) the Government 's action in issuing the impugned notification was arbitrary and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. HELD: (i) The Government had no authority to issue a Notification under section 6 after the expiry Of two years from 14th August, 1953. [168 E] (ii) The Government has power to issue notification under section 7 after the expiry or earlier publication of the notification under sub section (1) of section 4. The Government can issue a notification only after the expiry and before the publication of the same. The Government could not delegate its powers to issue such a notification. [169 F G] (iii) The Government could issue a notification after the expiry period of two years if it felt that there was sufficient reason for doing so. But the Government cannot delegate its power to issue notifications after the expiry. [167 H] (iv) The Government is entitled to issue a fresh notification after the lapse of two years when the Government considers that there is sufficient reason for issuing the notification

The Labour Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal holding that the dismissal of the respondents for misconduct was not justified. Held, that the word "retrenchment" in section 2 (oo) of 'the Industrial Disputes Act includes termination of service of all workmen by the employer and termination of service without any enquiry at all. The second meaning of the word is not restricted to cases where the employment of a temporary workman is terminated by way of penalty or he is removed from service after an inquiry. The word 'retrenchment ' in section 2A of the Industrial disputes Act means termination of service as a result of the determination of a contract of service and does not include termination of service simpliciter. The word .acquire ' in section 25

347: The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. He filed an application for revision in the High Court but it was dismissed. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain his revision application because the order of dismissal was not a "final order" within the meaning of section 439(6) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. If the accused had already unsuccessfully applied for revision against the order of the High Court, he would have been entitled to be heard in support of the plea of alibi. [1011 G H]

4656: The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death by the Sessions Court. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the circumstances that the appellant was previously convicted for murder and committed these murders were extremely heinous and inhuman, constitute a "special reason" for imposing the death sentence as required under Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973. It was further submitted that neither the circumstance that the appellant 's previous conviction for murder or even the possibility of his reformation was considered by the courts below nor any compelling reasons were recorded for awarding the death sentence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question whether the circumstances that have been enumerated in the judgment of this Court in Sunil Fuldrey vs State of West Bengal, [1979] 3 S.C.R. 935, are sufficient to justify the imposition of the death penalty must be answered in the negative. [367E F] 1.2 The fact that death sentence is provided in Section 302 of the Penal Code does not necessarily mean that death sentence should be imposed only when there has been an extreme cruelty or the like nature of the crime. [368A B] 2. The law regulates social interests, arbitrates conflicting claims and demands. Sunder Jew may pass wrong legal order and may have grave impact on social air but cannot do correct Canesque or stray episode can be bypassive and oppressive harsh treatment. That is why sentencing limitation has to be observed while considering the question of sentence. [369B C] 3. The law imposes an obligation on the court to impose the punishment of death penalty if the circumstances of the case and the evidence available are such which would answer the description of 'rarest of rare cases ' within the meaning of Section 354( 3) of the Criminal Procedure Code. The court must apply the same standard of proof and the law does not permit the court to do so in appreciating the evidence and coming to its own conclusion. [370D E] 4. The law prescribes the procedure for dealing with the question
2373: The respondent was a electricity company owning inter alia properties. On appeal by the respondent, the Judicial Magistrate fixed the valuation of the properties at Rs. 90,000/ . As a result of the High Court 's decision the valuation stood reduced to Rs. 90.000/ . In the appeals before this Court it was contended that the courts below had committed an error in relying upon the probable cost of constructing a new building of similar type in order to estimate the capital value as contemplated by Godhra Municipality and accordingly reduced the capital value fixed by the Sessions Judge to Rs.90,000/ which was not permissible under law. Dismissing the appeals, HELD : (i) The High Court has rightly held that the word "rate" used with respect to a tax is only for the purpose of estimating the annual letting value of lands and buildings and not for assessing the capital value of the lands. [485 B C] (ii) The High Courts have taken consistent view in interpreting the words "rates" or "grants", not defined in the Act, but having regard to the context in which they appear in the Act itself, they should be construed in a liberal way. The definition of "rent" given in section 3(1) of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act 1925 does not require any special meaning to be assigned to the expression "net annual value". It is intended to give a broad idea of the concept of "rent". The definition of 'rent ' is not exhaustive of all kinds of taxes; it can be made applicable to all types of taxes including taxes on land. [486 D E] (iii) The High court was right in holding that the word 'rate ' was not used in the sense of payment of rent and that the same rates were being levied on the net annual value of the land. [490 F G]

6452: The appellant was a candidate for the post of Principal in a college affiliated to the Uttar Pradesh University. She applied for the same and was selected by the Selection Committee constituted under Section 31(11) of the Uttar Pradesh State Universities Act, 1973. She did not satisfy the qualification of five years experience. The Management thereafter sought the approval of the University to appoint her as required under Section 31 (11) of that Act. The appellant challenged the decision of the University by way of a writ petition before the Lucknow Bench of the Allahabad High Court on the ground that the College being a minority institution any interference by the University under the Act is violative of Article 30(1) of the Constitution. The High Court rejected the challenge. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The requirement of five years ' experience in teaching is an integral part of the educational system. The requirement is relaxed in case of a Muslim minority institution which has been established and is being run in accordance with the provisions of the U.P. State Universities Act. [764F] 2. The appellant does not have the requisite qualifications. The college being a Muslim minority Institution prescribing five years experience is unjust to make her leave the post. Under the circumstances let the University reconsider the whole matter sympathetically. [765G] 3. In the view that we are taking it would be unjust to make the leave the post, the University shall grant the necessary approval to the appointment of the appellant as Principal of Karamat Husain Musiim Girls College, Lucknow with effect from the date she is holding the said post. [766A B]

940: The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1950 51 corresponding to the previous year 1949 50. The Income tax authorities sought to tax its profits and income for the assessment years 1950 51 corresponding lo the previous year, 1949 50. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the exemption stood good even after the amendment of 1953, when section 14(2)(c) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was in force, and that the fiction in the amended provision that the income tax was to be deemed to have been validly levied continued to exist until repealed by the Finance Act, 1950, which came into force on April 1, 1950. HELD:The appeal must be allowed. (i) Section 14(2) (c) of Indian Income tax is not retrospective in character; it only applies to cases where there has been no levy or collection of tax during the relevant period. [465 F] Kabra 's case, referred to. (ii)Section 14(2), as it stood before the amendment of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 provided that notwithstanding anything contained in any law, but subject to the provisions of sub sections (1) and (3) of section 4, all income, profits and gains shall be chargeable to income tax under the head "Income from other sources" and the expression "income from other sources", includes capital gains arising during certain periods. The fiction created by the amendment of section 14(1) of the Act is that the income, profits or gains shall be computed after deducting therefrom the allowances made for the expenditure on capital account. [466 B C] Kabrastanand Bhargava vs Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal, , applied.

Rule 25 (6) provides that the Committee shall prepare a list of all eligible candidates who are eligible for promotion to the Group 'D' category. Rule 25 provides that the Selection Committee shall consider the cases of candidates on merits and prepare a list if necessary for promotion to all other categories of posts in the State service as per the eligibility conditions laid down therein. Rule 25 C provides that the appointing authority may, at any time, either on his own motion or otherwise, after considering the proceedings of the Committee, if any, drawn up under sub rule(1) or (2), revise the list, pending amendment of the final select list. 4904: The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant tenant on the ground that he required the premises for his own use. The appellant contended that the proviso to section 14(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 was not applicable because the appellant had not given a notice to quit to the respondent landlord and therefore he was not entitled to invoke the provisions of section 15 (1) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree holding that though the first ejectment application was withdrawn by the respondents on the ground of default in payment of rent, no order for recovery of possession of the premises was made on the ground specified in clause (a) of the proviso to sub section (1)of section 14 of the Act, as such the appellant was not entitled under the proviso to subsection (2) of section 14 to apply for possession of the Premises on the ground mentioned in clause (b) of the said proviso. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The proviso to sub sections (1) and (2) is intended to protect the tenants from eviction except with the permission of the Controller. [395F] 2. In the first ejectment proceeding which was filed by the respondent landlord against the appellant, the latter had not obtained any benefit under that sub section. The proviso applies only where the tenant has committed default in the payment of rent for three consecutive months. There is nothing in the proviso to indicate that the benefit would accrue only if the default is condoned by reason of any default committed by the tenant. [394A B] 3. The proviso contemplates two situations where the tenant fails to make payment or deposit as required by section 15 (l) of the . [393C] 4. The proviso requires the Court to give an opportunity to the tenant to amend the plaint so as to enable him to seek relief which may be available to him on the ground contained in the proviso. The proviso does not contemplate that the Court should grant such relief to the tenant merely on the ground on which the tenant seeks to recover possession. [393E F] 5. The proviso cannot be construed as conferring a right upon the tenant to claim protection under section 15 ( l) of the Rent Act. [390B]
