2086: The appellant was the tenant of a non residential premises in Bangalore City. He had installed machinery in the premises and he had installed machinery therein. The landlord filed an application under section 8(3)(a)(ii) of the Mysore Urban Rent Control Act, 1976 for the eviction of the tenant on the ground that he required the premises for his own occupation. The Additional District Judge held that under section 8 (3)(a) (ii), the landlord was not entitled to possession of the premises in dispute unless and until he was prepared to vacate the shops in which he was trading at the time. The High Court set aside the order of the Additional District Judge and restored that of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the definition of the word "tenant" is wider than the ordinary meaning of the word and includes a person .continuing in possession after the termination of the tenancy in his favour. It was further submitted that the Act did not define the term "tenant" but only defined the rights of a tenant. HELD: Dismissing the appeal, (i) The definition of the expression "tenant" in section 2(1) of the Act is wide enough to include a person who is a tenant of residential buildings owned by him. [864 C] (ii)The definition of the term "landlord" in section 3(2) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act is wide as compared to the ordinary meaning Of the word "and" used in section 4 of the Act. [865 D E] (iii)Section 4 of the Karnataka Act deals with the right of tenant to deposit the rent in certain cases and time for deposit and exemption from payment of rent. Section 5 provides that where a landlord requires the premises in question for his own residence or for the occupation of a member of his family, he would be entitled to make an application before the authority prescribed under section 8. [866 F G]
3366: The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court, in appeal by the State, acquitted the appellants on the ground that the dying declarations made by the deceased were not corroborated by any independent evidence. In regard to the first two statements made by the accused, the High Court observed that the second statement was a dying declaration which could be used only for corroborating or contradicting other witnesses. In regard. to the third one, the High court held that it was unsafe to rely on the dying declarations since the prosecution had placed great reliance on them. In regard, to the fourth one, the Sessions Judge relied upon the dying declarations and convicted the appellants under section 302/34 I.P.C. and awarded each of them of the remaining three. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the oral statement which Bahadur Singh made cannot in the eye of law constitute a dying declaration because he did not give a full account of the incident or of the transaction which resulted in his death. It was further contended that the dying declaration was not voluntary and was not hit by section 32(1) of the Evidence Act. HELD: (i) The dying declarations are admissible under section 32(2) of the Indian Evidence Act. [766 F] (ii) The dying declaration is admissible in evidence. The question whether the dying declaration is voluntary or not depends on the circumstances of each case. If the court is satisfied about the truthfulness of the dying declaration, conviction can be based on such dying declaration. But if there is no corroboration of the dying declarations, the court may look for some evidence which would lend assurance to the dying declaration. [767 A B]
3199: The appellant was the owner of a consignment of goods. The goods were delivered to him on a certain date. The appellant filed a suit for the recovery of the value of the goods and claimed that they had been delivered in pursuance of the contract of bailment entered into by him with the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it and held that the appellant was not entitled to recover the value of goods as the respondent had no right to sue. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 87 of the , provides that if the cause of action arose wholly or in part within the jurisdiction of a court, the defendant is entitled to notice of action. [839 B] (ii)The rule is that when a man is sued in tort for the breach of some positive duty imposed upon him by an Act of Parliament, or for the omission to perform some such duty, either may be an act done or intended to be done under the authority of the Act, and if so done or intendedto be done under that authority, and if not done, the defendant, is entitled to a notice of action.[840 D E] (iii)Section 87 of the does not confer any right on the plaintiff to proceed against the defendant merely because he has instituted a civil proceeding for the alleged infringement of his right. It only gives a limited right to the defendant to show that the cause of actions did not survive against the defendant. [841 F G]
470: The appellants were the defendants in a suit for partition of joint family properties. They alleged that the marriage was performed on May 10, 1938, and that at the time of the marriage, a sum of Rs. 5,000 was paid to them by the father of the appellants as gifts of the houses. The further case of the appellants was that at the date of the marriage they made a "sankalpa" of the gift of the houses which was accepted by the father and the gift was later confirmed on the occasion of the Dwiragaman (Gowna) ceremony which took place in December, 1938, but the deed of gift was actually executed and registered on March 10, 1940 some two years after the marriage. The trial court held that the final settlement of the terms of marriage was not binding upon the parties and that the gift was not for any consideration and was not an act of profit making. On appeal the High Court affirmed the findings of the trial court. Held, that the final settlment of the marriage was not a condition precedent for its acceptance by the husband or his relations and the wife had no right to make a gift of the house to her. The mere fact that the husband had received a large sum of money as gifts from his wife would not necessarily show that he had acted mala fide in making the gift. The husband could not be said to have acted mala fide merely because he did not know that the wife was not prepared to go to the husband 's place where the husband was living.
256: The appellant and respondent No. 2 were candidates for election to the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly from a constituency in the State of Madhya Pradesh. Respondent No. 1, who was one of the contesting candidates, filed an election petition against the appellant and the other respondents under section 81 of the Representation of the People Act alleging that the appellant had committed corrupt practices within the meaning of section 123(7) of the Act and as such the election of the appellant was void. The appellant contended that the nomination of Vasant Rao was improperly accepted by the Returning Officer and the result declared on the 14th May, 1952, was not declared. The Tribunal held that the act of the Returning Officer in accepting the nomination of the appellant and/or the string of allegations made in it amounted to an improper acceptance of the nomination of respondent No. 1 and consequently declared the election void. On appeal the High Court held that the election of Vasantrao was materially affected by the improper acceptance of his nomination and set aside the election of respondent No 1. Held, that the election was not void but only voidable. The question whether the improper acceptance should be set aside or not is a matter which the Election Tribunal has to decide after considering all the evidence led before it. It cannot be said that the result of the election was materially affected thereby. The result of the elections must be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution and the Act. The Act does not provide for any further appeal and therefore the election of Vithu could not be set aside without giving the appellant an opportunity to contest the election. The Act provides for an appeal to the High Court against the decision of the Election Tribunal and the procedure to be followed by it in disposing of the appeal. The Act gives finality to the decision of Election Tribunal and lays down that all orders of the Tribunal shall be final and conclusive and subject to the provisions of section 100(1)(c), the order of the Tribunal is final and conclusive. The Act also provides for appeals to the High Courts and the Supreme Court and for special leave to appeal to this Court. The Act makes no provision for appeal to the Supreme Court against the decisions of the Election Tribunals. The Act is a self contained Code dealing with election disputes and the powers of the Supreme Court are limited to
826: The appellant, a textile mill and its factory were situate at Jalgaon. The respondent on behalf of the employees issued a notice to the appellant under section 42(2) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, demanding payment of reasonable bonus for the period from January 1, 1956 to December 31, 1955. Negotiations in this regard having failed, the respondent made a reference to the Industrial Court under section 73A of the said Act for arbitration of the dispute arising out of the said notice. The award was made by the arbitrator appointed by the Government under section 43A of the Act. The award provided that the amount of bonus payable shall be paid in lumpsum to all the workmen who had completed service for a particular year. The award also provided that the balance of the surplus shall be given to the workmen as rehabilitation grant and that the balance shall be utilised for rehabilitation purposes. The Industrial Court held that the reserves were used as working capital and that the reserves could not be used as working fund but only for depreciation. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the Industrial Court was right in holding that the reserves in question were not used as working funds but only for the purpose of rehabilitation and that they were so utilised and that it did not place any evidence before the Court to prove that the reserves had been used as working 'capital. The fact that the reserves are used as working assets does not make them part of the working capital of the company. The reserves may be utilised for the rehabilitation of the workmen or for the provision of additional machinery or plant which might have been acquired by the company but which would not have been available if they had been actually used for a bad purpose. The reserves can be utilised for depreciation and they should be utilised for meeting the liabilities of the company after deducting depreciation allowance.
888: The petitioner was the eldest son of one of his brothers. On July 5, 1943, the Ruler of Vadia State granted him in perpetuity a village Pithadia for enjoyment as 'Kapal Giras '. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the impugned order did not amount to a law providing for the extinguishment or modification of a right which accrued in favour of the petitioner before the date of the impugned order; (ii) the impugned act did not affect the right of the petitioner to the property which was his private property and (iii) the impugned Act did not provide for the extinguishing or modification of such a right. HELD: (i) The impugned act did neither infringe any of the fundamental rights of the petitioner nor did it abridge or take away any of his rights. (iii)The impugned Act did no more than to regulate the grant of jagirs to the members of the erstwhile rulers of former Indian States. The expression " Jagirdars" is used in the context of the personal privileges of the Ruler of an Indian State and in its legal sense, the Ruler has all the attributes of a sovereign sovereign. The Ruler of a merged territory is the holder of all the assets of the original grantee as also the income from
2685: The appellant, a partnership firm carrying on business in partnership at three places in Madhya Pradesh, in the name of the Jaora Slate Pencil Works and Bombay in the name and style of M/s. Pratap Singh and Preetam Singh carried on business in the name as M/s Jaora Slates. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant and the appellant 's brother for rendition of accounts of the deal. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to pass appropriate orders for protecting the subject matter of the suit was not excluded. HELD: (i) The Civil Court at Mandsaur was competent to entertain the application for appointment of receiver. The order of stay of the suit under section 34 of the was therefore effective only from the date of the filing of the application. [787 G] (ii) The Civil Courts have no jurisdiction to appoint a receiver. The Civil Courts are not courts of record or Additional District Judge. They have only the power to decide all questions arising out of the arbitration proceedings including the question whether the award is valid or opposed to justice. The Civil Court has no inherent powers apart from what is conferred by the Code of Civil Procedure. [788 A B]
53: The appellant brought a suit for possession of the ghatwali estate on the basis that the ghatwalis in suit were their joint family property and were im pendente ly possessed by them. It was alleged that the gattas were in the nature of joint family property, that they were separate from the rest of the g hatwals and were therefore governed by the Mitakshra School of Hindu law which admittedly governed the family of the parties. The defendant in her written statement denied this claim and contended that the ghtwas were not joint family property but were only joint family properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the ghosthas were joint family property. On appeal the High Court held that the gheewas being the exclusive property of the ghasthis, the rule of survival applicable to such ghatwales was also applicable to them. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the rule of espousal was applicable to the ghatwala charities as defined in section 2(1) of the , and that the rule was applicable to such charities. HELD: (i) The ghatwals in question were joint family properties and were therefore liable to be partitioned in equal shares. 176: The appellants were tried by the Sessions judge, Rewa for offences under section 120 B and 161 of the Indian Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act (II of 1947). The first appellant was sentenced to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000 under section 120B and the second appellant was sentenced under section 161 to two years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs, 1,000 each under section 161. The High Court confirmed the convictions and sentences but reduced the fine amount to Rs. 250. The appellants contended that the absence of a right of appeal may be a lacuna, but that inasmuch as it has not been expressly provided, it cannot be implied from the fact that a provision has been made for the exercise of powers by the appellate court. Held, that the absence or existence of a right in the accused to have his case considered in the light of the provisions of the Vindhya Pradesh Criminal Law Amendment Ordinance No. XLVIII of 1949 does not make any difference between the provisions of section 2 of the Vinding,ession of the Sessions Judge and those of section 3 of the Ordinance. The View taken by the High Court was correct and there was no reason to interfere with the same.
4581: The appellant, a registered dealer under the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947 (Orissa Act 24 of 1975) and the State Government in exercise of their powers under section 3(2)(c) of the Act levied additional tax on dealers who were not liable to pay sales tax as they had been selling goods in course of inter state trade or commerce. The appellant challenged before the High Court the levy of additional tax under the Orissa Additional Sales Tax Act. The High Court held that the levy was a single point levy and that it was not a single point excep tion but was a single unit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the levy of the additional tax was not a double taxation but was a multiple taxation and that the concept of multiple taxation being well known there could be no two taxable events in respect of same commodity. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The levy of additional sales tax is not a single tax but a multiple taxation. [850F] 2. The principal Act is a special Act which provides for the levy of a single point sales tax upon every sale or purchase of goods other than those declared under section 3 B of the Principal Act. [851G H; 852A] 3. Section 2(bb) defines 'turnover ' to mean the aggregate amount for which goods are sold either for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration. The definition of 'turn over ' is inclusive one. It includes the aggregate of the amounts of sale prices and tax. If any, received and receivable b, a dealer in respect of sale or supply of goods, classifying them into different categories, the aggregate of amounts of sale price and tax would be the aggregate of sales prices and tax would become due from the person making the transfer. [853C E] 4. The second proviso to section 2(bb), however, imposes an identical liability to pay tax irrespective of the gross turnover. The first Proviso does not impose an identical obligation or burden of discharging a burden of discharging the burden. [855B] 5
1614: The appellant was a cashier in the Municipal Board of Hardwar and had been working as such since 1932. He was prosecuted under section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for having committed an offence under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code and was convicted by the Special Judge. The conviction was upheld by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant had converted the money to his own use and had advanced the same to the officers and servants of the Board according to the practice prevalent for a number of years and that therefore he had converted the moneys which were not being deposited in the Bank or the treasury at Roorkee as required by rules. HELD : (i) The appellant was not guilty of any offence under section 5(2) of Act 1 of 1947. His case was covered by section 5(1)(c) of the Act. [94 E] (ii)The appellant could not be said to have converted the money so received by him into his own use. [95 A] (iii)It is not possible to accept the contention that the appellant was not concerned with the other accused who were charged with the offences alleged against them. It is clear from the evidence that the appellant himself was concerned with the money so advanced to the officers or servants of the board. [95 B] (iv)In view of the established facts that the appellant used the Board 's money in order to advance it to the officers, servants of the Municipal Board, the appellant cannot be said to convert the money so borrowed into his own money. 4503: The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death by the Sessions Court. He was also charged under section 201 of the Indian penal Code. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Sessions Judge erred in not recording a finding as to what he had to say on the question of sentence. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Sessions Court overlooked the provision contained in section 354(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 which provides in so far as is relevant that when the conviction is for an offence punishable with death, the judgment shall subject to the provisions of section 254 be recorded in the manner prescribed therein. [864F] 2. Section 354(3), Cr. P.C., 1973, makes it imperative that every such record must contain the grounds on which the opinion is based. [865A B] 3. The law requires that before recording a finding of guilt against the accused, the court must satisfy itself that there were "any" sufficient reasons for believing that the accused was guilty. [866B C] 4. The duty of the Public Prosecutor is to give the prosecution an opportunity to examine all witnesses who deposed to the commission of the crime. The examination of the witnesses would only lead to a quietus to the whole case. [867D E] 5. The law does not require that the Magistrate should record any particular number of witnesses at the police station. All admissible evidence is before the Judge but that evidence itself often gives a clue to the genesis of the crime and the motivation of the criminal. It is not necessary that the doctor who conducted the post mortem examination should have seen the injury or the cause of death. [868E F] 6. The High Courts are right in holding that the conviction of the appellant under section 302 IPC is not justified. [869H; 870A]

It was further contended that the rules have been made without any authority and are in gross violation thereof. The State Government contested the writ petition contending that the rules had been framed under Article 309 of the Constitution and the promotions were made strictly in accordance with the rules. It was also contended that the petitioners were not entitled to be considered for promotion as Executive Engineers since they did not come within the zone of consideration for promotion to the substantive vacancies in the category of Assistant Engineers. Allowing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The rules have been framed under article 309 of the Consti tution and the promotions effected thereunder are subject to the provisions of the Act and the Rules. The rules do not provide for any consultation with the Public Service Commission. The rules only lay down the procedure for selection by competitive examination and seniority. [378E] 1.2 In the absence of any statutory rule governing promotions, there cannot be any relaxation of the rules. The rules must be reasonable and fair so as to advance the object of the legislation. [379F] 2. The petitioners are not entitled to claim seniority over the direct recruits. [380B] 3. The petitioners were promoted as Executive Engineers by orders dated August 31, 1982 and August 8, 1984 respectively and they have been working continuously for more than 12 years without any break from the date of their actual appointment. The question of seniority does not arise as the petitioners have not been able to establish their claim to seniority. [385C D] 4. The petitioners have failed to make out a case of violation of any statutory provision or of the principles of natural justice. [387H; 388A] 5. 1769: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Sales Tax Laws Ordinance, 1949, and the notices issued to them under article 32 Of the Constitution. They contended that the impugned Act was a law relating to the imposition or collection of taxes on inter State sales effected by the respective Sales Tax Authorities in the country and as such fell within the purview of article 286(1)(a) of the Constitution and as such was not amenable to the jurisdiction of this Court under article 32 of the Constitution. Held, that the petitioners were not citizens of India within the meaning of article 19(1)(f) of the Constition and so they could not maintain the petition. 6677: The respondents were the principal debtors in a registered industrial concern. They filed a petition under Sections 31 and 32 of the Bombay City Civil Court for attachment and sale of their properties. The High Court passed an order on December 18, 1985 directing the respondents to deposit certain amounts with the Corporation within two months. On January 22, 1986, the respondents deposited certain amounts with them. The High court directed the Corporation to release the attached property to the respondents. The Corporation did not comply with the said orders. Thereafter, the respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the orders of attachment and sale. The High COurt dismissed the petition holding that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain it. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation: (1) that the High court had no jurisdiction since the respondents had already been served and they had appeared before the High court; (2) that the respondents could not be permitted to take advantage of its own wrong and seek to defeat the rights of the respondents; (3) that the provisions relating to enforcement of the liability of a surety were ultra vires Article 14 of the Constitution; (4) that the respondent could not be allowed to take advantage by paying the amount due from him to the Corporation; (5) that the Corporation was entitled to recover the amount from the respondents only as a liabil ity and not as a creditor; (6) that the proceedings against the respondents were barred by limitation; and (7) that the impugned orders were invalid because they were made without giving the respondents an opportunity of being heard. 2382: The appellant, a State Government employee, was appointed as a Medical Officer in the Andhra Pradesh State Government Medical College and Hospital on July 29, 1963. He was later promoted to the post of Assistant Professor in the Health Department on June 21, 1968. In the list of Scheduled Castes prepared by the Director of Medical Services, the appellant was shown at serial No. 1 in the order of priority with a view to selecting from that list those castes or communities which were "considered backward on account of the low standard of living, education, placement and upward revision". The appellant challenged the validity of the order dated July 29, 1966 passed by the State Government under article 16(4) of the Constitution on the ground that it violated his fundamental right guaranteed under article 15(1) of the constitution. The High Court held that the order was invalid because it contravened the provisions of article 16(2). On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of the State Government made on July 29. 1966 was not invalid for the reason that the order did not indicate that the Government had considered the social, educational and economic conditions of the backward classes mentioned in the list submitted to it by the Director. The order merely stated that the Government after considering the report of the Director formed the opinion that the backward classes should be taken into account in deciding the relative claims of various classes. It did not set out any reason why the order was bad. [599 F H] (ii) The order was not invalid because it did not specify the criteria on which the Government had applied its mind. The respondents cannot claim any better right than what is conferred on them by section 92 of Civil Procedure Code. [269D E] 2.3 The grant of leave without notice to the respondent does not amount to a valid institution of the suit. It is only a ministerial act which can be performed by the Court. [270E F] 3. 1567: The appellant was in occupation of the premises since prior to 1950. The Rent Controller struck out the defence of the appellant against eviction on the ground that he had failed to make the payment or deposit as required by the order dated April 2, 1960. Thereafter, the respondents made an application before the Rent Control Tribu nal for amendment of the plaint but the same was granted without permitting the amendment of the written statement. The appellant then filed a second appeal in the High Court which dismissed the same holding that the order striking out his defence was not a final order and it could be challenged in an appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the premises had been let out to the All India Postal & R.M.S. and (ii) the application for eviction was not maintainable because the appellant was only a licensee of the Union. HELD: Dismissing the appeal: (i) The order striking out the defence was not final and the appellant could not challenge it in an appeal against the order of the Rent Control Tnimber Tribunal. 1585: The appellant was the defendant in three suits filed by the respondent against the State of Madhya Pradesh. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in disallowing the cross objection of the State against the plaintiff 'S suit against the State because the plaintiff could not have filed a cross objection under Or. 41, r. 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The plaintiff did not file any cross objection under or. 41, R. 33 of the Code. The only remedy open to him was to file cross objections under Or.41, r. 33 of Or. 41. 3404: The appellant assessee M/s Kalyanji Mavji & Co. is a registered partnership firm dealing in various commercial activities. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. The Tribunal referred the following question to the High Court under section 66(1) of the Act: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in holding that the information of the Income tax Officer resulting in the notice under section 34(1)(b) of the Income 'tax Act, 1922 was not based on any fresh facts but was derived from the materials on the records of the original assessment ?" The High Court answered the reference against the assessee. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. [970 G] 2. The fact that the Income tax authorities had earlier disclosed before the Income tax authority that the income of the partner who had been admitted to the benefits of the partnership was not taxable in view of the fact that the income from the partnership was subsequently assessed to tax, would make no difference so long as the information was available with the Income tax department. [969 A B] 3. In the instant case, the information on which the Income Tax Officer sought to re opened the original assessment was based upon subsequent facts as would appear from the record of the original assessments. 3367: The appellant was a managing agent of a company in the taxable territories. Section 10(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922 states that the tax shall be C payable by an assessee under the head "profits and gains of business" or "profits & gains of profession". Sub section (5A) of section 10 of the Act provides that any compensation or other payment due to or received by, .any managing agent of an Indian company at or in connection with the termination of his agency agreement with .the company, is or becomes "profit and gains" of business. The Tribunal held that the compensation received by the appellant was not profits and gains of a business but was a payment made to the managing agents of a company which was not a business. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the compensation paid to the managing agent was not profits earned in the year of account ending June 30, 1954, but it was a payment to the managing director who was entitled to receive it in the same manner as the compensation received in the previous year. The word "income" in section 10(5A) means what it says and not what it says. The compensation received by a managing agent is not profits and therefore not exigible to tax.

6304: The petitioners are manufacturers of Brick Kilns. They manufacture and sell various articles including 'Bangles'. 2800: The appellant, a tenant of the premises in dispute granted to the respondent a lease for the purpose of constructing buildings for residential or business purposes. 6281: The appellant was a manufacturer of carpets. He manufactured carpets which were not covered by Items (a) and (b) of Schedule I to the Act. The High Court held that the products, viz., carpets were not covered either by item (d) or by item (e) of Schedule 1 of the Act. It has, having regard to newly developing materials, methods techniques and processes, a continually expanding content and new sets of weave must have changed hands. The use to he made of the word 'textify ' does not necessarily mean that the fabric which is woven comes into being only after the process of manufacture had been completed. What is necessary is that the fabric must have been woven into us before it was used in the process of manufacturing. The use of word "manufactures" is restricted to the final stage when the fabric is actually produced. 922: The appellant, a resident of Baroda in the State of Baroda, was carrying on business in India. He had a branch office in Baroda and its head office at Bombay was situated in Baroda. In 1947 he applied to the Income tax Officer for an assessment under section 12A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1948 49, but the Income tax officer rejected his claim holding that the Act did not apply to the business carried on in India. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the Act applied only to the business in India and not to any other part of India. The Tribunal confirmed this view. The High Court also took the same view on another ground which it had before it. Held:(i) The third proviso to section 12A is not applicable to the facts of the case because the business of the assessee in India was not controlled in India. (ii)The expression "business of a person who is resident but not ordinarily resident in the taxable territories" in the second proviso to section 42(1)(b) means that the profits or gains of such person would be received in or brought into India. (iii)The expression 'profits and gains of business ' in the second Proviso has no reference to the income of a particular business. (iv)The expression has to be construed as meaning the whole of the profits and gains of that business. (v)The expression means that the profit or loss arising from the business must have been earned in India.
5970: The deceased Hari Singh was a carpenter by profession. He left behind him his wife, the appellant No. 1 and a daughter, the appellant Nos. 2 to 4. The appel lants filed a petition before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Udaipur, claiming compensation of Rs. 1 lac as compensation for the death of their husband in a motor vehicle accident. The Tribunal held that the statutory liability of the Insurance Company was only up to a sum of Rs.4,000 and awarded a sum of RS. 10,000 as compensation. The High Court affirmed the award of the Tribu nal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was not justified in affirm ing the award of compensation as against the statutory liability. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the statutory liabil ity of the Insurance company was up to the amount of Rs. 4,000. [764F] (2) The High court was not justified, in affirm ing an award of the Tribunal for Rs. 10, 000 only as compensation. [765G]
4881: The Respondent, a Government servant, was in occupation of Government accommodation allotted to him by the Central Government. He filed an application under section 25B of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 before the Rent Controller on the ground specified in section 14A(1) thereof being Suit No. 48 of 1976 for recovery of possession of the premises. The Rent Controller held that the Respondent was in unauthorised occupation of Government residential accommodation and ordered eviction of the Respondent. The Respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority which dismissed the same holding that section 14A (1) of the Act did not contain a condition that the Government servant who made an application under Section 14A(2) should not be in possession of reasonably suitable alternative accommodation as was the case under clause (e) of the proviso to sub section (1)of Section 14 of the Act and that even if such a factor were to be taken into consideration, it could not be said that the Respondent, was in possession of reasonable suitable accommodation as was tended to be done by him. The Respondent then filed revision petition before the High Court which dismissed the revision petition holding that section 25B (8) of the Delhi Act did not include a condition that land lord must be in possession 'in his own name or in the name of his wife or dependent child '. Aggrieved by the order of the High Court, the Appellant has preferred this appeal contending that the High Court erred in its view that the respondent was in unauthorised occupa tion and therefore he was entitled to protection of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the respondent is not entitled to protection under section 14A of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act. [608F] 2. The word 'occupation ' has been defined in section 2(g) of the , to mean any position of waste,ujure or building, whether vacant or non-occupation of whatsoever character or activity or the use of any premises for human habitation. It means any work or thing in connection with or incidental or ancillary to agriculture, horticulture or animal husbandry or any building or place used as a means of access to or from any place passing or dwellingoor of a house. [610G
5483: The appellant was the tenant of the premises in question. On her husband 's death, respondent No. 2, who was the son of the deceased, filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that the appellant required the premises bona fide for his personal use and occupation. The rent in respect of the premises had been deposited on account of the appellant 's husband. The appellant contended that the rent was not paid as the appellant 'was in India at the relevant time. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant 'were the tenants and the appellant was not entitled to be joined as a party to the proceedings. The High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the tenancy was for the then tenant and the appellant 'self was an employee of the said company. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The land lady did not oppose the eviction petition because as per her version, the tenant had left the premises and closed her account while the notice terminating the tenancy was sent to the landladY where the appellant was residing. [311H; 312A] 2. The fact that the tenancy is for the then landlord or on his behalf and the company has no evidence to show that the tenancy had been terminated by the notice terminating tenancy. The notice could have been issued only after the landlord had come forward with the case that the tenancy in question had been terminated. But the landladies were not examined. They were not given any opportunity to lead evidence regarding the termination of tenancy. [313D E] 3. The tenancy in the instant case was for the erstwhile tenant. The tenancy having been terminated by notice, the landladily
1825: The appellant, a partnership firm, entered into a partnership with one of its partners, the first respondent. The Income tax Officer rejected the application for registration under section 26A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 on the ground that different firms could not constitute a valid partnership. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer but the Tribunal held that the partnership deed was not genuine and brought into existence only as a simulat er arrangement, that the profits which are distributed under the deed to the individuals mentioned therein were not the true profits of those individuals. On appeal by the appellant, the Tribunal held on a construction of the partnership deed and also on the basis of some other circumstances, that the said deed "is not genuine" and that the profits that are distributed under it were not the real profits of those individual partners. In further appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court has jurisdiction to entertain reference under section 66(2) of the Act. [864 C] (ii) The Tribunal has held that the Partnership Deed is not genuine. But the Tribunal has held in favour of the appellant on the basis that the partnership is not genuine for the following reasons: (a) earlier the firm entered into a part nership for the purpose of carrying on the business of manufacturing match products. The firm had entered into a contract with the appellant for the sale of the goods manufactured by it. The firm paid commission to the appellant. The firm did not include the profit in the firm 's capital account. The firm was assessed to income tax. The question whether the firm is a genuine or a new one depends upon the terms of the partnership agreement. If the firm is not registered, the assessment cannot be made on the partner who entered into the contract. [865 D E; 866 A B] (b) The Tribunal found that the firm was not a genuine one. It was not shown that the firm had been formed for the purpose for which it was constituted. The firm has been dissolved and the accounts have been closed. The firm is no doubt entitled to its assets and liabilities. But the firm has not been able to realise the commission realised from the sale of its goods. The firm cannot be said to have been formed
2270: The respondent made an application under section 11 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 for acquiring proprietary rights in certain lands. The Compensation Officer held that the respondent was a tenant of the Government and awarded compensation to him. On appeal by the respondent, the District Judge set aside the order of the Compensation Officer and remanded the case to the Compensation Officer for fresh enquiry. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of remand on the ground that the said land had been acquired by the State Government under the provisions of the Act and as such the respondent 's application under section I 1 could not lie against the Union. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the respondent 'was not a tenant but only a lessee of the said lands. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The scheme of the Act is that the land owned by the respondent must be deemed to have vested in the State Government free from all encumbrances and he cannot be regarded as a tenant. The Act does not bind the Government and an application under s.11 can not lie against it. [564 C] (ii) The Act does contain a provision which makes it obligatory upon the Collector to make an enquiry and determine the nature of the land to which the applicant belongs. The Collector has to hold an enquiry into the title to the land and determine whether the land is a forest or not. If he finds that the land is forest land, he has to make a report to the Government stating therein his opinion that the land should be acquired. The report of the Collector is then final and conclusive evidence of the fact that the land has been so acquired. But if he finds that there are no merits in the claim of the applicant for compensation or that any other claim is not justified, he has no further duty to make a reference to the Civil Court. [565 D F]
6716: The respondent instituted a suit for recovery of possession of a building on the ground of arrears of rent, etc. The decree was affirmed in appeal by the First Appellate Court as well as by the High Court. In the second appeal filed by the respondent, the High Court held that it was a tenant of the respondent and directed eviction of the appellant. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decree passed by the civil court in the present case was not a nullity for the Act had not barred the jurisdiction of the civil court, but only prevented the execution of the decree which was passed after the Act came into force; that the decree was in contravention of the provisions of section 30(ii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, and that the finding of the courts below that the suit was not maintainable was based on no evidence or was perverse. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 30(ii), which is the only provision under which the jurisdiction of civil courts can be ousted, is not attracted to the instant case. [857F] 2.1 Clause (ii) of section 30 of the Tamilnadu Buildings (Le ease and Rent Control ) Act, 1960 does not exclude from its purview any building or part thereof let out on a monthly rent of Rs. 400. The Act has not prohibited the passing of a decree for eviction otherwise than in accordance with the relevant statutory provisions. [858B C] 2.2 The Act does not forbid the passing of decrees for eviction otherwise then in accordance with law. The decree of the civil Court cannot be said to be without jurisdiction. [859C] 3. The decree passed by a civil court is not a nullity. It is not open to the landlord to challenge the decree on the ground that the decree is not a decree for money due. [860D E] Rattan Arya & Ors. vs State of Tamil Nadu & Anr. , ; , referred to.

On the basis of adverse remarks made against him by the reporting authority on May 4, 1982, he filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the author ity of the Home Secretary to write a confidential report assessing the performances, character, conduct and quali fication of the respondent as the Inspector General of Police, Haryana. The Single Judge of the High Court took the view that as the Home Secretary was specifically empowered by the State Government as the reviewing authority under Rule 2(e), he had the authority to write the report or make adverse remarks against the perform ing of the respondent for the aforesaid period during which he was the Inspector General oF Police, Haryana, and that the said power could not be delegated to the respondent. The Division Bench allowed the appeal holding inter alia that the Home Secretary being specifically empowered by Rule 2(a) to write the annual confidential report, he had the power to do so. 653: The appellant was a sugar factory in the State of Bihar. It had two factories one at Gaya and another at Guraru. The Gaya Sugar Mills Ltd., was taken over by the State Government under the provisions of the . On December 2, 1954, the State Government issued a notification under section 10(1) of the , directing that all the assets of the Gay Sugar Mills Ltd. including the assets of its management shall vest in the State Government free from all encumbrances and that all properties movable and immovable held by the said Gay Sugar Mill or its workmen shall stand transferred to and vested in the State government free from all encumbrance. The appellant challenged the legality of the said notification on the ground that it contravened article 31(2) of the Constitution as it purported to include within its sweep all the properties and effects of the Gayansthan Sugar Mills Ltd.; that the said Gayansthan was not a party to any adjudication proceedings before any Tribunal or before respondent No. 1; and that the reference made by the State of, Bihar to the Industrial Tribunal did not purport to include Gaya Sugar Mill Ltd. In the alternative, it was contended that the said Mill could not be deemed to have been taken over by respondent No. 3 after January 26, 1950, when the Act came into force. Held: (i) The effect of the provisions of sections 33 and 33A of the Act is that the ownership and control of the undertaking of the GAYU are retained with the State Government and the ownership and Control so long as the undertaking continues to vest in it is retained with the Government. The Act does not contemplate the vesting of the shares of the shareholders in the State but merely provides for the vesting of all the property movable and immovable which may belong to or be owned by the GAYUDHL, the appellant. (ii)The Act does not provide for the transfer of the shares by the Government to the appellant. The Act only vests the title of the Government in the appellant and the Government has no right to retain the shares. The Act is not intended to confer any title on the appellant. It is only a machinery for obtaining relief against wrongful act of the Government. (iii)The Act contemplates adjudication proceedings relating to the ownership and the possession of the

929: The mortgagor, in execution of a decree for money passed a mortgage decree on March 29, 1935. On October 26, 1936, an application had been made by the mortgagee decree holder under section 4 of the U. P. Encumbered Estates Act, 1934, for a final decree for sale of the mortgaged property and for the payment of the amount due on the mortgage to the mortgagor. The mortgagor 's claim was rejected by the Special Judge who directed sale of the property for recovery of the sum of Rs. 2,37,503 5 6 with future interest as in the preliminary decree. An appeal filed by the mortgagor decree holder was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The mortgagor 'S creditor was not bound by the decree. He could only get the amount due from the mortgagor on the date of the suit or the date of his application for revision. [601 D] (ii) The principle that a judgment debtor is entitled to the amount due to him on the date when he makes an application for revision is not applicable to execution proceedings. Section 14 of the Act provides that the court may make such orders as it thinks fit in respect of any application for revision which has been disposed of. The order of the court disposing of an application for review is not a judgment within the meaning of section 2(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure. [602 C E] (iii) The order of a court disposing of a proceeding for execution cannot be treated as a judgment within section 14 of the Usurious Loans Act, 1918. It is not possible to construe section 14 of that Act in the sense of giving effect to the intention of the legislature in enacting section 14 of Act 22 of 1939. The words "decree" and "order" are used in the same sense in which they have been understood in the Code of Criminal Procedure. [608 F H]

The learned Judge directed that the application be placed before a Vacation Judge with effect from 23rd June, 1986. On that day the complainant 'S advocate also appeared and filed his appearance. On this date the complainant was again requested by the Court to adjourn the case but the request was turned down. The High Court allowed the application and recalled its previous order dated 3nd June, 1985. The appellant has come in appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts should not have been swayed away by the conduct of the parties as it is not possible for any one to remember what they are doing. [839E] 2.1 In the instant case, the respondent had already been released on bail by the Trial Court. He did not make any attempt to produce any material to show that there was any change in the circumstances which would justify the grant of bail to the respondent. The High court erred in granting bail to the other accused persons. [840F G] 2.2 It is unfortunate that the High Court has not taken into consideration the fact that the trial was delayed and the witnesses were being examined. The High has failed to take note of the fact that there was no change in the circumstance after the rejection of the bail applications. [841C] 2.3 The High Court ought to
4083: The appellant was a public servant. He was charged with offences under sections 403, 409 and 477A read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted him but the High Court convicted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the search warrant issued by the Magistrate was not valid because (a) the search was not in accordance with law; (b) the seizure of books, documents etc., from the appellant were illegal; (c) the search and seizure were in violation of article 20(3) of the Constitution; (d) the provisions relating to search and seizure contained in section 93(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, are not hit by Article 20(3); (e) the search is contrary to the provisions of section 94(1), and (f) the provisions of the Code of Criminal Proce dure are not attracted. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether there is any element of compulsion in issuing a summons to a person accused of an offence under section 94(old) to produce a document or thing in his possession or power was kept open. [857F] 2. The question as regards the constitutional immunity of the accused from search and seizure under the Code of criminal procedure 1973 has been considered by this Court in several cases. [858G] 3. The question of the constitutional immunity under article 20(1) is not res integra. [859H 860A] 4. The question about the validity of the search and the legality of the seizure of the books, documents and other things seized during the search is essentially one of fact. It must be made clear that the question whether there was any element of pressure on the police to produce those books, documents or things in the custody of the accused is left open. [886B C] 5. Section 93(1)(f) of the Code does not bar issue of warrants for search and seizure of books and documents or things found in the premises of the accused. [894C] 6. The question regarding the constitutional immunity from search and sale of books, etc. is left open [859D]
4498: The respondent Corporation framed a scheme for the purpose of providing uniformity in scales of remuneration and other terms and conditions of service to employees of the Corporation. The scheme provided that the employees were entitled to be paid monthly salary and dearness allowance at the rate of one month 's salary in lieu of notice, but it was made clear that the payment would not exceed Rs. 500 per month. The scheme also provided that the Corporation would pay bonus equal to three months ' salary in lieu thereof. The employees filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the scheme on the ground that the provisions of the Act violated their fundamental right under Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the scheme did not violate any provision of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the scheme was arbitrary and violative of Article 14; (ii) the scheme discriminated between employees of the same class of employers who had been granted benefits of different schemes; (iii) the scheme violated the guarantee of equality guaranteed by article 14 of the Constitution; and (iv) the scheme offended Article 31(2). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme is arbitrary and discriminatory. It does not contravene Article 14 of the constitution. [864F] 2. The scheme was not discriminatory nor was it discriminatory as there was no discrimination between employees of similar undertakings situated similarly. [865B C] 3. The scheme did not offend Article 14 of Constitution. [866A] 4. The scheme being reasonable and having regard to the objects sought to be achieved by it, it cannot be struck down as offending Article 14 or Article 19 of the Constitution merely because the scheme has been so framed that it could have received some benefit of the classification. [867D E] 5. The scheme in question is not discriminatory. [868G] 6. The scheme provides that the employees will be paid monthly wages and dearness allowance for each year of service subject to a ceiling of Rs. 500/ per month. [869H; 870A] 7. The scheme further provides that the payment will not include the annual increment. The scheme however does not provide for the payment of
7056: The appellant, a sitting M.L.A., was elected as the Chief Minister of Goa State from the Goa State. He filed writ petition No.48 of 1991 in the High Court challenging the order of his disqualification made by the Speaker under the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground of laches and allowed the same holding that the writ petitions were filed after considerable delay, and therefore merits of the contention that the Speaker had no such power of review was not considered. Aggrieved by the said decision, the appellant preferred the present appeals. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the writ petition was maintainable against the Speaker who was the only person exercising the power of review vested in him under the Tenth schedule. [831D] 1.2 In Kihoto Hollohan vs Union of India & Ors., ; , this Court observed that the power of the High Court to review its judgment is a part of the appellate jurisdiction of the court which is conferred on it by the Constitution. It cannot be exercised as an appellate jurisdiction. [832C D] Kihotos Naik vs Union of lndia & Anr., ; , referred to. 1.3 The High Court was right in holding that the orders made by the Acting Speaker in purported exercise of the power of Review under the Tenth ' Schedule to the constitution, have to be declared nullity and ignored, then writ petition No 48 of 1991 by Ravi section Naik was dismissed as not pressed on 22.4.1991 because the order of the disqualification made by him had to be declared as nullity and ignored. [830E F] Kioteliak & Co. Ltd. vs Maharashtra Legislature, [1990] 3 SCC 682; Kiote lal vs Union oflndia, ; , referred
1992: The mortgagor 's land was part of a larger holding of 23.69 acres under a mortgage executed in favour of the mortgagee. The mortgagee purchased the land in the farzi name of Dwarkalal, and the mortgage deed provided that the mortgagee would pay Rs. 68 10 9 3 per acre as rent to the mortgagee annually on account of the total rent. The mortgage deed provided for payment of the entire rent payable by the mortgagee annually, but did not pay the balance of 10 annas pies. The mortgagee consistently paid the rent of the entire holding and the mortgage money became substantial. The mortgagor ' sold the land to the mortgagee and the sale certificate was issued to him. The mortgagee filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage and for recovery of arrears of rent. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court dismissed the appeal in part. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The purchase at the rent sale and the certificate sale were made by the mortgagee by availing himself of his position as such and having regard to section 90 of the and Illustration (c) to it, the purchases were made by availing himself. of his position and not by virtue of any contract or compromise. [166 B] (2) The mortgagee was entitled to redeem the entire mortgaged lands. But he could not sell them without the permission of the mortgagor. He could not thereafter sell them without paying the entire rent due from him. [164 C] (3) The mortgagee had no interest in the land. He could only get back the amount paid by him to the mortgagor. The mortgagor could not therefore claim the benefit of the proviso to section 90. [165 A]
6522: The appellant, a resident of the estate in which the land applied for nautor was granted nautor land on payment of Rs.552.50 as Nazarana. The Forest Department filed an appeal against the said order before the Deputy Commissioner Simla which was accepted and the order of the Revenue As sistant Chopal sanctioning nautor lands in favour of Gopinder Singh was set aside. The Financial Commissioner accepted the appeal and restored the grant of nautor to Gopinder singh. The Financial Commis sioner accepted the appeal on the ground that the law in his own hands had not been followed by the Revenue authorities. The Financial commissioner accepted the appeal. The Financial Commission allowed the appeal on two grounds: (i) that the appellant felled the trees on the land without waiting for necessary approval of the Divisional Forest Officer and as such he took the law in its own hands; and (ii) that the service for the defence of Army or civilian, who were in the armed forces and military or civil service, could be considered as service for the Defence of India. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The second part of clause (a) of Rule 7 makes it clear that an income of less than Rs.2,000 per annum should be from all sources including lands. [799H] 2. The second limb of clause (d) of Rule 2 is applicable only where there is a bona fide income of more than 10 bighas of land but has not been derived from any other source including lands. In the instant case, the income of less then 10 bighas of laud was derived from the trees standing on the land. The second ground is not applicable because the income of the appellant falls short of 10 bighas of agricultural land. [800C E] 3. The second reason is also not applicable because there is no evidence to show that the income derived from the fruit bearing trees was derived from any source other than the source of income of the land. [800D] 4. 5159: The respondents in the appeals were the owners of a distillery in which spirit was manufactured under a licence granted by the State Government. D 2 licence for manufacturing liquor in the distillery was granted to each of the respondents on certain conditions. D 2 was granted licence for manufacturing country liquor and D 1 was granted licence on certain terms and conditions. On 30th December 1984, the State Government issued a notification under Section 17(2) of the M.P. Excise Act, 1915 granting the right to all distilleries and warehouses in the State of Madhya Pradesh to obtain a licence for manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquors. The respondents challenged the said notification before the High Court by filing writ petitions contending that under the policy decision dated 30th December, 1984, D 2 licence was to be granted to each D 1 only for a limited period of 5 years commencing from 1st April 1986 or it was to be renewed from year to year after the expiration of the period of five years so that all other persons would be totally excluded from enter ing the field and a monopoly would be created in favour of D 1 and D 2 licence would not be renewed. The High Court allowed the writ petitions holding that under the scheme of the M P Excise Act, the State had no power to issue any direction contrary to the policy decision of the State Government and that the State Government had no power under Section 17 of the Act to alter the terms and conditions of licence granted to a licensee. Aggrieved by the judgment of the High Court, the State has preferred these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, the Court, HELD: (1) The policy decision dated March 30, 1986 is not an executive order but an executive decision. It is true that the policy decision was taken by the State in the public interest to protect the interest of the people of the State but then the policy decision cannot be struck down unless it can be shown to have been vitiated either by mala fides or colourable exercise of power. [839E F] (2) In the instant case, the policy decision taken by the Government in public interest was not vitiated by mala fides nor was there any abuse of power. The policy decision was made bona fide and not arbitrary. [840F G] (3) The policy decisions are not

1423: The appellant was the principal debtor to a loan taken by his father from the respondent Bank. The loan was overdue and the appellant gave a surety bond for the repayment of Rs. 25,000/ . The appellant 's case was that he never stood surety for the respondent Bank but that he stood surety for Rs. 20,000/ which was subsequently altered to Rs. 20000/ and that any change of figure was a material alteration resulting in the avoidance of the contract, even though the alteration might have been advantageous to him, the guarantor entrusted to the appellant a letter of guarantee dated May 24, 1947. The trial court decreed the suit against the appellant but the High Court on appeal held that the letter of guarantee was not proved to be a new document but only an improvement made by the appellant with the knowledge of the respondent Bank that it was due to the act of the appellant that the letter remained with the principal debtor. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The letter of guarantee is a fresh document. It does not create or extinguish any rights in immovable property. It merely makes up the initial liability of a third party in respect of a loan. [864 H] (ii)The letter of guarantee clearly mentioned that the appellant would give a letter of Guarantee to the principal borrower and the principal borrower made alterations without the consent of the appellant. The alteration was made in order to carry out the common intention of the appellant and Sankaran, the appellant and the Bank that for the overdraft accommodation of Rs. 20 thousand/ allowed to the appellant would given a letter of guarantees to the principal debtor, and the principal debtor had no authority to alter the guarantee without the consent or knowledge of the appellant, and the alteration was made for the benefit of the principal debtor in this case. [865 A C; 866 D E]

4861: The appellant entered into an agreement with G.E.C. for purchase of a certain flat in a building known as "Green House" situated at Bombay. 607: The respondent, who was the Karta of a Hindu undivided family, executed an agreement in 1934, referring their disputes relating to partition of the family properties to arbitration. On June 21, 1936, the arbitrator made an award which stated that out of the G. Daropadi and the remaining Notes and various immoveable properties including agricul tural land, gardens and houses should be endorsed in favour of the appellant. On November 15, 1939, the respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 7,310 11 3 as damages on account of the alleged breach of contract. The appellant contended that the award was not binding on him because it was not signed by the arbitrators. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the award did not bind the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The award was not a speaking one. It was not a judgment within the meaning of article 31 of the Constitution. [813 D] (ii)The award was not an executable one. The award was a document between the parties and could not be challenged under article 14 of the Constitution on the ground that it was not a judicial or quasi judicial order. [814 E F] (iii)It is well settled that a party cannot rely upon a non speaking award. [815 B C]
3065: The accused was convicted by the High Court under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death on the former count. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the accused. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable and that the statement of the deceased was not corroborated by any independent witness. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) It is well settled that in a case where there is direct evidence regarding the fact of last seen together, the mere non production of the accused at trial may not affect the prosecution case adversely. [902 D E] (2) There is no doubt that when two views are possible, the view favourable to the accused should be adopted. But if the view favourable 805 to the accused is taken, then the benefit of reasonable doubt will have to go to the accused. [903 F G] (3) In the present case, the evidence of PW 1, the wife of the deceased, who had accompanied the deceased to the place of occurrence, and the evidence of other witnesses, who were close relatives of the deceased and who saw the accused and the deceased together with her daughter in law, clearly established the presence of the accused with the crime. The evidence of these witnesses also established the presence and participation of the accused in the crime. [904 A B]
80: The appellants were the tenants of the lands in question. On appeal, the High Court held that the mortgagees could not be said to have acquired permanent occupancy rights in the lands. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The suit was barred under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. [787 C] (ii) The suit is not one for recovery of possession but it is one for redemption of the mortgage. [788 D E] (iii) The suit for possession was not maintainable because the mortgagors had no proprietary title to the lands. [789 F G]

The consultation contemplated by section 133 is meant the formal and informal consultation with the Commission and not the subject matter of their consultation. The requirement of sub section (2) (a) of section 133 is therefore satisfied when the Commission makes a recommendation to make the appointment of respondents Nos 3 to 46. 26: The respondents were the tenants of a building in Bihar. They paid one month 's rent in advance and agreed to pay it as per the scheme of the Act. In the course of their tenancy, the appellants paid one month "s rent in advanced by them and the respondents accepted the same. The respondents did not vacate the premises within one month from the date of the payment of the rent but continued to deposit the rent with the Controller on the ground that the building was non payment of rent. The appellants filed an application under section 11 of the Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 for eviction of the respondents on the ground of non payment of arrears of rent. This application was resisted by the appellants on the ground inter alia that there was no non payment of the rents due from them and that they had been paying the rent regularly. The respondents contended that the Act was applicable only to Bihar and not to Bihar. Held, that the Act applied only to Bihar where the landlord himself was the tenant and not to other States where he could be said to have committed default in payment of rent for more than six months. The Act did not apply to Bihar where there was no default because the Act did not provide for any appeal against the order of eviction passed by the House Controller. The Act was intended to protect tenants from being evicted except on the grounds specified in section 11. The Act does not confer a right upon the landlord to evict his tenant if he brings into Court all the rent due from him before the order of his eviction is passed. The Act confers a right upon a landlord to apply for eviction of a tenant on the ground specified in section II of the Act, and the Act does not give such a right to the landlord. The Act gives power to the Controller to determine whether or not there has been non payment of rents and if so, what rent should be paid by a tenant. The Act empowers the Controller to decide whether or not the non payment of any rent has occurred by reason of non payment. The Act authorises the Controller to hold an enquiry and decide whether the non payment has occurred by reasons of the non payment or by reasons of any other cause which justify non payment or non payment of a rent. The Act also empowers the Controller, in appropriate cases
4426: The appellant polled votes as against the votes polled by the respondent No. 1, who had won the election. The result of the election was declared on 24 10 1977 and the appellant was declared elected to the Assembly. The appellant filed an election petition challenging the election of the appellant on several grounds including the allegation that he had filed a false return of the expenses and had incurred more than the permissible limit which amounted to a contravention of section 77 of the Act. The High Court accepted the election petition only on one issue and set aside the election of appellant on the ground that the appellant had committed corrupt practice under section 123(6) of the Act in incurring the expenditure exceeding the permissible limit. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: (1) It is not necessary for the candidate to show that he had committed any corrupt practice at the time of filing his nomination paper. [634F] (2) In order to succeed on the basis of the allegation made in the petition it is not necessary that the candidate should have been guilty of some corrupt practice at all. [635A B] (3) The allegations made in the election petition were not proved. [636C]
1851: The appellant, a defeated candidate, challenged the election of the respondent on the ground that he had committed corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court held that the appellant was guilty of a corrupt practice under sub section (4) of section 123 and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the statement in question was not an offence under sub section 4 of section 123 but only a statement of fact which is false and which can be said to have been calculated to prejudice the prospects of the respondent 's election. HELD : Dismissing the appeal: (i) It is well settled that the burden of proving the commission of corrupt practice by a returned candidate or his agent or by another person is on the party who alleges it. The onus probandi lies in every case upon the person who challenges the allegation made against him. The allegations are required to be proved like any other fact. The allegations must be such as to make them inconsistent with the possible defence of the person charged. [864 H] (ii)The appellant has failed to prove that the statement published and circulated by him was not offending the personal character and conduct of the respondent. [865 D E]
5060: The petitioners in the two sets of writ petitions, who were direct recruits to the posts in Grade IV of the Indian Economic Service and Grade III of the Indian Statistical Service respectively, challenged the validity of the Indian Administrative Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1954, the Indian Statistician service Rules, 1961 and the Indian Stational Cadre (Appointment by promotion) Regulations, 1955 made under Article 3I of the Constitution as being violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The regulations do not provide for any alternative method of recruitment except those prescribed in the regulations. The regulations also do not prescribe any particular procedure or method for filling up the vacancies existing as on the date when the regulations came into force. The regulations have been framed with a view to regulate the recruitment and conditions of service of the various categories of the services under the Union Government. The regulations are not inconsistent with the rules made under article 309 of the Constitution or section 9 of the . [873G H; 874A B] 3. The regulations make it obligatory for the Union Public Service Commission to hold competitive examinations for appointment to the various grades of the Services before the appointments can be made to these grades. The regulations, however, do not provide that not less than 75 per cent of the vacancies should be filled up by direct recruitment through an open competitive examination to be held by the Commission in the manner prescribed in Schedule II to the Rules. The regulations only lay down the principle of rotation and if there is no quota, then the rotation itself is bad. [875H; 876B C] 4. The regulations provide that not more than 25% of the vacancies in Grade IV will be filled up from amongst officers serving in offices under the Government in Economic
4113: The respondent Nathi, who was the widow and mother of two sons of one Nathi, filed an application under section 10 A(b) and 10B of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 for declaring her as surplus land. She claimed that she had inherited the land from her husband in equal shares and that she was entitled to allotment of 30 standard acres of land. The Collector (Surplus) held that Nathi had been allotted only 30 standard acres and that the remaining 30 standard acres were not available for allotment. The Commissioner dismissed the application on the ground that the "surplus area" declared in Nathi 's life time had already been allotted to other tenants and could not be excluded from the holding in the hands of his widow and mother. An appeal against this order was dismissed by the Commissioner on the ground of delay. The respondent moved a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed on the ground, inter alia, that mere allotment of land to other tenants did not amount to utilisation of "surplus areas" within the meaning of clause (5a) of section 2 of the Act and no part of it could therefore be utilised for allotment to other tenants. The appellant contended that the " Surplus Area" declared in the life time of Nathi was merely an initial stage in the process of utilisation of the "surallotment". Held:The allotment of 30 Standard acres of land to the respondent Nathi was not in excess of the permissible area of 30 standard acre but was only an initial stage when the resettled tenants had not taken possession of the land. The allotment of 30 ' Standard acres was made in the year 1958 and the same was completed in the year 1961. Therefore, the "sur surrendered area" declared by the Collector in his order dated November 25, 1959 was not in existence at the time of the making of the "additional area" under section 10A(a). [650 E]

The Collector rejected these applications on the ground that they were not revisable under the Code. In the appeals to this Court it was contended that the Revenue officers had a dual capacity (1) under the Abolition act and (2) under the Code; that under the Code, both the Commissioner and the Board were appellate as also revisional authorities; that under section 84 of the Abolition Act, an appeal lay to the Commissioner or the Board of Revenue under the Code only when there was a right of appeal provided thereunder; that under sections 84 and 85 of the Abolition act, the Commissioner and Board had power to revise the orders passed by the Revenue Officers and that the Board had no jurisdiction to entertain any revision or appeal against such orders.
