[804 E F] (iii) The Revenue Officers have the power to revise orders passed by them either by the Commissioner or by the Board of the Revenue under the provisions of Ch. Xl of the Code. But the Board does not exercise the said powers. It is the Board which has the power to decide whether
247: The appellants were the mortgagees of certain lands in Pakistan. They filed a suit for redemption of the mortgaged properties on the 10th March, 1926, and obtained an order of attachment of the properties. On the 13th December, 1937, the decree holders purchased the properties at auction sales held on the 8th August, 1939, for Rs. 3,899 and delivery of possession was duly given to them on the 6th July, 1940. The personal decree of the mortgagors was also executed and some properties of the mortgager were purchased by the decree holders on the 8 th August, 1939. The mortgagees were ordered to put the mort gagee into possession of all the properties which had been purchased by the mortgagees on the 8 nd August, 1939 and delivered possession to them on that date. The decree holders applied under section 36 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1940, for reopening the mortgage decrees and for passing fresh orders as regards the payments due on the mortgages. The decree holder contended that the execution proceedings were barred by limitation. The executing court overruled the objection and passed a new decree in favour of the mortgangers. The decreeholders appealed to the High Court. The High Court confirmed the decree with some minor modifications. The decree debtors appealed to this Court. HELD:The appeal must be allowed. (i) The decree holders were not entitled to reap the benefit of the period of limitation prescribed for the institution of the execution application by the decree holder. [159 E] (ii) The decree holder was not entitled to claim the benefit of section 14(1)(c) of the Limitation Act because the period of one year prescribed therein is computed from the date when the decree was passed. [160 B C] (iii) The decree was not therefore executable. The decree was a money decree and could not be executed unless it was redeemed. The decree being a money decree it was governed by section 14(2) of the Act. [165 D]

Section 14 provides that no agent shall make any sale of goods belonging to the principal without the permission of the agent. Section 15 provides that no licensed vendor shall purchase any article in the name of another person unless he has obtained 'the consent of the owner of the article. 1707: The appellant was declared elected to the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly. He filed an election petition before the Tribunal alleging that the Returning Officer had improperly rejected a large number of votes which were tendered at the time of counting and in consequence thereof the election was materially affected. The Tribunal dismissed the application for inspection on the ground that it would be too early to grant inspection of ballot papers. The High Court held that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to order inspection of ballot paper even if there was some defect in the counting, and that the Tribunal should have allowed inspection of the ballot papers by the Returning Officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Tribunal has power to allow inspection of ballot boxes after the counting of all ballot papers had been completed.[939 G] (ii) It is not necessary that an order for inspection should be made and that the secrecy of the ballot paper should be maintained. An order for inspection may not be granted as a matter of course; having regard to the insistence upon the secrecy of ballot papers, the court would be justified in granting an order for inspecting the ballot papers. [940 H] (iii) The Tribunal is prima facie satisfied that in order to decide the dispute and to do complete justice between the parties inspection of ballots papers has been permitted by law and that the ballot papers ought to have been called for. If the Tribunal finds that in order not to allow the ballot papers to proceed further without inspection, the result of the election is likely to be doubtful or if any error is discovered in the process of counting it must give notice to the persons concerned to remedy the defects within 7 days from the date of its receipt and if they fail to remedy the defect, the Tribunal will make an order for cancellation of the result of election. 3475: The appellant, a registered dealer under the Madhya Pradesh Sales Tax Act, 1948, was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of certain goods. He had been assessed to sales tax for the period from 1st April, 1956 to 31st March, 1957 under the Madhya Bharat Sales Tax Act. The assessment order was passed by the Sales Tax Officer on 30th September, 1958. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner reduced the assessment to nil. In revision, the State Government set aside the order of the Assistant Commissioner and directed that the assessments be re completed after making deductions in respect of the amounts already paid. The appellant contended before this Court that the Explanation to section 8(2A) of the Central Act read with section 5(2)(a)(iv) of the State Act is not an exception to the exemption granted under section 5(1). It was further contended that the Explanation should be given a liberal interpretation so as to give full effect to the exemption clause. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The Explanation to section S(2A), read with section 2(b) of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act is an exception to section 5(ii) (a) (iv) of State Act. [999 G] (ii) The Explanation provides that where goods are sold by a registered dealer to another registered dealer for use by him in the production or manufacture of goods for sale, such sale shall be deemed to take place in his case if they are purchased by the registered dealer themselves as being for resale or for use by them in the course of inter State trade or commerce. [997 H; 998 A] (iii) The Explanation does not say that the goods must be used by the assessee in the production of goods for the purpose of consumption in the State. The Explanation only means that the goods cannot be utilised by the assessee for any other purposes except for the purposes of consumption in that State. [998 B C] (iv) The Explanation contemplates cases where the goods are not used for the purpose for which they were purchased but rather seeks to avoid taxation on the same ground. [996 D E]
4136: The assessees were the owners of a large number of shares in a private limited company. They applied for valuation of the shares made by Mafatlal Gagalbhai Pvt. Ltd., Chartered Accountants, by applying the profit earning method of valuation of shares without making any adjustment in the profits of the company. The Wealth Tax officer valued the shares at much higher figures than the market value arrived at by applying the break up method. Since the valuation of the share was not accepted by the Revenue, the assessees preferred appeals to the Tribunal. The Tribunal accepted the contention of the assessees and adopted the valuation of shares made by the Chartered Accountants. The High Court dismissed the assessee 's cross objections and held that the method of valuation adopted by the Wealth Tax officer was not proper. [904 D E; 905 C]

The letting out of the building is not a mere change of user from the date of the lease itself. It is a new transaction. The letting of the building has been completed before the Act came into force. 4349: The Delhi Development Authority is a local authority. It has been constituted under the Delhi Development Act, 1957. Section 32(1) of the Act provides that the Authority may take into consideration any plan it appears to it to be fair and reasonable or may not be just. Section 33 empowers the Central Government to place at the disposal of the Authority all lands vested in the Central Government. Section 33(2)(a) provides for an appeal against the order of the Authority to the Central Government which shall have power to reverse or modify any order passed by the Authority. Section 33A provides for penalties for contravention of the provisions of the Act. Section 33B provides for appeals against the orders of the Authority. The Delhi Development Act was amended by the Delhi Development (Amendment) Act, 1981. By the Amendment Act, the Authority was again placed with the same powers as were conferred on the Central Government under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, and the Central Government had also the power to make rules. The Delhi Municipal Corporation had framed the Master Plan for Delhi and the Master Plan had also laid down the manner in which the land should be utilised. The Delhi Town Planning Act, 1961, was repealed by the Delhi Town Planning (Amendment)Act, 1983. The Delhi Improvement Trust Act, 1960, was enacted to provide for the improvement of Delhi according to plan, of the development area known as Delhi Development Authority 's jurisdiction, development of land, improvement of streets, parks, gardens, playgrounds and community facilities, and for the purpose of planning, the provision of open spaces, roads, buildings, transportation facilities, special areas development schemes etc. The Delhi Housing Board Act, 1961 was repealed by Delhi Development Act , 1983. Section 33C provides for the levy of fine for carrying out any of the purposes of the Act, which would include the imposition of penalties for carrying out the provisions of section 33D. The Delhi High Court allowed the Writ Petition filed by the Union of India and the Delhi Development Authority and directed the Authority to carry out its duties and functions under the Act. The Delhi Administration appealed to this Court. The Delhi Laws Act, 1958, was enacted by the Parliament to provide for certain measures to protect the interests of weaker sections of society and to ensure the production of goods and material
544: The appellant, a religious denomination of Gowda Saraswath Brahmins, instituted a suit under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure for framing a scheme for the temple. This was the position when the Madras Temple Entry Authorisation Act (Madras V of 1947), was passed by the Legislature of the Province of Madras. The question arose whether the right of a religious denomination to manage its own affairs in matters of religion guaranteed under article 26(b) of the Constitution was subject to, and could be controlled by a law protected by article 25(2)(b). Held, that the Act did not infringe the fundamental rights of the appellant under article 26 of the Constitution. The Act did not offend against the provisions of article 26(d) of the Con stitution. The Act was enacted with a view to put certain religious institutions within the scope of the Act and it provided for their regulation and control by prohibiting them from taking any form of worship which they were not entitled to do. It was not therefore an interference with the religious denomination 's right to manage its property but was only incidental to the regulation and control of the said institution. The Act had been enacted to provide for the better administration and governance of Hindu temples and of the properties thereof. The Act also authorised the trustees of such temples to take part in the management of the said temples. The Act, however, did not in express terms or by necessary implication prohibit the taking of part in the administration of such tempers. The Act merely laid down the duties of the trustees and laid down the procedure for their performance. The Act provided for the appointment of a committee of management and the powers and functions of the trustees. The Act gave power to the Government to frame rules for the proper administration of temples and to make provision for their management. The Act made no provision for the appointment or removal of any trustee or manager and the delegation of the power of appointment or removal to the trustees was not authorised by the Act. The Act conferred on the Government power of superintendence over all temples and their endowments and the Government exercised its power of supervision over them. The Act created a body of persons who were members of a particular religious denomination or community and empowered them to administer the temple and to pass
233: The first petitioner was a servant of the Government of Madras. The second petitioner was a public servant of the State of Madras. The first petitioner filed a complaint against the second petitioner before the Magistrate alleging that he had committed offences under sections 409, 477A and 120B I.P,C. The Magistrate after issuing notice to the first petitioner and after considering his explanation passed an order directing the first petitioner to be tried in accordance with section 241(2) Cr. P.C. In appeal the Sessions Judge confirmed the order of the Magistrate but the High Court set aside the order of acquittal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the sanction given by the Government under section 197(1) Cr. p. C. for the prosecution as against the first petitioner is invalid inasmuch as the order of his sanctioning authority specifying the Court before which the trial is to be held is not placed before the sanctioning authority; (ii) even if the sanction under section 197 Cr. P C. is valid, it is for the very Government which accords the sanction to specify the Court before whom the trial is held under section 241 (2); (iii) even if it refers to specification of the Court by the Government, the power under section 14 of the Criminal Procedure Code of appointing a Special Magistrate for trial of the case cannot be exercised by the Madhya Pradesh Government. HELD : (i) The sanction given by Government under section 19 of the Criminal Proce dure Code of appointing the Special Magistrate for trials of cases triable by him is not obligatory and it is open to the Government to specify the court before which the prosecution of such Judge is to be conducted. [175 G] (ii) The power under section 197 of the Criminal procedure Code of appointing Special Magistrates is discretionary and optional but if in an individual case, that power is not exercised by the Government then section 14 of Criminal Procedure Code cannot be invoked. It is only when the Government has discretion that the power can be exercised. [176 D E] Anwar Ali Sarkar vs King Emperor,

Under the terms of the agreement the appellant entrusted the work to an Indian Company who had accepted the contract. 2026: The respondent concern was engaged in the manufacture of pharmaceutical products. It applied for leave to her husband and she was granted leave on the condition that during the period of absence the woman would be at liberty to employ any other woman who may be willing to take up employment. On the failure of the woman to join duty, the respondent filed a reference under section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, claiming reinstatement with full back wages. The Industrial Tribunal held that there was no justification for the rule requiring un married women to resign as soon as she marries and that the rule was not in existence when the respondent 's husband was employed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the rule could not be enforced against the respondent because she had been denied the benefit of leave which was available to married women. HELD: (i) The rule is not in existence in other departments of the respondent concern itself. It only provides that such a rule is in force in other departments. [495 F] (ii) There is no reason why the rule should be so construed as to exclude married women from availing themselves of the leave facilities. The fact that the work has got to be done as a team and presence of all those workmen is necessary is in our opinion no disqualification so far as married women are concerned. [496 B C] (iii) The rule cannot be said to be in existence when one of the parties to the dispute is the respondent 'son or wife. The rule is in existence when both the parties to a dispute are married. The rule can be said to have been evolved merely to secure to employees an implied power to relieve them of the evil sought to be avoided by such a rule. In order that such a construction may serve the purpose of the legislation it is necessary that the interpretation should be placed upon the provision of the statute itself. [497 G H; 498 A]
3405: The appellant Bank is a banking company within the meaning of section 5 of the Banking Companies Act, 1949 and has its Head office in London and branch offices in different parts of India. The dispute between the Bank and its workmen represented by the All India National & Grindlays Bank Employees Federation was referred to an Industrial Tribunal under section 10(1) of the Act. The Tribunal held that the bonus payable to the workmen for the accounting year 1965 was not available to the Bank as it had no reserves and directed the Bank to pay the workmen and non work men staff a sum of Rs. 27 lakhs (Rupees twenty seven lakhs only) in full and final settlement of all claims including the development rebate reserve. In appeal to this Court, the workmen contended that the Tribunal had exceeded its jurisdiction in directing the payment of the balance of Rs. 2 lakhs which was the available surplus. HELD: (i) The Tribunal had erred in holding that the available surplus was available for distribution as bonus to the workmen. The Tribunal had itself determined the available surplus at Rs. 2 1/2 lakhs. The Tribunal could have directed the payment of Rs. 1 1/2 lakh only if there were any surplus after deducting therefrom the amount already paid. [137 E F] (ii) The Tribunal was wrong in directing the award of interest on the amount of Rs. 20 lakhs from 1st January, 1956 to 31st December, 1964. Interest should be calculated on the amount due from 1st December, 1963 till the date of payment. Interest should also be calculated on a certain percentage of the salary or wage earned during the accounting year. [136 D E]

1056: The appellants were assessed to income tax for the year of account July 1, 1949 corresponding to the assessment year 1949 50. For the year of assessment 1949 50 they submitted their return showing a loss of Rs. 1,37,000. The Income Tax Officer passed an order "no proceeding" and closed the assessment. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the appellants not having exercised their option under section 2(ii) of the Indian Income Tax Act in so far as it was materialised, the only course open to the Income Tax Officer was to take the financial year ending March 31, 1950 as the previous year for the income from an undisclosed source and to consider this credit in the assessment for the year 1950 51 after giving opportunity to the appellants to explain the nature and source thereof. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order on the ground that the same was without jurisdiction and also on the ground of non compliance with the provisions of section 34(1). The High Court dismissed the petition but granted certificate of fitness to appeal to this Court. HELD: (i) Section 34(1) of the Income Tax Act at the relevant time in so far it is material provided: " no proceeding" and "no proceedings" mean any proceeding which may be commenced otherwise than in accordance with the provisions contained in this Chapter. [657 G] (a) The Income Tax officer had no power to close the assessment because he was not competent to do so. He could have proceeded with the assessment himself or could have adjourned the hearing of the case for a reasonable period not exceeding 15 days. But the Income Tax officer did not do so. The order of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner was a final order and the question whether the order was a provisional one or a mere tentative one must depend upon the facts of each case. [658 A C; 659 B D] (b) The Income tax officer 's failure to issue notice within the time allowed by law does not necessarily result in the reopening of the assessment. It is only when the Income tax officer has reason to believe that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment and the explanation offered is satisfactory that the income chargeable to income tax could not be said to have escaped

2374: The decree holder obtained an order for eviction of the judgment debtor from the premises in dispute. The judgment debtor applied to the executing court under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure for delivery of possession of the premises. The decree holder applied for execution and the High Court held that the decree was not executable as it was not a case of collusion between the decree holder and the judgment debtors. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The decree holder had not challenged the proposition that the court could not order delivery of possession without the requisite sanction for dismantling of the factory. [750 G] (ii) The decree is a composite one involving several distinct rights and each right has its origin in a separate set of provisions. It is a single right which can be enforced by resort to the provisions of the Code. If there is no separate claim or right in respect of any property, such property cannot be proceeded against in execution proceedings. 4013: The appellant company was a Government Company. The prosecution case was that there was an exchange of abuses between the deceased and the appellant near the shop of the First Informant, and that the latter was trying to snatch the knife from him. The Sessions Judge acquitted both the accused but convicted the appellant under section 302 read with section 114 I.P.C. and sentenced him to transportation for life. On appeal the High Court reversed the order of acquittal and convicted the appellant on the ground that the evidence against him had not been corroborated by the eye witnesses. It also held that the appellant had no motive in the commission of the offence. Held: (i) The mere fact that the witnesses have turned hostile does not necessarily mean that the prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The effect of their testimony is that the court is entitled to believe that it is true. If a witness gives a false statement during the course of his evidence he cannot be believed unless he reverts to the position hears. The reason is that a witness who gives a false state ments during the course o f his evidence can as well 'become reliable. [465 D] (ii)The evidence of the two eye witnesses is consistent only with regard to the occurrence and they are independent witnesses. There is nothing in the evidence which would render them unreliable. The evidence of the three eye witnesses is fully corroborated by the medical evidence and the circumstances. [466 B C]
3452: The appellant brought a suit in the court of Assistant Collector, Baran for possession of land comprised in khasra Nos. 513 and 678 situate in village Balakhera under sections 180 and 183 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955. The respondent pleaded that he was a trespasser as he had been inducted by Kishori Lal as a tenant without any authority or that he had not occupied the land duly let out to him. The appellant contended that he was not a trespasser but had only a right of occupancy. The trial court decreed the suit holding that Birdhi Lal being a trespasser was not liable to be ejected from the land. The appeal preferred by the respondent was allowed by the Board of Revenue. The High Court held that Birdhah lyow did not fall within the definition of "evacuee property" contained in section 2(42) of the Act and hence the appellant was not entitled to eject the respondent. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have power to interfere with the decision of the revenue authorities on questions of fact which are final and no other. [608F] 2.1 In order to succeed in his suit, Kishori lal had to show that Birdhiku was a trespass er and there was no error apparent on the face of the record. The High COurt has rightly held that the appellant was entitled to evict Kishori Lai. The High Com missioner had correctly found that the appellant had failed to establish his claim. [612E] 4. The High 'Court has rightly affirmed the judgment of the Assistant Collector. [613D] 5. The High 905 Court has rightly held on the facts of the case that the appellant could not
1385: The appellants were the Directors of a Co operative Insurance Society. They filed a complaint in the Court of the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta, under sections 467, 471 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code and section 120B of the Indian penal Code against the two appellants. The complaint was dismissed by the Magistrate under section 203 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on the ground that it did not disclose any offence against the accused persons. An appeal to the High Court was summarily rejected. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order dismissing the complaint was not one of dismissal for want of prosecution but one of conviction. [314 D] (ii) The order of the Magistrate dismissing the complaint is not one of conviction and an order of acquittal cannot be made without giving an opportunity to the complainant to prove his case by cross examining the witnesses produced by him. [315 B C] (iii) The order passed by the Magistrate dismissing a complaint under section 203 does not require interference as no notice has been given to the appellants before filing their respective complaints. [316 A]
3425: The respondent was a member of the Punjab Civil Service (Executive Branch) and retired from service on October 1, 1949. In June 1961 he received a copy of letter No. 5137 ED I 60/9269 dated May 2, 1961 addressed by the Secretary to Government, Punjab, Education Department to the Director of Public Instruction, Punjab, Chandigarh, conveying sanction of the Governor of Punjab to the grant to him i.e. the respondent of superannuation pension and death cum retirement gratuity under rules 5.27 and 6.13 of the Punjab civil Service Rules, Vol. II read with para 9(1)(a) of the New Pension Rules, 1951. The said order was passed in exercise of the powers conferred by rule 6.4 of the Punjab Cricket School,natural lyabai jan, 1959, as amended from time to time. The respondent challenged the aforesaid decision of the Government to apply the cut in his pension and gratuity under clauses (a) and (b) of rule 6. 449 of the Punjab Service Rules, Volume II read with paragraph 9(1) (a) of New Pension Rules 1951. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the order imposing the cut in the respondent 's pension and gratuity was not one of punishment within the meaning of article 311(2) of the Constitution and that it could not be made without complying with the provisions of article 311 (2). On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order imposing the penalty of cut in the pension and gratuity of the respondent was an administrative order and the case did not fall within the purview of article 311 of the Constitution. [258 B] (ii) The order was not an administrative order but a quasi judicial function. It was not required to be made by the authority empowered to dismiss or remove a person from service. [255 D] (iii) The order is not an administrative act. It is purely executive acts. The fact that the order imposes some other administrative order after the decision of the High Court does not make such order a legislative activity. [256 F G] Deokinandan Prasad vs State of Bihar & Ors. , referred to.
87: The plaintiff 's case was that the parties were Sudras and belonged to the Nanak Shai sect of Fakirs, and that the parties formed a joint Hindu family. The plaintiff alleged that the parties had been dasipu tras of Nandkishore Das by another concubine, and that he and the third defendant, Shibgarh Das formed a joint family. The trial court dismissed the suit holding among other things (1) that the plaintiff not being in joint possession of any of the properties, the suit for partition was not maintainable, (2) that the parties being Sudras, the plaintiff could not be made the subject of partition, and (3) that the defendant No. 5, Kuldip Das pleaded to the same effect and further alleged that the plaintiff had no cause of action against the defendant No 5. On appeal the High Court held that the plaintiff having failed to prove his claim against the defendant, the suit was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The findings which have given rise to the present appeal are findings of fact based on appreciation of evidence and they do not give rise to any question of law. [839 E] (a) The finding is one of fact. It is open to the High Court to reappraise the entire evidence for itself and to come to its own conclusion. But it cannot be said that the High Court has acted illegally or with material irregularity so as to attract the provisions of article 227 of the Constitution. [840 G H] (b) The High Court has rightly pointed out that the findings of fact arrived at by the courts below are findings of law and need not be interfered with unless they are shown to be palpably wrong or manifestly perverse. [841 A B] (c) The High Courts are not constituted as appellate authorities over the decision of the subordinate tribunals within their jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution and therefore, the jurisdiction of this Court is limited to seeing that the tribunal functions within the limits of its authority. [842 C D]
2200: The appellants, who were dealers in iron and steel, purchased iron scrap from various dealers in Punjab and outside for making rolled steel section and selling the same. They filed writ petitions under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the orders of assessment passed by the assessing authorities and for restraining them from levying purchase tax on the goods purchased and for refund of the tax illegally collected from them. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the amended provision, section 2(ff), was void as the legislature had not authorised it; (ii) the amendment made a mere change in the charging section which provided that the entire Act shall be operative only with prospective effect so as to make any change or alteration in such charging provisions within the meaning of the definition clause; and (iii) the amendment was invalid because it contravened sections 14 and 15 of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. HELD : (i) The amended provision, Section 5, was validated by the State Legislature by the East Punjab General Sales Tax Amendment Act, 1948. [764 E] (ii)The amended provision, s.2(ff) was also void because it contravened the provisions of sections 14 and15 of the Central sales Tax Act, 1947. [765 F G] (iii)Section 2(ff) is not ultra vires the State Legislature inasmuch as the said section is stillborn and that, as the said Section is the charging section, the entire Act was void. 1307: The appellant, a money lender, filed a suit under section 36 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act for an order reopening the personal decree against him. The trial court decreed the suit and directed that a new decree be drawn up and that the amount due under the personal decree be paid in three annual instalments. Against this decree an appeal was preferred to the District Court. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the cross objections filed by the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the High Court had no jurisdiction to rehear a second appeal under section 100 C.P.C., (ii) the High Courts ' decision was erroneous as the provisions of Order XLVII Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure were not applicable to such a case; (iii) the High court had wrongly decided the question whether the decree passed by the trial court was legally enforceable or not. HELD: (i) The High Court had rightly decided the question. The High Court could have remanded the matter to the trial court for deciding the question afresh after taking evidence. [891 F] (ii) The High court had rightly decided that the decree passed in the second appeal was not legally enforceable. [890 G] (iii) The High Courts ' decisions were correct on all material points and they had correctly decided the question of law. [892 B]
2933: The respondent was a watches carrying on the business of keeping and selling watches. He carried on the same business in the name of Walton Watch Company, which had been seized on March 19, 1963 under section 110(1) of the Customs Act. The Collector of Customs granted extension for a further period of four months on September 19, 1963, but the respondent 's application for extension was rejected by the Collector on September 19. The respondent filed an appeal before the Central Board of Revenue which allowed the appeal on the ground that the Collector could not extend the time for giving notice under section 124 (a) of the Act beyond six months of seizure. The appellant contended that the proviso to section 1 10 (2) of the , did not contemplate any notice to the respondent as the considerations which would weigh with the Collector or which would be relevant for granting extension would be of such a nature that they could not be disclosed; that the Collector should have given a reasonable opportunity to the respondent to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him; that the proviso did not contemplate a notice to the Collector as the considerations that would weigh with him and that therefore there was no question of any right being vested in the respondent on the expiry of the time prescribed under sub section (2) or that the extension was within one year. Held: (i) The proviso to section I10(2) does not contemplate any fresh notice to the person concerned after the initial period of six months expires. [808 E] (ii) The proviso contemplates a notice to be issued to the person affected by the extension of time. The expression "reasonable belief" has reference to a substantial act of personal character and cannot mean mere conjecture or suspicion. The onus is upon the person who seeks to explain his conduct to prove that he knows nothing about it. If he fails to do so, the extension of the period must be held to be ineffective and unenforceable. In the present case, the Collector of Customs had applied his mind to the question whether the extension for a period exceeding six months could be granted. The Collector had also examined the matter in detail and had come to the conclusion that the extension for more than six months was justified. The Collector was not
975: The appellant was a resident of Bombay in the taxable territory and had his place of business at Bombay. He filed returns for the assessment years 1955 56, 1956 57 and 1957 58 but did not file any return. In proceedings under section 34(1)(a) he disclosed income from his own business in the year of account ending March 31, 1954, but did not disclose the income in the year ending March 31. The Income Tax Officer issued notices to him under section 34 read with section 22(2). The appellant contended that the notice was invalid as it was served beyond eight years from the end of the year of assessment. Held, that the notice under section 22(1) was valid and the period of limitation prescribed by section 34(I)(a) was not applicable to the issue of such a notice. Section 34(1) (a) does not apply to nonresident assessees because the words "any person who has taxable income" are used only where there is omission or failure on the part of an assessee to make a return within the time allowed. The omission or failure must be one which occurs every day during the course of the year. The omission and/or failure must be the same as the omission or failure referred to in section 22(l). The omission or default must arise out of the omission or default of the assessee and not out of his fault. The omission must be one done by him within a reasonable time and if the omission or delay arose out of the omissions or default of an assessee, then the time taken in prosecuting the matter must be excluded.
1488: The appellant company was a jute mill company which purchased raw jute and manufactured finished goods therefrom. HELD: (i) The contracts in question are not void under s.9 of the Act because they do not contravene any of the provisions of the Act and the appellant is not entitled to enforce the contracts against the respondents. [957 G] (ii) The contracts were not hit by the provisions of s.55(1) Of the , and the appellant was entitled to invoke the provisions of that section. [958 B C] (iii
5826: The appellant company entered into an agreement with the respondent No. 1 Madhya Pradesh Electricity Board for supply of electricity in accordance with the terms and conditions mentioned therein. The Board was not able to generate sufficient electricity to meet the full demand of the consumers and with a view to ease the situation two orders were issued by the States of Madhya Pradesh under section 22B of the called as the Madhya Pradesh Electricity Supply and Consumption Regulation Order 1975 and the Madhya Pradesh electricity generation, Control and use regulation Order, 1975. The Board had to supply 2,500 K.W. power on A.T. basis with effect from 1.11.1973. The Divisional Engineer, Gwalior informed the appellant Company that the Board would supply 2,000 K.W power on AT basis with effect form 12.11.1979. The appellant Company replied by its letter dt. 17.5,1975 stating that the Board was entitled to recover the additional energy drawn by it from the appellant without any prior approval of the Board and a letter Annexure `T ' dated 5.8.1980 was sent to the Company explaining the position and requesting the Board to reconsider the matter. The Company also wrote a letter to the Board on 5.880 stating that the supply availed by it with effect from 12.11 1979 would be billed at the penal rate. The Company further stated that the Board may, however, reduce the contract Demand charges if the Board is not willing to do so. The Company was asked to furnish the details of the additional power drawn by it. The Company furnished the details of additional power drawn and the Board accepted the same. The Company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the reduction of contract demand. The High Court dismissed the writ application. Hence this appeal
6596: % The appellant, a tenant of the respondent Bank, was in occupation of a shop under a lease agreement executed between the parties. Clause (iii) of sub section (3) of Section 1 of the Jammu & Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966 provides that the provisions of the Act shall be applicable to every tenant of residential premises also. The appellant filed an application before the Rent Controller for eviction of the tenant on the ground of his income from business and other factors. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that clause (iii) was attracted in respect of the appellant 's income. The appeal preferred by the appellant against the said order was allowed by the District Judge. The High Court held that clause (ii) of sub s.(3) of section 1 of the Act is not hit by the provisions of Article 14 of the Constitution. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned clause does not take into account the nature of the building, but only the income of the tenant. It is submitted that the impugned provision is discriminatory and arbitrary because it draws an artificial distinction between tenants on the basis of their income. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The test adopted by the legislature for the purpose of clause (iii), namely, whether the tenant is a tenant of an industrial or commercial concern, is not an intelligible classifi cation, for the income of a tenant may vary from year to year depending upon the nature of his business and other relevant factors. [839E F] 1.2 The object of the Act being to protect the tenants from exploitation, the Act has to be interpreted in such a way as to give protection to the tenants who are poor and helpless. The classification is reasonable and cannot be said to be unreasonable. [841F G] 1.3 The object of clause (iiia) of sub sec tion (3) is to prevent exploitation of the tenants by the tenants. The word "income" is used in contradistinction to the word "profits". The word "profit" is used to convey the idea of an income. The word is used to denote the profits of the business carried on by the tenant.
4229: The respondent was searched by the customs authorities and currency notes were seized. An appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the confiscation of the currency notes was dismissed. In second appeal before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, the assessee represented that if he was regarded as engaged in the business of smuggling gold he was entitled to a deduction under section 10(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Tribunal held that the assessee was carrying on the business of transporting currency notes across the border and that he was not concerned with the actual smuggling or the actual smugglers. On reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The loss incurred in carrying out the illegal business must be allowed as a deductible expenditure under section 10 (1) of Income Tax Act. [803 G] 2. The test for determining whether the loss is an allowable deduction is whether the amount sought to be deducted is one which the assessee knew that the necessary incident involved in the business is detection by the Customs authorities and the consequent confiscation of the notes. If it is, no question of any notional income arises from the activity of smuggling. [804 A B] 3. The test is whether the assessee has been able to establish that he had knowledge that the necessary event took place at the time when the notes were seized and that he did not know that the necessary party was aiding him in carrying on that business. If he is so aware, he will be entitled to deduct the said expenditure under section 1o of the Act. [894 C E] 4. The test of the nature of the business of the assessee is to see what is the net income of the assessee? What is the net profits brought to tax by the assessee would depend upon the facts of each case. [805 F] 5. The test laid down by this Court in Badridas Daga vs Commissioner of Income tax, is that for the purpose of Section 10(1), the deduction must be allowed. [806 A] 6. The test to determine whether the assessee had been able to prove that he had information that the necessary act was detection by the customs authority and the consequent seizure
932: The Rajpramukh of the State of Rajasthan issued a notification under section 15 of the (V of 1861) under which " the Harijan and Muslim inhabitants of the villages in which an additional police force was stationed, were exempted from liability to bear any portion of the cost of that force. " The Rajpramanik appealed to the High Court against the order of the State Government. The High Court dismissed the appeal as not maintainable on the ground that the Rajpramukhs were not " confined to the area within their own police force" and that they had no locus standi to file the appeal. Held:(i) The exemption of the Harijan & Muslim inhabitants of these villages from liability to pay the cost of the additional force was not based on the ground of caste or religion or the other criteria set out in article 15(1). (ii)The exemption of the Rajpramanhik was not based upon the ground of religion or race or caste but on the ground whether the persons belonging to these communities were found to be peace loving or law abiding citizens. The exemption could only be for those who were found to have been peace loving and law abiding people. (iii)The exemption was not applicable to the Rajprakashs of the villages where the Rajputana and the Muslims were posted. The exemption was applicable only to those who were born in the community or community which actually belonged to the Rajputan or community.
3105: The respondent company was a fairly prosperous concern and one of the biggest of its kind in Asia. It had Central Repair shops in Calcutta and other places and a Purchasing Depot in Kerala. The Company and the appellants represented by Unions were entering into various agreements from time to time, the last of which was on August 30, 1962. The agreement provided for payment of bonus at the rate of 15% of the profits made during the year. The company paid bonus to the workmen as per the Act in addition to what has been paid under the Agreement exhibit A.5. The company refused to accede to the demand of the workmen for payment of Bonus for the year 1964 at the rates mentioned therein. The State Government on June 25, 1966 referred to the Third Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal, for adjudication the following dispute : "Whether the employees of the Company represented by the Union and the workmen are entitled to Bonus for year 1964 under the in addition to the Bonus paid to them and whether in view of the Agreement exhibitA. 5 is applicable to such employees ?" The Tribunal held that the general bonus paid under the agreement exhibit A. 5 was an amount paid as production bonus or incentive wages. The Tribunal also found that the demands of the workmen were as pro duction bonus and that it was not an annual payment nor was it paid in lieu of bonus based on profits. The Tribunal further held that the demand of bonus was ex gratia payment and not a term bonus and that the claim for profit bonus was not admissible under section 32(vii) (a) of the Act. The Tribunal accordingly directed the Company to pay the bonus at the rates specified in the agreement exhibit B. The Company filed an appeal against the award before this Court contending that the Tribunal erred in holding that the general scheme of the agreement exhibit 'A ' was not applicable to the case. The Company contended that the general terms and conditions of the agreement were not identical with those of exhibit 'B ' and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the same. The Company also contended that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that there was no general bonus payable to the workmen. The Company further contended that the award of the Tribunal was contrary to the terms of the agreement and the evidence
931: The respondent firm which is not a licensed dealer under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, was assessed to sales tax for the year 1952 53 on the basis that it had obtained licences under the relevant provisions of the Act. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the assessment but this petition was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The rule regarding the operation of rr. 16(5), 16(5A) and 16(5B) of the Turnover and Assessment Rules, 1939, framed under section 5(1)(b) of the Act, were not ultra vires as they were inconsistent with the provisions of the statute under which they were made. [156 E F] V.S. Syed Mohammed & Co. vs State of Madras, ; , followed. (ii) The rule relating to the operation of the rule regarding the benefit of single point taxation in the case of hides and skins was not ultra vires section 5(vi) of the Madras General Sale Tax Act, 1930. [155 G H] V. S. Syed Mohammad & Co. V. State of Madras A.I.R. , referred to.
1225: The respondents entered into three contracts for the construction of a aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and other works at Ranchi. They entered into two contracts for the work of construction of a tente e. The first contract related to the construction of an aerodrome and the second was of a building which had been completed before the agreement was signed. The arbitrator who made his award in respect of these contracts was not a party to the arbitration proceedings but he was a party to another arbitration proceeding under section 17 of the . He sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The Subordinate Judge who tried the suit held that there was no valid agreement of reference to arbitration and decreed the suit. On appeal by the appellant the High Court confirmed the decree. Held, that the agreement for reference to arbitration did not comply with the requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, and the award was therefore not binding on the Government. The agreement was not an instrument relating to the execution of works within the meaning of section 175 (3). The award did not require any legal action against the Government. It was not executable as a decree. The award did nothing more than to direct the Government to execute the agreement. The agreement did not provide for arbitration nor provided for setting aside or refusing to set aside the award.
1982: The appellant, a sugar mill, was levying cess on sugarcane purchased by it. Section 23 of the Madhya Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1961 provided for the method of collection of cess. Section 21 of the said Act prescribed for the constitution of the Council which was proposed to be constituted under section 5. The appellant submitted its bill to the Council. The Council considered it desirable that the Council should have a re look at the Bill before it could pass the resolution. The Council, however, did not consider it necessary to give its opinion as to whether the Bill was in law or in legislative competence. The appellant thereupon filed writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act. The High Court held that the Act was intra vires and valid but the Council was not justified in passing the impugned order. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Act is a piece of colourable legislation with a view to make provision for the constitution and composition of the Council and the Council are not competent to pass any legislation in respect of the levy, assessment and collection of cess, cess or fee. [532 C] (ii) The Act does not represent the whole scheme of the legislation. It represents the entire scheme of the statute. The Act is not intended to confer power upon the Council to collect cess or tax from the occupier of the land. The cess or tax has been levied and collected in accordance with law. [533 D E] (iii) The Act, in other words, does not represent a part of the levy which is sought to be imposed. The Act does represent the whole purpose of the levy. The Act cannot be challenged on the ground that it is ultra vires the State Legislature. [534 F G]
4832: The Appellant, a publisher of books for general reading to be kept in school and college libraries was selected by the State Government as a supplementary list of 105 books out of the said 1,718 books which had been submitted for selection. The Selection Committee restricted the list of 466 books out of 1,719 books submitted for selection to the year 1982 and also directed that the same should be made available to the State Government for approval. The State Government 's decision with respect to purchasing books out of 446 books was not challenged before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition under Article 226 of the Constitution filed by the Appellants. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The procedure followed by the State of Orissa in setting up a committee for the selection of books for purchase of books from the grant made by the Central Government was neither arbitrary nor against public interest inasmuch as the procedure followed by it was neither arbitrary or violative of any fundamental rights of the appellants. [329F] 1.2 In the instant case, the procedure followed was that the State Government approved the selection of the books for purchase and sale of books from grants made by the central government. The State of Orissa did not choose to make any further selections for purchase of book from the grants made by it. It only reserved the right to reject any book recommended by the Assessment Sub Committee and the same was subject to approval by the State Govt. The State Govt. decided to select a supplementary list for purchase of the books from the grants so made. This decision was not challenged at all. [334G H; 335A] 2.1 The State Government has no power to change the rules of the game after its game is over. The process of selection is governed by the rules of business and not by the executive instructions issued by the Government. The State has power to make the selections even in cases where there are no rules governing the selections. [338B C] 2.2 The State Government cannot change the rules relating to the purchase of books. [339C] 3. The State is entitled to fix the time within which the books have to be purchased and the same can be rejected if they do
2885: Section 7 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 37 of 1954 provides that no person shall himself or by any other person on his behalf manufacture for sale, store, sell or distribute (i) any adulterated food; (ii) any article of food in contravention of any other provision of the Act or of any rule made thereunder. Section 13 provides that no prosecution for an offence under section 7 shall be instituted except with the previous sanction of the Central Government or such authority as may be specified by the Central Government in this behalf. Section 19 provides that no court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under section 7 except upon a complaint in writing made by the Food Analyst or some officer duly authorised by him. Section 20 provides that no Court shall take cognizance 'of any offence punishable tinder section 7 unless there is a complaint in respect thereof by the Food (Health) Authority. Section 21 provides that no civil court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which the Central Government, or the State Government, as the case may be, is empowered by or under the Act to determine and no injunction can be granted by any court in respect of anything said or any 898 act alleged to be done under the Act. Section 22 provides that no criminal court shall take cognisance of any offence under the Act except upon a report in writing of the facts constituting such offence made by a person who has been concerned in the distribution of the food grains. Section 23 provides that no objection shall be taken to any search or seizure under the Act and every such objection shall be deemed to be a valid Royalty. Section 24 provides that no order passed by a Magistrate under the Act shall remain in force for more than twelve days after the making of the same. Section 25 provides that no sentence of fine shall be imposed by a Magistrate on the accused unless the trial has been had in the Court. Section 26 provides that no direction for the arrest of any person under the Act or any rule made under it shall be given by any Criminal Court after the expiration of one month from the date of the performance of an agreement between the parties to arrest the offender. 4973: The appellant and respondents 1 to 3 were the Shebait of a temple known as "Ganguli Ji" situated in the town of Panna. 1518: The appellants purchased the properties in dispute by a sale held on February 27, 1946. They filed a suit for recovery of the arrears due from them under section 128(f) of the Act. 1785: The petitioner was selected by the Madras Public Service Commission as a Lower Division Clerk under the Madras Ministerial Service Rules in 1949. He was allotted to the Revenue Department and posted in South Kanara District. In 1956, the Government of India issued an order reducing the petitioner in rank from the post of Upper Division Clerk to that of a temporary Upper Division Clerk. On May 11, 1957, the Government passed orders varying the conditions of service of the petitioner with retrospective effect from November 1, 1956. The petitioner challenged the validity of this order on the ground that the Mysore General Services (Revenue Subordinate Branch) Recruitment Rules 1959 were not made with the previous approval of the Central Government under section 115(7) of the State Reorganisation Act, 1956, and therefore did not govern the petitioner insofar as the conditions of his service had been varied to his disadvantage. Held, that the Mysore Government had no power to make any rules under article 309 of the Constitution after November 1,1956, when the Central Government had made its order. The Mysore General Services Rules, 1959, which were made in exercise of the powers conferred by section 115(1) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 were made before November 1, 1966. The Mysore Government had the power to make rules under article 313 of the Constitution for the more convenient transaction of the business of the Government of the State. The Mysore Goverment had the power under section 115 (7) of Act 1 of 1960 to make rules regarding conditions of service applicable immediately before November 1. 1956, to all persons who were members of the service in connection with the affairs of the State of Mysore. The Mysore Rules of 1959, which are made under section 115 of the States Reorganisa tion Act, 1956 do not affect the rights of the petitioner to be considered for promotion to the post of a temporary Lower Division Clerk.
351: The petitioners were tenants of jagirs in the former State of Pepsu. They had been paying rent to the Government for their lands and buildings on the basis of a rate sanctioned by the Board of Revenue, but were not being assessed to land revenue. In 1955, the Government issued a notification under section 81 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887, fixing the rates of rent payable by the petitioners for the jagir lands and buildings. The petitioners challenged the validity of this notification in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the notification was bad as it contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it fixed the rates without any modification and made a provision for revision of the same. Held, that the notification did not infringe any fundamental right of the petitioners guaranteed by articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution. The classification of jagirdars into tenants and non tenancy was based upon the rent which they paid for their lands. The rent rate was fixed on the basis that the tenants were liable to pay rent from the first day of July next following the date of settlement; and if the rent rate was to be fixed on the first day after the date of the settlement, then there would have been no discrimination between the tenants who were liable to be evicted on the ground of rent being fixed from the first of July next succeeding. The classification was founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group, and was reasonable and valid. The classification is not unreasonable and cannot be said to violate articles 14,19 and 31 of Constitution.
44: The appellant was convicted by the Sub Divisional Magistrate of Darjeeling under section 7 of the Essential Supplies Act, 1946, and sentenced to six months ' rigoro us imprisonment. The High Court set aside the conviction but granted a certificate under article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution. Held, that the Governor 's notification of 14th December, 1946, continued the operation of the Essential Suppi sions Act in the district of Darjeellaba beyond the expiry of the life of the Act. The Governor 's Notification of 14th March, 1947, did not extend the period of one year from the date of the emergency. The Governor General had power to extend the period within which the Governor General could issue a notification extending the period of the Emergency. The notification of 14 th March, 1947 extended the period of emergency only.
1643: The appellant was the husband of the respondent. He had a wife and two children out of his wedded wife. On the question whether he had established that the respondent had an irrevocable determination to break up the matrimonial home when she left the matrimonial home on February 26, 1954, and did not return to him thereafter, the Court held that the appellant bad no reasonable cause for not returning to the husband 's house after the expiry of the period of one month from the date of his marriage and that the respondent 's conduct in not returning to his parental home at Bombay with her parents in law amounted to desertion under section 10(1)(a) of the Indian , as such the appellant was guilty of desertion. Held, that the appellant was entitled to a decree for judicial separation under section 10 (1) (a) of Act 2 of 1955. The fact that the appellant had been living separately since November 11, 1946, would not make any difference between them and the respondent could not be regarded as deserting her. The appellant was not guilty of any conduct unbecoming of a husband which would justify the passing of a decree for divorce against him.

The question arose whether the appellant company was liable to pay sales tax on the value of the spare parts supplied by the respondent company as a result of their use in the process of repairing servicing and overhauling of the specified aircraft. The mere fact that the appellants accepted the sum in respect of another building does not by itself establish that they accepted it as consideration for the first building. 3092: The respondents were carrying on business of manufacturing bidis in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The Divisional Forest Officer seized two quantities of such leaves from the respondents ' factory and took them to the factory premises. The respondents moved the Sub Divisional Forest Officer Saugor who seized two quantities from them. The Sub Divisional Forest officer seized the remaining quantity of the leaves from the factory and seized the remaining stock from the factory. The respondents filed a complaint against the appellants before the District Magistrate, who was authorised by the State Government under section 3(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Tendu Patta Wyapar Viniyaman Act, 1964, alleging that the appellants had committed offences under sections 5 and 7 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned Act did not infringe any fundamental right of the respondents guaranteed by articles 14, 19(1) (f), 25 and 26 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (a) The Act does not infringe article 19(5) of the constitution. [85 C] (b) Section 3(3) of the Act provides that no person shall transport or cause to be transported any specified class of tendu plants from any place within the State to any other place in the same state. The Act does provide for control of transport of certain specified kinds of tendu
4281: The appellant was the adopted son of a Hindu. He executed a deed of adoption in favour of his adoptive father Mansaram, who was then a minor. The deed recited that the appellant had been adopted by Mansaram on August 10, 1944, and that he had been appointed as a guardian of the property of the minor. The appellant filed a suit for compulsory registration of the deed of adoption and for an injunction restraining the respondents from interfering with his possession. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court decreed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The deed of adoption did not contain any recital that Mansaram was not in a fit state of mind at the relevant time. [597 G] (ii) It is clear from the plaint that the appellant was not present when the deed of adopt ment was executed and even if it be assumed that he was not in sound disposing state of mind, he could not have been prevented from entering into a transaction which was not within his competence or jurisdiction. [598 B] (iii) There is no evidence whatsoever to show when and where the adoption took place and even whether the necessary ceremonies were performed. The mere fact that the adoption took pacts of the appellant in the year 1944 does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that he was born in a state of mind before he entered into a transaction of adoption. [599 D E]
7035: The appellant was charged with the offence of murder and convicted under section 302 IPC. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the evidence of PW3, who is sister of PW3 and PW4, who had seen the occurrence on 21.3.1976, being inimical to the appellant, was not reliable; that the evidence given by PW3 was unreliable because he had been declared hostile and had not supported the prosecution case; and that the possibility of PW3 having been won over could not be ruled out. On behalf of the State, it was submitted that PW3 had stated before the police that when he went to the house of the appellant on 21.1.1976, he told him that her uncle had been killed by Anil and his brothers but his uncle did not tell him that he had been woning by the deceased. It was further submitted that the evidence regarding PW3 having witnessed the occurrence was unacceptable since he had not named the appellant as one of the assailants. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of PW 3, who is a sister of PW 3 and PW 4, who has also turned hostile cannot be rejected merely because she happens to be the sister of PW4. [813F] 2. The possibility that PW3 might have been wonful or some other person may not be totally excluded from consideration. The possibility of PW4 having been wrecked by the appellant and his uncle would not stand scrutiny because even according to PW3, when he ran from the place of occurrence, he told her that her uncle was killed by Anil. [814C D] 3. The evidence given by PWs 3 and 4, who are sister and brother of PW3 cannot be discarded only on account of their being related to the deceased. They were closely related to the appellant. Their testimony about the presence of PW3 at the scene of occurrence is acceptable. The possibility, therefore, that both the injuries had been caused to the deceased by Mahendra, with the crowbar, who came first, gave a blow to the deceased on his head which resulted in his death cannot be ruled out.[815E F] 4.
2097: The appellant was a manufacturer of T.B. Hospital and T.B., Hospitals in the State of Rajasthan. The Government of Bharatpur issued another notification on January 16, 1956 revoking the tax concessions granted to the appellant. On appeal the High Court held that item No. 3 of the Bharatpur notification was a term of the contract of sale between the parties and the State of Saurashtra had no authority to revoke the tax concession. HELD: (i) The notification dated January 16,1956 was a term Of the contract of sales between the appellant and the State and was not a part of the contract. [92F] (ii) The notification merely extended the concession granted to the State of Bharatpur by its notification dated January 15, 1956. It did not impose any obligation upon the State of Banswara to perform its obligations under the notification. Nor did it make any provision for the payment of any duty on the import of goods into the State from other States. [93A B] (iii) The notification was not a law imposing or authorising the imposition of any duty. It was only an executive order issued by the Central Government in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the . [94C]
6937: The appellant was a member of the Maharashtra Legislative Assembly. He filed a writ petition in the High Court for a direction to the State Government to take action against the two Hon 'ble Judges of the High Court who dismissed his Writ Petition on 2.4.79 and thereafter the Review Petition on 23.4.1979 and also impleaded Shri R.P. Thorat, the then Judge of the Bombay High Court as respondent No. 3. The Division Bench of the High court took cognizance of criminal contempt and directed issue of notice on 13.5.80 to the appellant directing him to show cause why he should not be punished for contempt of Court to which the appellant filed reply raising certain preliminary objections stating that the notice was bad for the reasons, namely, (1) the Section of the Act under which cognizance had been taken was not specifically mentioned; (2) though the offending portions were marked the notice did not show sufficient cause as to why the words and expressions used therein have been construed as contemptuous; (3) the procedure followed by the High Court was contrary to the rules framed by it; and (4) no consent of the Advocate General had been obtained. The Division bench held that the cognizance of the criminal contempt was taken by it on suo moto basis and non quoting of the provisions of section 16 of the Act was immaterial and that the contemner was informed that the Court was invoking its jurisdiction under Article 215 of the Constitution of India to punish him for contempt. The Division appeal filed by the appellant was allowed and the order passed by the Single Judge was restored. 873 In the review application, the petitioner contended that there was error apparent on the face of the record because the High Court in its suo motu action had taken cognizance of the contempt petition without giving a clear 1575 notice to the contemnor. The Division Beach of the High COurt, on the other hand, contended that the contempt petition was maintainable before the High Court. Allowing the review application and remitting the matter to the High Court, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has committed an error in entertaining the review application. [872F] 2. The High court while exercising power under Article 215 is not entitled to act as a court of appeal against the decision
1090: The appellant, a company, was in the service of the respondent company. In respect of leave to its staff members, the respondents applied for privilege leave which was refused by the appellant. The appellant contended that the refusal was arbitrary and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the refusal to grant privilege leave amounted to denial of equal protection of law guaranteed under article 16(1) of the Constitution and so it was void. It was not discriminatory but was based on an intelligible differentia having a rational relation to the object of the Act. The classification made by the award did not violate article 14 of 'the Constitution. The grant of privilege leave was not dependent upon any condition precedent which would justify the grant of privilege or sick leave. The grant could be restricted only to cases where there was no special benefit to the workmen concerned. The grant was not arbitrary nor was it unreasonable. The grant had been made in the interest of industrial peace and public safety. The refusal to grant leave was justified as it was not based on any extraneous grounds.
1705: The respondent was an Assistant Commissioner of Police in the Calcutta City and the appellant had made a complaint against him alleging that he had committed offences under section 120B/420, I.P.C. and section 420, I. P. C. He also filed a complaint before the Chief Presidency Magistrate against the two other persons for cheating. The Chief Presidency Magistrate took cognizance of the offence on the basis of the said complaint and issued process to the appellant. The appellant contended that the High Court should not have quashed the process as it would amount to quashing the entire proceedings which were pending before the Magistrate. Held: (i) The order passed by the High Court quashing the process is set aside and the Magistrate will proceed further with the case. [801 F] (ii)The High Court has no jurisdiction to quash the process at the stage of taking cognizance of the offences alleged to have been committed by the accused. It is only when the Magistrate decides that there is sufficient ground for proceeding further that he can be proceeded against. In the present case, the Magistrate did not decide whether there was sufficient ground for proceedings against the appellant or not. He merely decided that the complaint should be dropped. The High Court could not, therefore, interfere with the order of the Magistrate. [802 B D]

1611: The respondent was convicted under section 323 and section 324 read with section 511 of the Indian Penal Code. He was detained in jail custody for a period exceeding forty eight hours. His application to the High Court for release on bail was rejected by the District Magistrate who ordered him to be taken into custody. On an application by the respondent, the High Court directed that Bipat Gope should appear before the District Magistrate on Monday following which he was released. The State filed a petition under article 226 challenging the order of the District Magistrate and the High Court ordered on May 1, 1958, that Bipta Gope should be taken into detention and sent him to jail. The High Court held that the order of release by the District magistrate was an order for his unconditional release and therefore he could not be rearrested. The State appealed to this Court. Held:(i) Rule 4 of the Rules framed under section 49 of the Prisons Act does not provide for the grant of conditional release to a prisoner on his appearing before court or being allowed to go through the prison authorities and the rule is only directory and not mandatory. (ii)The rule does not provide expressly for the grant to a prisoner of conditional release by the High Court. It merely provides for the conditions under which the convict may be released. The rule is intended to serve a different purpose than the one mentioned in the rule. The rule cannot be construed as conferring a right upon a person to be released on parole. (iii)It is not correct to say that the rule is directory because it will be applicable where there are no alternative arrangements. But it can be made applicable only if there is some other provision in the rules which provides for the grant or non grant of such remission as is contemplated by r. 549 of the Bihar Jail Manual.

[833F G] 1.2 If the investigation of a Criminal Case is stinking with the sole purpose of delaying the proceedings in the criminal case, the same cannot be permitted to be continued against the erring officers.
