468: The petitioner was a Sub inspector of Police in the then State of Bhopal. He was prosecuted and convicted for offences under section 161, Indian Penal Code, and section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, on a charge of accepting a bribe to the tune of Rs. 100 by the Sub Inspector of Police. The Judicial Commissioner held that no sanction had been given for the prosecution of the petitioner and the Special Judge, Bhopal, took cognizance of the offence without a legal sanction. On appeal by the petitioner, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed against him but granted a certificate under article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution. Held, that the Special Judge was not a Court of competent jurisdiction to try the case. Section 403 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, which corresponds to section 423 of the Code, provides that all offences under any law shall be tried by a Special judge within the local limits of his jurisdiction. Section 404 (2) of the code of Criminal Procedure provides that when trying any case, a special Judge may also try any offence other than an offence specified in section 6 with which the accused may, under the Code of criminal Procedure, 1898. be charged at the same trial. The words "any trial" in section 403 (2) are wide enough to include all such trials where the accused is convicted and sentenced.
2791: The appellants were charged with offences under section 395 and 412 of the Indian Penal Code. They pleaded that they had been falsely implicated in the case by the police. The trial court accepted the plea but the High Court acquitted them holding that there was no evidence to show that the police party had come to search for the buffalo or that it was a police party. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) It is not necessary that there should be an elaborate enquiry as to facts and circumstances of each case before ordering a search under section 166(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [1130 E] (ii) There is nothing in section 165 of the Code which makes it incumbent on the police officer to make an enquiry before a conviction can be recorded against any person. [1131 F] (iii) The police officers who are entrusted with the investigation of a cognizable offence cannot be said to have knowledge that the investigation was being conducted by the police without their knowledge. [1132 D] (iv) Section 165 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not require that the police must hold an enquiry before arresting any person. The power of arrest is subject to the condition that if the officer has reason to believe that it is in the interest of justice to investigate the same he shall immediately give notice in writing to the person arrested and take his statement into confidence. The police officer may, however, arrest a person without warrant when he suspects that his presence would be unlawful. But the arrest is only for the purpose of investigation and does not amount to voluntary arrest. [1133 G 1134 A] (v) The police officer has a duty to conduct the investigation in accordance with law and to inform the public prosecutor about the commission of an offence. He has also a duty to assist the public prosecutor in obtaining relevant information. [1135 B]
1559: The appellants were dealers in sugar. They sold sugar to the Government of India under a contract entered into by them with the Government of Madras for the supply of sugar. The Government of India Act, 1935 was passed for the purpose of levying sales tax on sale of goods and the Provincial Legislature had power to legislate for levy of tax on sale or purchase of goods as defined in section 4(1) of the Indian Sale of Goods Act, 1930. Under the Government of Indian States Act, 1935 the Provincial Legislature was empowered to enact laws imposing liability to pay sales tax on the value of goods used in the execution of building contracts. The Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Act prescribing rates of tax on the sale of sugar. In exercise of authority conferred by the notification the Government of Bihar made the Bihar Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1947, which amended the definition of "sale" given in the two Acts. By section 2(g) of the Act the expression "sale" means any transfer of property in goods .by one person to another in the course of trade or commerce .and includes a transfer of goods on hire purchase or other instalment system of payment . , but does not include a mortgage, hypothecation, charge or pledge. The appellants contended that there was no sale by the assessees of sugar in their hands and that the State Legislature had no power to impose tax on such transactions. Held, that the definition of 'sale ' in the two enactments at all material times was not confined to the sale of goods only, but it included a transfer of property and that the expression "transfer of goods" in the two statutes could not be limited to the mere physical act of transferring property in goods. The expression "transfer" in the three Acts did not mean merely a mere change of ownership but meant an actual transfer of property for the purpose Of securing price or payment or promised, or partly for personal consumption or for any other purpose, so that where there is no transfer of goods, the property in the goods would not pass to the person from whom it was received unless the transaction had been SET, sale of goods. 3193: The appellant and the respondents were candidates for the election to the Haryana Legislative Assembly. The first respondent was declared elected. The appellant filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the first respondent on several grounds, namely, (1) that the requisite number of spare copies of the petition had not been filed along with the petition; (2) that the delay in filing the election petition was due to the fact that the requisite numbers of spare copies had not been furnished by the appellant; and (3) that the spare copies were actually filed beyond the period of limitation. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that it was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The requirement of section 81(3) is mandatory and if the election petition contains only one ground, then the election petition cannot be said to have been presented within the time prescribed therein. [278 D] (ii)The election law does not require that every election petition should be accompanied by as many copies thereof as there are respondents mentioned in the petition. It requires that all such copies must be filed before the commencement of the trial. [279 A B] (iii)Section 80(3) provides a complete machinery for obtaining relief in respect of a corrupt practice alleged but it does not provide for any particular type of remedy. Section 81(3), read with section 100, makes it clear that the election petition must contain only one ground of corrupt practice alleged against the returned candidate. [280 C E] (iv)In the present case, the election petition did contain only one allegation and the election petitioner could not make out a case of corrupt practice. [281 F]

2297: The appellant, a former Judge of the Supreme Court and a retired High Court Judge was appointed a Commission of Enquiry for the purpose of inquiring into certain allegations made against him by some of the Judges of the High Court. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the said Commission. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Chief Justice had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition as he was not a sitting Judge of the High court while functioning as a Commission of En quiry and that the order passed on November 3, 1968 by Dutta J., which was an interim order, could not be regarded as a judicial order within the meaning of article 222(1) of the Constitution. HELD : (i) The Chief Justice was not right when he held that Dutta J. had no jurisdiction while at Sibsagar. [617 E] (ii) The Chief justice of India has been conferred with the power to appoint a Commission of Inquiry for the purpose or to remove the Commission from office. The Chief Justice is given the power to make rules for the more convenient transaction of the business of the Commission. The Rules of Procedure and Functionaries of the High Courts are framed under article 225 of the Constitution and they have statutory force. The Rules framed by the Chief Justice are part of the procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure for the trial of warrant cases by Magistrates and the powers vested in the High Courts under section 423 of the Code of criminal Procedure. The power of the Chief Justice to make rules regarding the manner of conducting inquiries and the procedure to be followed by such Commis sioners and Sub Judges is also provided for by the Rules of Procedure. [618 A B; 619 C]

2618: The first respondent joined the State Service in 1937. He was absorbed as a Sales Tax Officer, Class III in the former State of Bombay after merger. In May 1958 he was served with a charge sheet containing allegations of attempt to obtain illegal gratification from certain cloth dealers. A departmental enquiry was held and on March 15, 1963, the Enquiry Officer made certain recommendations regarding the punishment which in his opinion should be inflicted on the first respondent. On March 15, he was dismissed from service. In May, 1958, the City Civil Court decreed the suit holding that the order of dismissal was illegal. On April 1, 1964, the High Court decreed the Suit holding that the enquiry was vitiated because the report of the Enquiry Officer was not sent to him. The first respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of the High Court contending that failure to supply the report of Enquiry Officer in the matter of imposition of penalty had resulted in violation of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The High Court granted a certificate under article 133(1)(c). Allowing the appeal, HELD : (i) The first respondent was entitled to a copy of the report of enquiry by the Enquiry Officer. The Enquiry Officer had also made certain recommendations about the punishment which was to be imposed on the first Respondent. The Enquiry officer had also made some recommendations regarding the punishments which were wholly redundant and irrelevant. The first Respondent was entitled to an opportunity of making a representation against the findings of the Enquiry officer. [254 E F] (ii) The first Respondent 's contention that the Enquiry Officer did not make any recommendation about the punishment was without force. The first and second respondents are brothers. There is no provision in the Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules for giving copies of the reports to the Government servant concerned. The only provision is that the Government servant shall be given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. [255 G H; 256 A B]
2435: The petitioners were detained under section 3(3) of the Bombay Police Act, 1951. They challenged the order of detention on the ground that there was undue delay in sending the report to the State Government and that they had been working at the time when the Commissioner sent the report. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the delay in sending a report could not be avoided by the Commissioner and that when they were sent by him they were working at high pressure in maintaining law and order; (ii) the Commissioner was hard put to for time and the surrounding circumstances explain the very short delay; (iii) the reasons given for the delay were vague and unintelligible; (iv) the representations made by the petitioners against the detention were rejected without application of mind; (v) the representation made by the petitioner was not considered by the State Government; (vi) the grounds of detention were not communicated to the petitioners within the meaning of section 8 of the Act; and (vii) the statements of two witnesses recorded during the investigation were not voluntary and were not relevant. HELD: Dismissing the petitions. (i) The law requires that the detaining authority must be satisfied that the detention is justified and that there should be no delay in doing so. The detaining authority is answerable to the State government, Sub section (3) gives validity to the order for a period of 12 days even without approval. The reason of rule 30A(8) is that it is in the nature of an independent decision and further detention can be justified only if the decision is recorded as required by the rule. [10B C] (ii) There is no provision in the Act that such an approval must be communicated to the detenu. The reasons of the rule are clear and definite. The detaining authorities have to apply their minds to all the facts and circumstances before they can come to the conclusion that there was sufficient cause for the detention of the person concerned. The detaining authori ties have to act with promptitude and take action on objective considerations. [11E F]
1748: The petitioners, who were members of a joint Hindu family governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law, claimed that they and respondent No. 2, his wife and children were members of the Ruling Family and that the said income was not liable to be included in their total income for purposes of section 87B of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Central Government refused to sanction the application on the ground that the said section was ultra vires the State Legislature as it contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The petitioners filed a writ petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of section 87 B of the Code on the ground inter alia that it contravenes articles 14 and19(1)(b) of the Constitu tion because it contravenes article 19(1) (f) of 'the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. Held, that section 87B is intra vires the State Legislatures and the condition precedent prescribed by it which requires previous sanction of the Central Government before filing a suit against the Ruler of an Indian State in a competent court of law is not invalid on the ground of contravention of article 19(i)(f) or article 31(2). Section 86(4) does not offend article 14 of the Constitution and is not ultra vires. The provisions of section 87 are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act. Section 87 provides that all laws in force in a merged State immediately before the commencement of the Act shall continue to have effect subject to such adaptations, whether by way of repeal or amendment as may be necessary or appropriate to the length of the sentence. The provision of section 87 is not inconsistent with any of the provisions of Part III of the Constitution, and the conditions requisite for its applicability are satisfied if the Central Government sanctions the same. The provisions in section 87 are only enabling provisions and do not affect the power of the Central Govern ment to make rules regarding the conditions subject to which the sanction may be accorded.

1145: The appellant Mill Owners ' Association, Bombay, in respect of disputes relating to bonus for the years 1952 and 1953 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality of the notification dated July 31, 1956 issued by the Government of Bombay under section 114(2) of the Act. The appellant contended that the notification was invalid as it purported to be made under section 114 (2) of Act 1 of 1936, which was not applicable to the Mills and that the award of the Industrial Court in respect of the dispute relating to bonus was without jurisdiction and therefore void. Held:(i) The notification dated July 13, 1956 did not contravene article 14 of the Constitution. It merely gave power to the State Government to issue such a notification if it was satisfied that the mills were being managed in a way manner oppressive to them or that they had become uneconomic properties or had become subject to exploitation by the State. The notification did not purport to be either expressly or impliedly expressed to be made applicable to the mills. The notification merely directed that the agreement, settlement, submission or award shall be binding upon the Mills. The notification was not intended to apply to mills which were not profitable to the Mills. In the present case the mills were not profitably affected by reason of the notification. The mills were not affected by the notification. [110 G H; 111 A B] (ii)The notification did not infringe any fundamental right of the appellant. The notification only authorised the State Government "to make a reference to the Industrial Court for its opinion" and not "to give directions to the State Industrial Tribunal in regard to the payment of bonus. The notification also did not violate article 14 of Constitution. The notification in question did not contravene articles 19(1)(g), 21 and 31 of the Constitution and was therefore void.
5346: The appellant landlord filed a petition under section 10(3)(c) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 for eviction of the respondents on the ground that he required additional accommodation for his personal use. The Rent Controller upheld the claim of the landlord and ordered eviction. On appeal by the appellant, the Appellate Authority reversed the findings of the Rent Controller and also held that the respondent were not entitled to recover possession of non residential premises for their residential requirements and dismissed the petition for eviction. The High Court allowed the revision petition and set aside the order of the Appellate Authority and restored the order of eviction passed by the Rent Controller. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the respondent 's shop is situate in an adjoining building and the ground floor of the same building is being used as godown for storing his business ware; that the respondent has no other reasonably suitable accommodation; that the ground floor is not sufficient for residential purposes and that the ground Floor constitutes a non residential building within the meaning of Section 2(2) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in interfering with the findings of fact rendered by the Appellate Authority while exercising its revisional powers under Section 25 of the Act and the High Court was in error in interfering with those findings. [1082F] 1.2 The scope of revisional jurisdiction is very limited. It can be exercised only in cases where there is total or complete misapplication of law or injustice takes place because the decision is reached by the appellate authority after hearing the parties. [1083A B] 1.3 In any event, the High Court has been very lenient in interfering with findings of fact. [1084C] 1.4 In any event the factors of relative hardship be tween the parties weigh more in favour of the appellant than the respondent. [1085D] 2. The High court was right in interference with the findings recorded by the Appellate authority while exercising its revisory power under Section 25. [1086E]
1091: The respondent company was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1952 53 under section 16(3) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer by an order dated January 25, 1954 rectified this error and imposed a further tax at one anna in the rupee on the assessee. The respondent filed a return showing an income of Rs. 3,21,284 without taking into account the amount allowable under section 15C of the Act. The Income Tax Officer by his order dated January 24, 1954 rectified the mistake and imposed additional tax at the rate of one anna. The respondent challenged the order before the High Court which held that the orders made were without jurisdiction and therefore granted a writ of certiorari quashing the orders and the Income tax Officer had brought this order to appeal. The appellant came up in appeal to this Court by special leave against the judgment of the High Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the order of rectification could not be said to have been passed without jurisdiction because the amendment of the law by the Finance Act, 1956, did not apply to the case as the Income tax officer had no power to pass any order prejudicial to the interest of the Revenue under section 35 of the Act; (ii) even if it was assumed that the Income tax authorities had power to rectify their mistake under section 35, they had no jurisdiction to make the order that they did, (iii) even assuming that the order of the Income tax officers was erroneous, the order of their own was not correct in so far as it related to the computation of income from the business of the respondent company and the question whether the Income tax Officers had jurisdiction to rectify their mistakes or not was immaterial when the order is corrected under section 35. HELD: (i) The order of rectification was not a mere correction of a mistake but was an integral part of the order making the order. [864 E] (ii)The order of rectification can be said to be an order of the nature described in section 2 of the Finance Act of 1952 and therefore the Income tax Authorities had no jurisdiction under section 35 to rectify their orders. [865 F G] (iii)The order was not a nullity and could not be set aside under section 35 by reason of
6912: The respondent landlord filed a suit for possession of the premises in question on the ground that the tenant appellant had defaulted in payment of rent. The appellant contended that the notice dated 7.8.1980 was not served on them and they were not aware of the contents thereof. The trial court held that the service of notice dated 7th August, 1980 on the appellant company was not proved. The appellate court reversed the finding holding that the evidence of the plaintiff showed that the copy of the notice was sent to all the defendants by registered post. The High Court allowed the revision petition filed by the tenants and set aside the order of the courts below. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 is mandatory and enjoins upon the Court to draw a presumption that the defendant had accepted the notice. [10A] 2. In view of the provisions contained in section 114 of the Evidence Act, it is necessary for the Court to find out whether the person who issued the notice was aware or not of the contents of the said notice. It is also important to note that the presumption under section 114 of Evidence Act can be drawn if there is nothing to show that the addressee was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing before the Court when the notice was duly served. [11B C] 3. In the instant case, the defendant company was served with the notice dated July 7, 1980. The same was received by the appellants on August 16, 1980. There is no explanation as regards the receipt of the aforesaid notice by the appellants. The presumption under section 12(3) (b) of Bombay Rent Act is rebutted by the defendant. The burden of proof that the defendant was not in knowledge of the contents was on the defendant. [12D E] 4. The Additional District Judge erred in drawing an inference of service of notice on the appellants. There was no rebuttal on behalf of the appellants. [11E F] 5. The Additional Distt. Judge was right in holding that the presumption of service of the notice in the facts of the present case was drawn under section 114 Indian Evidence Act. [11F G
7118: The respondent in the appeal was serving as a Lecturer in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology in the Medical College, Jabalpur. 6184: The appellants are the tenants of certain intermediary landlords known as Girasdars. Respondents Nos. 1 to 3 are statutory authorities, namely, the Mahalkari Kutiana Deputy Collector of Porbandar Division and the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal respectively. They have no interest in the result of these appeals but they are represented by counsel before this Court. The appellants filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the allotment of land to respondents Nos. 4 5. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. The main contention on behalf of the appellants was that the Girasdari lands were not liable to assessment under section 4 of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951, because they were held by tenants jointly and the separate allotments made in respect of the land held by them separately were not binding on the tenants. The appellants also contended that the Girasadars were entitled to separate allotment of land for their personal cultivation. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (i) The Girasdidars are entitled to separate allotments one allotment in respect of land held by tenants joint in estate and any bid land or cultivable waste land and other land of a kind set out in the proviso to sub section (1) of section 24 of the Saurashtra Act. [864F] (ii) The Girasadari lands are not liable to be assessed to land revenue under section 4(2)(a)(iii). Section 4(2) (a) provides that all land of whatever description held by a Girasdar is and shall continue to be liable to payment of land revenue to the State of Gujarat. The Girasdar who is a tenant of Girasdar is also a tenant of the Girasdar. He is also a member of the Girasahandari Union. The Girasahandaris are not included within the meaning of 'Gairasi ' in the Saurashtra Land Reform Act, 1951. [865H; 866A B]
1946: The plaintiff, the eider sister of the first defendant instituted a suit for declaration that she was the owner of half share in the suit properties and for partition and separate possession of her half share. According to her, the property was the absolute property of her mother Puttananjamma and upon her death, this property devolved on her and the first defendant as her mother 's heirs. Since,according to her,the mother 's heir had relinquished her right in these properties, she was joined as a party. It is common ground that the property was in the possession of the second defendant, who did not want to join her as coplaintiff, and she was added as a party to the suit. The trial court decreed the claim of the plaintiff but held that the first defendant was estopped from claiming possession of her share in the properties left by her mother. The first defendant preferred an appeal before the High Court challenging the correctness of the decision of the trial court. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the first defendant and passed a decree in her favour for possession of her 1/2 share in the property. The plaintiff appealed to this Court by special leave against the judgment of the High Court. The main contention raised by the appellant was that the High Court was wrong in awarding a decree to the first defendant for possession of the half share in her properties, because, according to her, she was entitled to the entire property under section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act, and that the High court was wrong in granting a decree to her. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in awarding a decretal amount against the other defendants. [864F] (a) Section 51 of the Act provides that where a person has only one half share in joint family property, he is entitled to a certain proportion of the property. But the right to share is not an essential part of the property which can be acquired by him without being divided amongst his co sharers. [865H; 866A] (b)The right to share arises when there are two or more co sharers in the same joint family property. In the case of a co sharer, if there are several co sharers, each
1277: The respondent, a Railway employee in the Southern Railway, was promoted to the post of Superintendent Grade II. He challenged the order of promotion by a writ petition before the High Court on the ground that the said order violated his fundamental right under article 16(1) of the Constitution and also the guarantee under article 16 (4). The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the circular which provided for giving preference to initial appointment to Class III posts in the matter of seniority did not violate article 16(2) of the constitution. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned circular had been issued as a result of the decision of this Court in A. K. Roy vs Union of India, ; , that the Railway Board had no power to make any reservation in favour of selection posts in the same grade and therefore the impugned circular could not be construed as a provision enabling the State to give preference to the respondent over the appellant who was promoted to Class I post. HELD : (i) The Railway Board had the power to reserve the numerical strength of Class III posts for the purpose of employment in its Secretariat. The reservation of selection posts was not confined only to initial appointment but also to promotions made by selection and that too for reasons of efficiency and administrative expediency. [617 D E] (ii) The Railway Administration had the power under section 3 of the Act to reserve the number of posts or number of posts in the service of the Government to be filled up by promotion from amongst the members of the Subordinate Judicial Service. The reservation was not confined to initial appointment. It was open to the Government to provide for reservation in the matter either by providing for appointment of persons with disabilities or by making appointments of persons with such disabilities. [616 F G] (iii) The Railway administration had the power in the matter. The Railway Board has the power to create posts and fill them up according to the roster. The Railway Administration has the power in this regard. [618 B C]
2660: The appellant firm was assessed to tax in respect of an amount of Rs. 3,99,587 received by it as profit on sale of shares. The firm paid a sum of Rs. 7 lakhs as profit on the sale of shares and claimed that it had taken over the entire share capital issued by the firm. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the transaction was one to facilitate acquisition of capital asset and since the firm had entered upon a well planned scheme for earning profit and that in furtherance thereof the profit was made taxable, he taxed the profit at Rs. 60,278. The firm appealed to the Appellate Tribunal which dismissed the appeal holding that the receipt of Rs. 1,00,000 was not taxable. The Tribunal also found that the price paid by the firm was not a capital expenditure but a revenue expenditure. In reference the High Court held that the receipt was not taxable because it was not a business activity carried on by the assessee firm. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The word "not" has by inadvertence been omitted in the second clause of the first sentence of section 10(2)(XV) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The intention of the legislature is to treat the purchase and sale of shares as a business activity. [902 D] (ii) The fact that the tax payer had borrowed loans at interest to purchase the shares was of no consequence. The loan was advanced to the company with a view to obtaining a capital asset. It was not a commercial venture. The money was purchased with a view of acquiring a capital asset and the payment of the money was not a part of the normal and usual course of purchase or sale of shares but was a capital investment. The mere fact that the assessee had borrowed loans from the company would not make any difference. [903 E F] (iii) The Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that the receipt could be regarded as a capital receipt. [904 A B]
1910: The appellant was a tenant of a market in the district of Barpeta. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutionality of the impost on a number of grounds. The High Court held that the impost was not unconstitutional and that it was not within the competence of the State Legislature to tax the market. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The power to impose fees is conferred by entry 46 List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and it can be validly exercised only by a law made by the legislature. The power to levy fees has been expressly conferred by article 277 of the Constitution. It is well settled that the entries in the three legislative lists have to be interpreted in their widest amplitude and they should receive a large and liberal construction so as to confine the language of the entries to its necessary purposes and bear a meaning which will carry out the intention of the legislature. [657 D E; 658 B C] (ii)The power to legislate for levying fees is conferred under entry 77 of List 1 of the Seventh schedule to the Constitution. Entry 49 of List 1 deals with taxes on land. Entry 36 relates to fees taken in relation to the proceeds of trade and other services mentioned in entry 62 of List 11. Entry 47 of List 11 provides for fees taken in respect of licences for obtaining an i 'licence or a permit for the manufacture, storage, etc., of articles specified in sub section (1) of section 62. Section 62 empowers the local board to levy fees on persons bringing any goods for sale or purchase of such goods. Section 63 provides that the fee payable on licences for the retail sale of any goods specified in sub s.(2) may be paid either in cash or through a bank or by money order at the option of the licensee. The appellant was the tenant of a Kharma market in the District of Barpetah. He had also a shop in the market. The market was being run by him through a broker. The market could not be run without the consent of the appellant. The local board fixed a certain amount as the maximum rate per maund for the occupation of the market. On the question whether the market was a market within the meaning of the Act, HELD:
1487: The respondent company was a sugar mill. It entered into an agreement with the appellant company for the sale of sugarcane to it at current market rates and to have advances adjusted towards price of sugarcane. The agreements were not on a par with the agreements between the parties in respect of sugarcane. In 1948 49 due to drought, the assessee company could not work its sugar mills and the advance made in 1948 49 remained unrecovered because they could only be recovered by the supply of sugarcane to the assessee company. The Income tax Officer assessed the assessee company under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as a trader of sugar and the Appellate Tribunal confirmed this assessment. The High Court held that the expenditure was not in the nature of a capital expenditure but was a revenue expense and therefore, the deduction was allowable under sections 10(3) (xi) and 10(2) (xv). Held, that the expenditure incurred was not in respect of any business or a trade carried on by the assessee and was not allowable as a revenue expenditure. The assessee had to prove that the amount expended was in fact profits or gains. The assessee was entitled to deduct the amount paid to the cane growers from out of the price paid to them. The assessee could not claim deduction of the amount paid as a revenue expense.
5432: The respondent landlord filed an application before the Competent Authority under section 19 of the Slum Areas (Improvement of Clearance) Act, 1956 for permission to execute the order of eviction passed against him. The Competent Authority dismissed the application on the ground that the application was barred by limitation and it was also held that supplementary objections were not maintainable. The Rent Controller ordered that the execution be maintainable and the same had become barred by limitation. The High Court held that the application under section 19 was not barred by limitation as it was filed beyond the period of 12 years from the date of the decree. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. Section 14(1)(b) of the Limitation Act is applicable only when there is a subsisting decree or order of the court. [902B] 2. The application under section 14(1) (b) was made in March 1975. The application was filed in March 1975 i.e. within a period of 12 year of the decree or order. The application for permission to executing the decree was filed in June 1979. The application is clearly barred by limitation because in the opinion of the said Rent Controller till such time the permission of the Competent Authority was obtained, no execution application could have been filed. [903C D] 3. The application filed in March, 1975 was within a period barred by limitation, and it was rightly rejected by the Executing Court. [904A B] 4. The application dated May 15, 1980 was filed after the expiry of 12 years of the decree and the Execution Application was barred by law of limitation. [905D] 5. The application of May 15,80,000 was barred by the principles of res judicata. [906E] 6. The application made in March,1975 was barred by res judicata. The application having been made more than 12 years from April 1975, the application was clearly
710: The Uttar Pradesh Transport Service (Development) Act, 1955, was passed by the State Legislature of Uttar Pradesh and came into force on January 26, 1956. Under section 68B of the Act, the U. P. Transport Service (Regulation of Trade) Act, 1947, was repealed and replaced by the U.P. Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1956. Section 68C provided that the provisions of the Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any law other than the Act or in any instrument having effect by virtue of any law other then the Central Act. The appellants were holders of stage carriage permits for plying their vehicles on the route in question. They challenged the validity of the U.p. Act on the ground that it violated article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it did not provide for the classification of the operators on the basis of their number of years of service to be rendered and that the U. p. Act had been made with a view to preventing the operators from carrying on their business of motor transport. Held:(i) The U. P Act did not infringe the fundamental rights guaranteed by articles 31 and 19 of the Constitution. The U.P Act did not offend against the provisions of article 14 of Constitution because it did not impose any unreasonable restriction on the right to carry on trade or business in motor transport nor did it impose an unreasonable restriction on such right. The U P Act did no more than make provision for the regulation of the transport industry in general and for the regulation and control of transport vehicles in particular. It was not a piece of legislation providing for the regulation or control of transport vehicle but one for the purpose of giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing the principles laid down in clauses (b) and (c) of article 39 of the Constitution that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good and this is apart from any other power to ensure the economic progress of the earth which is social and economic justice and its goal is achieved by giving preference to security agencies in the matter of carrying out their duties. The U .P. Act did not contravene article 14 of 'the Constitution because it gave arbitrary powers to the Government to frame rules under section 68
2966: The appellant company was manufacturing and selling electricity. It manufactured cloth by means of powerlooms which were used for the manufacture of cloth. The question was whether cloth manufactured by a particular process could be regarded as "cloth" within the meaning of the word "mill". The High Court held that cloth manufactured by means of electricity could not fall under the term "meanings" used in the notification. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The word "mills" has been used in the Act in its popular sense as understood in trade parlance. The word "ma chine" is defined in section 2(a) of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 as meaning "the total amount produced or obtained by a dealer by way of sales of goods made on his own account or By hand or by power". [644 C] (ii)The word "milling" has been employed in the definition of "grass" in section 2 (h) of the Act. The word 'ma chine ' has also been used in other articles like electricity. [645 D] (iii)In interpreting a taxing statute, it is always necessary to ascertain the intention of the legislature when such words are construed in their ordinary sense. But when the words are clear and unambiguous then the presumption is that they have been so interpreted that certain things will be said against each, no matter what the context requires. [646 F G]
2721: The appellant, a company incorporated in the United Kingdom, was appointed as the managing director of a company known as the Rampur Company. On March 19, 1953, the company reappointed V Dalmia and others to the Managing Agency with effect from August 15, 1960, and applied for extension of the managing agency till March 31, 1970. On December 10, 1963, the Rampur company reappointed Govan Brothers, Managing Agent for ten years with effect from April 1, 1970, and applied to the Central Government that the extension be approved. The Central Government granted extension for five years under section 326 of the . On December 10. 1963, the company filed an application before the Central Government under section 326(1) of the Act for approval of the company Law Board for extension of managing agency for a further period of five years. The Central Govern ment refused to accord its approval on the ground that the company had not been able to appoint or reappoint any person as managing agent after July 8, 1960, without obtaining the prior approval of the Central Government. The company then moved a petition in the High Court of Delhi on June 10, 1967 for quashing the decision of the Board and for an order extending the term of the managing agents till March 31. 1970. The Company 's appeal against the order of the Central Govt. was dismissed by the Division Bench of the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (i) the company was not a fit and proper person to be appointed or reappointed as managing agent; (ii) the company had no power to appoint or accept the appointment of a managing agent; and (iii) the company 's acts and conduct were not bona fide. HELD: (i) The company was not entitled to appoint or repudiate the company 'S. The company had no right to appoint or to accept the appointment. The company 's act and conduct were wholly irrelevant in so far as the affairs of the company were concerned. [864 C] (ii) The company had the power to appoint a managing agent. The managing agent proposed was a Director of the company. The company was the only person who could appoint the managing agent. It was therefore competent for the company to appoint or reject the proposed appointment
6204: The respondents were recruited to the Indian Forest Service and the Indian Police Service after the first respondent joined the service in 1954. They were later appointed to the Indian Police Ser vice in 1955. In 1956, the Government of India issued a notification under Rule 3(2)(d) of the Indian Forest Services (Regulation of Seniority) Rules, 1954, providing that the year of allotment of an officer appointed to the service shall be the year in which he would have been so appointed but for those rules. The respondents challenged the validity of the said rule by filing a writ petition before the Calcutta High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the rule was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India and quashed the impugned rules. Hence this appeal by the Union of India. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The rule is intra vires the provisions of Article 14 of the Constitution. [864F] 2. The rule has been framed under the All India Services Act, 1954. It is not in conflict with any provision of law. The rule cannot be struck down as offending article 14 of the constitution. [865G] 3. The rule does not offend article 14 of Constitution. The rule must be held to be valid. [866A] 4. The rule can be struck down only if it is found that it is contrary to the provisions of the law or the rules made thereunder. [867B] 5. The rule should not be arbitrary nor should be shown in such manner as to enable an employer to pass a strange order in the matter of fixation of inter se seniority. [868C] 6. The rule in question is not violative of article 14 of constitution. [886D] 7. The rule, is not unconstitutional on the ground that it contravenes article 14 of 9. The rule applies equally to all persons who are holders of civil posts in connection with the affairs of the State. [894E] 8. The rule may be struck down on the ground of legislative incompetence. But it does not contravene article 14 of. The rule will apply to all persons against whom orders of supersession have been made. [895H] 9. The rules do not infringe article 14 of 'the
2971: The appellant company was a managing agent of a company in which the public were not substantially interested. In respect of certain shares held by it in Elphinstone Mills Ltd., Bombay, the Income tax Officer cancelled the orders of its managing agents and issued notices to them under section 23A(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The appellant contended that the cancellation of the orders amounted to forfeiture of its rights as managing agents and therefore the Income tax Authorities could cancel the said orders without giving any reasons therefor. Held, that the cancellation did not amount to forfeiture of the appellant 's right as managing agents. The cancellation contemplated by section 23A (1) is only an administrative act and the Income tax authorities had no power to cancel the order of cancellation without giving any reason therefor. The cancellation of the order of the Income tax Offi cer could not be made without giving the assessee an opportunity of being heard. The cancellation was not for the purpose of making profit or loss but for the purpose,of preventing the assessee from carrying on his business. The cancellation could not be for the purpose Of preventing the assessee 's claim for dividends which he might have declared. The cancellation would be in effect a reduction of the assessee 'S profits and would not amount to a forfeiture of the assessee. The cancellation did not affect the right of the assessee to carry on its business. The Income tax Officer could not cancel the order merely because the assessee had failed to declare dividend in respect of those years in view of the provisions of section 23A of the Act. The cancellation, however, did not amount either to a forfeiture or a reduction of assessee 's right. The cancellation related back to the date when the order of assessment was made and it was not necessary to give any reasons for the same.
2140: The respondent, a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1953, purchased cotton from unregistered dealers and paid purchase tax of Rs. 5,932/ under section 10(a) of the Act. During the assessment period from April 1, 1956 to March 31, 1956, it purchased unginned cotton worth Rs. 5.93,266/ from unregistered dealers. During the course of assessment proceedings, the respondent applied for refund of the purchase tax paid by it. During the pendency of the assessment proceedings, however, the respondent sold the cotton seeds which form the bye product of the ginning process to another person. The Sales Tax Officer refused to allow any refund on the ground that the conditions of r. 12 (1) read with r. 6 (ii) of the Rules had not been fulfilled. The revision filed before the Gujarat Sales Tax Tribunal was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The sales tax authorities were right in refusing to allow the refund to the respondent and that the High Court erred in answering the second question in favour of the respondent. [318 E] (ii) The use of the word 'sale ' in r. 12(1) is not conclusive but only indicative of the intention of the parties. It must be left to the discretion of the purchasing dealer to determine whether or not the goods are intended to be used by him in producing any goods falling under the entry specified in column 2 of the Schedule to the Act. [319 C] (iii) The use in r.12(1) of the rules made under section 9 of the Act indicates that the purpose of the sale of unginned or unpressed cotton cotton was to enable the purchaser to produce the same for consumption in the State of Bombay. [320 B]
1892: The respondent was a licensee under the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951. He moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the resolution of the Corporation fixing the scale of fees on the basis of the annual valuation of the cinema houses made by a method which did not appear on the record. The High Court held that the levy was not a fee but a tax and quashed the resolution. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the levy was in substance a tax and no quid pro quo was necessary to sustain its validity beyond the grant of the licence; (ii) the fee fixed was not a tax as it was not a quid pro tempro; (iii) the fee was not a price for a service rendered to the licensee; (iv) the fee could be levied only by a special order or by issuing a notification under section 443(1)(b) of the Act; (v) the fee imposed was not a "tax" within the meaning of article 110(2); (vi) the levy did not amount to a fee but was a tax; (vii) the levy had been authorised by section 548(2) read with section 443 of the Act and was therefore invalid; (viii) the levy being in the nature of a fee was outside the purview of the Act. HELD : (i) The levy is not a fee and does not fall within the scope of any of the clauses of article 110 of the Constitution. [646 F] (ii)The expression "tax" has been used in the context of a fee and not a tax. The word "taxation" is defined in the General Clauses Act as including everything by which one person can do something. It connotes some matter which one may put to another by means of anything, then it includes what is done in the ordinary course of law. The word 'taxation ' in article 110(1), therefore, must mean a tax as well as a fee. The distinction between a tax and a fee lies primarily in the fact that a tax is a compulsory exaction of money by public authority for public purposes enforceable by law and is not payment for services rendered. A tax is a fee and is generally speaking neither a tax
4851: The appellant Corporation paid to its employees incentive bonus at the rate of one month 's salary in lieu of notice. The High Court held that the incentive bonus was wages and not additional remuneration. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The definition of 'wages ' is an inclusive one. It includes remuneration paid or payable to an employee in respect of any period of authorised leave, lock out, strike which is not illegal or lay off service, or for keeping a constant watch time with more than half an hour or no odd days. [718F G] (2) The definition is exhaustive and it provides that "gratuity" means gratuity payable on discharge. [719A] (3) The definition does not include any contribution paid by the employer to any pension fund or provident fund, or under the Act any travelling allowance or the value of any traveling concession, if any, paid at intervals not exceeding two months. [720B] (4) The definition being inclusive and not exhaustive, it excludes any payment made or payable to any person as an incentive bonus. [721C] (5) The definition consists of three parts. The first part says that "include" something other than basic wage, basic pay, dearness allowance, house rent allowance, non residential allowance, medical allowance, all interim relief etc., but does not include "any other additional remuneration", if any paid to an employee, in respect of his employment". The second part of the definition states that "includes" something other then "basic wage" and "nightry,urnool and to what extent" are the terms of the contract of employment. [723D F] (6) The definition, therefore, contemplates only those payments which are made or payable in respect of the period of employment. The definition is inclusive and not an inclusive one; it is a part of the contract itself. [724E] (7) The definition has been enacted to provide for a scheme of incentives and benefits to be extended to employees who have either retired or died. In order to attract the definition, there must be a relationship of master and servant between the parties. [725G] (8) The definition cannot be read
2331: The appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge for various offences, as indicated in the judgment of the High Court. The third accused was also charged with offences under sections 467/471 read with section 471 and 120 B I.P,.C. Both the appellants were further charged under section 476 read with section 34 I.P .C. The fourth accused was also convicted under section 420 read with section120 B I. P. C. The conviction of the appellants was set aside by the High Court on the ground that sanction under section 196A of the Code had not been obtained. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (i) since the charges against the appellants were framed under section 468 read with section 469, the trial was illegal; (ii) since the necessary sanction under section 195(1)(b) Cr. P.C. had not been secured, the trial must be held to have been illegal; (iii) since the prosecution had failed to obtain the requisite sanction, the trial could not be said to be illegal; (iv) since the sanction under section 197 Cr. P C had not been applied for, the trial would be illegal; and (v) since the appellants were prosecuted for non cognizable offences under sections 466/471 and 120 B IPC, sanction under section 473 was not necessary. HELD: Dismissing the appeals, (i) The question whether a particular offence is cognizable or non cognizable has to be decided on its own facts. P .C. is valid or not has to be determined having regard to the nature of the offence and other relevant circumstances of each case. Section 6 provides that the compensation payable to the holders of the land shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of section 7. Section 8 provides that all lands vested in the State Government under section 4 shall vest in the Board free from all encumbrances. Section 9 lays down the procedure for collection of compensation. Section 10 provides that the amount of compensation to be awarded should be determined by the Collector in the manner prescribed. Section 11 provides that the Collector shall determine the amount of compensa tion and if he does not act under section 11, his decision would be final. Section 13 provides that the cost of eradicating or other ancillary and subsidiary operations in the areas notified under section 4 will be defrayed out of the compensation pool. Section 14 provides that the surplus land shall be disposed of in the manner laid down in sections 8 and 9. Section 15 provides that the decision of the Collector under section 10 shall be final and conclusive. Section 16 provides that the rates at which the compensation is to be paid are to be fixed by the Board. Sections 17 and 18 deal with the mode of payment of compensation. Sections 19 and 20 deal with the procedure for recovery of the amount of the compensation. Section 21 provides that the amounts due to the holders under the Bhopal Land Revenue Act, 1954 shall be recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Section 22
2165: The respondents filed a suit against the appellant on the ground that he was in illegal possession of certain lands. They claimed title to the said lands by adverse possession and limitation. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondents were not entitled to claim adverse possession. On appeal, the Additional District Judge held that the respondents had failed to prove their title to the lands and dismissed the second appeal. The respondents preferred an appeal before the High Court which was also dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decision of the revenue court on the question of title to the land was vitiated by error of law and that the suit was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The decision of the Revenue Court on the question whether the respondents were in possession or not is not liable to be interfered with under article 136 of the Constitution. [623F] (2) Section 89(1) of the Act provides that no civil court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit in respect of any dispute between the landlord and tenant regarding the recovery of possession of any land or premises on the ground of non payment of rent or use of the premises for purposes other than the purpose of cultivation. [624A B] (3) Section 92(1) provides that nothing contained in section 92 shall affect the provisions of sections 13 and 14 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959. [625B C]
435: The Bengal Chamber of Commerce, Calcutta, was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act and its workmen were employed by the company. In 1956 the company made an award fixing dearness allowance for the employees of the company at Rs. 7/8/for each of the two classes of workmen. On the question whether the dearness allowance should be on the same scale as decided upon by the Bengal Chamber of commerce, the Industrial Tribunal held that those recommendations were made to the mercantile firms where the workmen consist practically of clerical and subordinate staff as opposed to Tramways Company where the large percentage of workmen belong to other categories, the clerks and Depot cashiers being only a small minority, though they found that the cost of living index found by the Bengal Chambers of Commerce should be accepted as the criterion for awarding increased dearness allowance in the case of the employees of company as well. The company appealed to this Court against the decision of the Tribunal and also applied for special leave to appeal to this Court. Held, that the award of the Tribunal fixing the dearness allowance in respect of the employees in the company was not vitiated by any legal principle or acted in violation of any statute. The recommendation of the Bengal Chamber Of Commerce was made to the company 's rise in the cost of production and it was accepted by the company and the workmen. The company had been paying the wages to the employees of its own accord without any distinction between the clerical and subordinate employees. The company was not entitled to fix the dearness allowance on the basis of the recommendations of the Bengal Chamrat Committee. The recommendation did not amount to a reduction in the cost structure of dearness allowance fixed by the Bengal chamber of Commerce. The recommendation was not binding on the company. The recommendation could not be said to have been made in contravention of any statutory provision or of the principles of natural justice.
6500: The appellant, a non resident Indian, was the owner of certain lands in the State of Punjab. He had been granted rights under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887. In the year 1942, he executed a lease deed in favour of the respondent for a period of twenty years. The said lease deed provided that the lessee would be entitled to remain in possession of the land for a period not exceeding six months at a time. The appellant 's father died on 8th May, 1945 leaving behind him his widow and two sons. The respondent, who was the son of the original grantee, applied for mutation of his name in the revenue records. The appellant claimed that he was the owner ship of the lands in question which were included in the forest lands. The respondent filed a suit claiming ownership in respect of the lands. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the grant made by the erstwhile ruler was in respect of revenue yielding lands only admeasuring 263.4 bighas and not in respect of forest lands. On appeal, the District Judge held that the grant was in respect only of forest lands and the respondent was not entitled to any right in the forest land. The respondent preferred an appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the respondent was the owner in possession of a particular forest and that the grant could not be treated as a grant in respect of a forest land. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. It was a grant of a specific area of land. The grant did not create any interest in the land. The said grant was merely a concession given to the respondent to enjoy the land without any right to alienate the same. The grant could not have been treated as a transfer of a specific forest land. [865H; 866A] 3. The grant is not in respect only to
3897: The appellants are the tenants of a house in Jammu city. They let out to the respondents a house for running a hotel. The respondents were not in a position to continue their business because they required it for their occupation and, at any rate, having regard to the comparative advantages or disadvantages of the landlord and the tenant, there was no equity on the side of the appellants to evict them under section 13(1)(h) of the Jammu & Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966. The respondents filed a suit for eviction against the appellants on the ground that the appellants required the house for their personal use and that the appellants had not merely a desire to occupy the building but they actually needed it for their own use. The appellants claimed that they required the house in order to extend their business by running a hotel and pleaded that the respondents required the house bona fide for their personal necessity. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellants did not have any personal need and that the respondents were entitled to evict the appellants under section 13 (1) (h). On appeal, the High Court held that the appellants ' case was covered by section II(3) of the Act which applied only to such cases where the landlord required the house or the premises for his residence. In the present case, the appellants had no personal need of their own and the respondents had no other reasonably suitable accommodation. The High Court further held that the respondents had proved their personal need and the appellants had failed to prove their comparative advantagi9ity or disadvantages. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts ' decision is based on a consideration of the evidence and circumstances of the case and the High Court has taken an erroneous view of law on the nature of the need of the appellants as also on the question of the comparative disadvantage or disadvantages or disadvantage of the landlord. [839 C] 2. Section 11 of the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shop Rent Control Act provides that if the landlord requires the house for the occupation of his wife or dependent child, he shall be deemed to have made the application for the purpose of obtaining a decree. The proviso thereto states that the landlord may apply the provisions of section 11 for the protection of the dependents of
3930: The appellant was the owner of certain lands situated in Hyderabad. He had a wife and two minor children. The father of the appellant, who was a Minister in the Nizam 's Government, was alleged to have been cheated by the appellant and his step brother. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of possession of the lands and mesne profits. The trial court dismissed the suit but the first appellate court decreed it. In second appeal the High Court held that the appellant was not the owner of the lands but was only benamidar. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant was not a benamidar as he was neither a minor nor a mere owner. He was merely an agent of the owner of a land. [864 C] (ii) The power of attorney executed by the appellant in favour of the father of the plaintiff was not a deed of conveyance. It did not confer any title on him. [865 D E] (iii) There is no evidence to show that the father of appellant was ever a party to the agreement for sale. The father was not a party to Ext. P 1. His father was not made a party to Exts. P 1 and P 2. [863 F G] (iv) The appellant could not be said to be the owner of lands in question. [866 A]
5488: The respondent landlord filed a petition for eviction against the appellant tenant on the ground of non payment of rent. The appellant contended that he became liable to be evicted from the premises in question under clause (d) of sub section (1) of Section 11 of the Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 which provided that on failure to pay two months ' rent a tenant was liable to be evicted from the premises taken on lease. The respondent pleaded that the appellant had become liable to be terminated the tenancy by forfeiture of his right to possession as well as the non payment of the rent. The Additional Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was not entitled to adjustment of the amount paid by him towards the rent in advance on the ground that he had not requested the respondent to adjust the same. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the order of the Additional Subordinate Judge. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had failed to prove that he was in arrears of rent for any period prior to September 7, 1973. It was further contended that since the respondent had been paying the rent regularly every month, the appellant could not be considered to be a defaulter in payment of rent for purposes of clause (d). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent was entitled to claim adjustment if it was necessary or required. [813F] 2. The respondent has failed to establish that he was a defaulter in paying the rent for the months of September and October, 1972. The receipt under which the said advance was received does not state that the amount received was liable tobe adjusted towards the arrears of rent only on the appellant informing the respondent orally or otherwise. The respondent did not ask the appellant to adjust the amount paid towards the rent due for the months September and October. The respondent also did not ask for adjustment of the rent which he had paid in advance. The receipts issued by the appellant were not sufficient to show that the amount paid in advance was liable to he adjusted towards the rent payable by the appellant. [814E F; 815A B]
2728: The respondent landlord filed a suit for ejectment against the appellants on the plea that he had been in occupation of the shop allotted to him. The civil court decreed the suit and the decree was confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the order of the civil court was without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) Section 3A of the Act provides for an appeal to the District Magistrate against an order made under section 7 or section 16. The District Magistrate is given power to revise any order passed under section 7(2). But the order of eviction has to be made by the State Government or the District Magistrate. The District Magis trate must be satisfied that the order is not one passed under section 3A but one passed under sections 4 and 5 of the Act. [367E F] (ii) The order of the District Magistrate is final. The order of eviction is not final as held by this Court in Khem Chand vs Delhi Administration. [369F] (iii) The order is not final because the District Magistrate can revise the same order if he thinks fit. If he does so, he may do so at any time before the passing of the order. [370B]
2302: The petitioners challenged the vires of the Taxation Laws (Extension to Union Territories) Regulation No. 3 of 1963, which introduced a new regulation in the Pondicherry Administration Act, 1962, with retrospective effect from April 1, 1963, providing that all laws in force immediately before August 19, 1958 would continue to be in force in Pondicherry until amended or repealed by a competent legislature or other competent authority. The petitioners contended that the impugned Act was not within the competence of the State Legislature and that the impugned legislation was invalid as it contravened articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution. Held:(i) The Regulation made under section 4(2) of the Pondicherry Administration Regulation, 1951, is not ultra vires the powers conferred on the State Government by article 240 of the Constitution of India. (ii)The power conferred on the President under article 240 of Constitution is subject to the provisions of Part III of the Constitution and the Parliament can make any law for the whole or part of the territory of India for implementing any such law. The power conferred on him by article 240 is subject to certain constitutional limitations. (iii)It is well settled that the power conferred on a State Government by a statute is subject to two limitations, namely, (1) that the power must be exercised in good faith; and (2) that it cannot go into extraneous matters. (iv)The power given to the President under the proviso to article 309 is subject to his satisfaction that the conditions precedent laid down therein are satisfied.

4772: The first respondent secured 11268 votes as against the appellant who secured 11260 votes. The appellant was declared elected to the Assembly seat by a notification dated 13th May, 1982 issued under article 324 of the Constitution. The first respondent obtained more votes than the appellant and the appellant secured 11260. The appellant challenged the election of the first respondent in an Election Petition before the High Court on the ground that the first respondent had been duly elected to the assembly seat. The High Court upheld the validity of the voting by machine and held that the first Respondent secured 11260 but he did not secure 11260. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Commission being a creature of the Constitution itself, its plenary powers flowing directly from article 324 must prevail over any Act passed by the Parliament or Rules made thereunder. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Commission being a creation of the Constitution, its plener is the creature of its power. [191H] 2. Article 324 confers upon the Election Commission the power to make rules for the conduct of elections to the Legislature of every State and for the reservation of number to members belonging to Scheduled Castes 'sity. The said power is conferred upon the Election Commissioner. It is open to him to regulate his own procedure and the orders made by him and to confer degrees on persons who are not entitled to vote in the matter. The Election Commission has to act within the four corners of the statute. [1918A B] 3. Article 324 does not authorise the Governor to make laws in respect of matters relating to or in connection with the elections to the Parliament or the State Legislatures. The Election Commis sion can only exercise such powers as are vested in it by the statute. The Election Commissioner cannot be equated with the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners. [1920C D]

3992: The appellant company was incorporated under the Rampur State Companies Act, 1932. On 10th May, 1933 it leased 2,000 acres of land and in 1946 another 2,000 acre of land to the Agricultural Company, Rampur. In 1939 the Rampur Sate leased 2,500 acres of land to a company which was required to pay fair and equitable land revenue which was to be agreed upon by the parties. On 5th May, 1935 the Rampur state leased 2,400 acres of land on which the appellant firm had been carrying on business. 150: The petitioner was detained by an order of the trying Magistrate under section 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He challenged the validity of that order in a petition under article 32 of the Constitution and contended that the order of remand was not made by the trying magistrate on the 9th March, but only by the 11th March, because, there was no order of remand committing him to further custody till the 11th of March, and that as the case had been adjourned from time to time, it was not possible for him to appear before the Court on that date. Held, that the order passed by the trying Magistrate on the 9 th March, was not illegal or improper and the petitioner could not be released on bail pending his trial. The fact that the case had already ended in the middle of the day when the affidavit on behalf of the Government was filed showed that the case was still at that stage and the petitioner did not have any opportunity to make any representation against the detention. The order of remand dated 6th March, 1951, was therefore illegal and must be set aside.
1018: The respondent was a Sub Inspector of Police in the U.P. Police Force and was posted as officer incharge of a police station. On November 17, 1952, he was promoted to the rank of head constable and in May 1952, he went on leave for two months. On December 17, 1952 he was placed under suspension and on August 18, 1953, he was charge sheeted and punished by order dated February 22, 1954. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said order of dismissal which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) as the respondent had been honourably acquitted by the criminal court on September 20, 1955, and (ii) the trial was vitiated by reason of the fact that the Superintendent of Police had not made any recommendation for his transfer, the order of dismissal was invalid. HELD: (i) The respondent could not be said to have been dishonest at the time when he committed the offence charged. [864 E] (ii) There is no provision in the Police Regulations which requires an authority holding a departmental enquiry to make a report about the conduct or character of an employee. [865 F G] (iii) It is not necessary that the nature of the allegations against the delinquent should be such as would induce a reasonable man to think that they are true. All that is required is that the nature and quality of the evidence in support of the charges levelled against the delinquent must be exactly similar. [866 A B]

He also noticed marks of identification on some documents seized by the Directorate of Inspection. The Income Tax Officer then issued a notice to the assessee to show cause why penalty should not be imposed under section 271(1)(c) of the Act for failure to comply with the directions given by the Directorate. The assessee filed an application before the Commissioner of Income Tax requesting for copies of all the documents seized by him. The Commissioner rejected the application. The High Court held that the Commissioner 's order was erroneous because he did not give any reasons for his decision. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Commissioner 'was not competent to issue the notice under section 276C of the Act; (ii) the Department could not have issued the notices under section 275D of the Act as the department itself was not the assessing authority; (iii) the Department was not entitled to file a return of income under section 139(1); (iv) the Department had no opportunity to examine the correctness or otherwise of the returns filed by the assessee; and (v) the Department having accepted the explanation offered by the assessee, the Department could only justify its action by filing a return of the income under section 143(1).
