5431: % The appellants are the owners of a building in which a flat was allotted to them. They filed an application under section 14 of the for requisition of the premises, and claimed interest on the amount awarded by the Land Acquisition Collector. The Land Acquisition Collector made an award for the amount of compensation payable to the appellants. The appellants challenged the award before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the appellants were entitled to interest on the entire amount awarded by Land Acquisition Collector from the date of requisition till the date of payment of the amount. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the appellants had been deprived of their property without authority of law, and that the appellants should be paid interest on the balance amount which remained to be payable to them. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The appellants are entitled to interest at 6% per annum on the amount of the principal amount of compensation determined by the Land acquisition Collector from the respective dates of such deposit to the date of actual payment. [287H; 288A] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellants have not been able to establish that they were entitled to any interest on the said amount. The appellants have also not been able (to satisfy us) that there was any difficulty in calculating the amount. [288B C] 1.3 Interest is payable on the amount due minus what has been paid from the respective date. The amount is directed to be paid within three months from this date by the respondents. [289D E]
927: The appellant was a Sub Inspector of Police in the Patiala State. He was dismissed from service by an order dated August 16, 1950, under Rule 92 of the Regulations framed under the Patiala State Regulation. On August 18, 1950, he wrote to the Chief Secretary of the State stating that by his retirement he would be put to heavy loss, i.e., about Rs. 50,000 which he would have earned as pay and allowances etc., during this period and that this decision of the Government tantamounts to his removal from service. The Government referred the question whether the appellant should be retired from service or not. The Government decided to retire him on administrative grounds. The appellant filed a suit challenging the order of the Government on the ground that it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution and also the provisions of the Patiala State Regulations relating to pay, allowances, leave, pension and travelling allowance. The trial Court held that the order of compulsory retirement did not amount to removal from service within the meaning of article 311 of the Constitution, but held that the termination of service effected by the order of August 16,1950, amounted to his removal within the meaning Of article 311 of 'the Constitution and as the requirement of that Article had not been complied with, the order of compulsorily retiring him was void in law. The High Court agreed with the trial court that the order was not one of punishment and so article 311 of ,he Constitution had no application. Held, that the order passed by the Government was not one by way of punishment and the rule regarding compulsory retirement did apply to the case. The order of compulsory reemployment was made under r. 92 of the Patiala States Regulations and the rules framed thereunder were applicable to the case of the appellant. The order was therefore not one of dismissal or removal within the contemplation of article 311.
3306: The appellant was found guilty of the offence under section 379 read with section 34 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. He preferred an appeal to the High Court but the same was unsuccessful. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended that the provisions of section 6 were not applicable to the case because (i) the date of the offence was not a fixed or pretended date; (ii) the appellant had not done anything since the date of his conviction and sentence to undergo imprisonment for life; and (iii) the appellant did not commit any act which would be likely to cause physical injury to the person of the deceased. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 6 of the Probation of offenders Act, 1958 is clearly attracted in this case as the appellant had neither committed nor misappropriated any property or valuable security of the deceased or any other person. [638C] 2.1 Section 6 of 'the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 provides that if any provision of a law is repugnant to any provision of an enactment, which, being repealing the provisions of an enactment so provides, shall prevail over such repugnancy. The object of the Act is to provide a summary remedy for determining the liability of juvenile delinquents who have been convicted and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The Act does not contain any provision similar to sub section (2) of section 6 of the Act. The offences of which he is found guilty are under sections 379 read with Section 34 and they are punishable with imprisonment but not with imprisonment for life.[636D E] 2.2 Section 6 of , which deals with the procedure for dealing with persons found guilty and punished, provides that if the court is satisfied from the evidence adduced before it or elsewhere, that there is necessity in public interest to deal with any person consensually convicted or having been, tried for an offence, then it may direct further inquiry against him. It is obvious that even though the point relating to the applicability of section 6 was not raised before the learned Presidency Magistrate or the High Court, this Court is bound to take notice of the provisions of that section and give its benefit to the appellant particularly since it is a section which is intended for the benefit of juvenile delinquency reflecting
5056: The plaintiffs filed a suit for infringement of the patents (Numbers 104120 and 125381) by the defendant, an Indian Private Limited Company. The defendant claimed that the patent was not in accordance with the specifications of the patent and that the patent did not contain any standard form of bio data or other details. The plaintiffs also alleged that the defendant had been using the patent for a very long period without any reference to the specification of the patency. The defendant denied that he had ever used any standard form or standard. The plaintiffs further asserted that the defendant was selling phytotoxicides and was selling the same in the market as a result of which the plaintiffs were entitled to be registered as manufacturers of phytosanitary granules under the Patents Act, 1970. The defendant further asserted that he had been manufacturing phytocuric acids and had been selling pesticides in the market at a very low prices. The plaintiffs prayed for a decree for permanent injunction restraining the defendant from selling pesta 53619 or any other product or part thereof in the market. The defendant also prayed for mandatory injunction directing the plaintiffs to pay damages of Rs. 1,000/ each to the plaintiffs. The defendant contested the claim of the plaintiffs on the ground that the patent applied for was not in conformity with the specifications and that the plaintiffs were not entitled to get a decree for specific performance of the contract. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their case. The High Court allowed the appeal filed by the defendant and held that the plaintiffs could not succeed in establishing that they were entitled to have the patent amended so far as it related to the phytopoically abnormal composition of the phthalateol. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The grant of a temporary injunction is a discretionary relief. It must be exercised taking into consideration the nature of the relief sought. [969E] 2. In the instant case, the plaintiffs had not made out a prima facie case. The plaintiffs had not even made out a case of infringement of the patent. [970F G] 3. The plaintiffs are entitled to interim injunction pending disposal of the suit.
3921: The appellant was a Government servant. He was charged under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code for having demanded and received illegal gratification from one R. N. Sharma, a public servant. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 18 months on each of the charges. On appeal the High Court acquitted him but confirmed his conviction and sentence. In the appeal by special leave the question arose whether the sanction granted by the President in exercise of the powers conferred by sub rule (2) of rule 11 and clause (b) of sub rule ( 2) of rule 14 of the 1957 Rules is valid or not. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order granting sanction under section 6(1)(c) of the Act is not invalid merely because it contains the words "the authority competent to remove the appellant from service". [864 C] 2. The word 'authority ' in sub rule (3) of rule Il is used in contradistinction to the word 'shall '. The word "may" in sub rule Il has been used in contrad sense and it means that the authority should be empowered to make an order of suspension or dismissal either in the same class or grade or post as envisaged by the rule. The word may also mean that the authority can pass an order of dismissal, etc. in respect of a class or category of persons. The word is used in relation to the authority competent to dismiss or remove a person from service. [865 G H; 866 A B] 3. The word authority in sub rule 1l is used to convey the idea of a discretion depending upon the nature of the authority. The power to appoint, suspend, dismiss or remove is vested in the authority competent under sub rule IIl. The authority competent to impose the penalty of dismissal, removal or reduction in rank is the President. [867 D E] 4. The President in exercise Of the power conferred by sub r.(2) of r. 11 and cl. (b)of sub rule (1) of r, 14 has made a special order as contemplated by rule 11(2) and rule
2950: The appellant firm was prosecuted for cheating the State of Andhra Pradesh by issuing a policy and printed pamphlets containing false statements that it was a Government of India Registered Firm. The appellant 's case was that the said scheme appeared to be speculative and did not contain any element of a transaction relating to purchase or sale of Policies, and that the appellant had received the original amount of Rs. 5.50 in full after the sale of three policies. The trial court acquitted the appellant but the High Court convicted him under section 420 read with section 120 B I.P.C. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The offence of cheating is the off shoot of an offence where one has been guilty conscience and dishonestly inducing another to part with his property or authority in favour of either of them. In other words, it is an attempt to deceive another. It is a question of intention, motive and consequent evasion of payment. The essence of cheating consists in a deliberate or intentional fraudulent disposal of property with intent to cause harm or injury to the third person or to the public. [128 F H] Hari Das Barat vs Emperor, A.I.R. , referred to. (ii) The object of the provision being to prevent fraud and avoidable harassment of payers of the public, the legislature could never have intended to make such offences punishable even if they are connected with the particular crime committed by the public. The object may well be to prevent the giving of a status to the offender who is alleged to have cheated a person in the name of money, or as a gambling person, or to put it differently, a gangster who is generally in charge of a business, but who does not know the nature of the business he takes in, and who knows what is going on in the market place. The Legislature could never have contemplated that a person who is charged with cheating should be made to face similar criminal liability for the same act or omission which he has committed. [129 E G] Hari Das Bhargava vs The State, A.l. R. , referred.
1429: The respondents were workmen in the appellant company. They claimed that the chemical works was an integral part of the company and therefore the over all position of the company should be taken into account and the wage structure etc. fixed accordingly; in particular it was contended that though the chemical works being one unit of a large number of industries controlled by the company, some of which were situate in the same area in Delhi, the various units were independent industries and each unit had to be considered on its own and the wage scale etc. fixed on the basis of the financial position of each unit in the industry should be treated on the same footing ; furthermore, the claim of the respondents that the chemical work should be treated as an independent unit was untenable on the ground among others, that it would be against the principle of industry cum region. The tribunal held that the chemical department was an independent unit and the wage scales, dearness allowance and gratuity were not comparable with the other workmen in the same industry and that the respondents were entitled to get the same pay. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal has given good reasons for accepting the claim of equal pay for equal work. It is true that the Tribunal has made certain observations regarding the nature of the work done by the chemical works but those observations cannot be regarded as conclusive evidence of the fact that the respondents are the workmen employed in the chemical works. [864 E] (ii)The Tribunal has also found that the respondents have been working for more than one year in the same concern. The finding of the Tribunal that the respondents ' status was that of a permanent employee is not supported by any evidence. The Tribunal has also pointed out that the respondents did not raise any objection at the time when they filed their respective claims before the Labour Commissioner or even thereafter that the respondents should be paid the same wages as are being paid to the other workmen of the same concern, and that the question of equal pay could not be raised at the instance of the respondents. [865 G H] (iii)It is well settled that if a body of persons functions through different departments and is run and managed by a common officer, it will be difficult to think of a single individual having separate seniority list for the purpose of promotion to higher post. In respect of the accounting year ending with 31st December 1954, the appellant had claimed exemption from payment of sales tax under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act. The assessing authority disallowed the claim on the ground that the declaration forms were not signed by the registered dealers and that they were not properly stamped. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was entitled to exemption under section 5 (2)(a) (ii) of Act. On further revision the Revenue Board allowed the same. The High Court also dismissed the Revision Application filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (i) the requirement of a declaration form duly filled in and signed by the purchasing dealer was directory and therefore the failure to issue such a certificate did not render the dealer liable to pay additional tax; (ii) the requirement was inconsistent with section 5(1)(b)(ii) inasmuch as the declaration forms duly filled in were required for the purpose of resale by the purchasing registered dealer; and (iii) the requirement under r. 27(2) made under the Orissa Act was directory and, therefore, it could not be said that the furnishing of the declaration forms was condition precedent for claiming exemption. 3805: The appellant, who was the decree holder of a decree for money passed away in 1953. The sale proclamation was not made available to the judgment debtor and he did not pay the decretal amount within the time allowed by law. The Court auction sale was held on October 12, 1953 and the appellant purchased the properties in village Devanoor and the appellant applied for permission to bid at the auction sale. The first sale was held in which the lands situated in villages Devanoor, Gudipadu were put to sale. But this sale was set aside as there was some delay in payment of the sale price. Thereafter a second sale was held and the property sold was sold. The appellant filed an application under 0.21 r. 64 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale but the Court dismissed it holding that no such application had been made by the appellant. The appellant then filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the Court not allowing him to participate in the second sale. The High Court allowed the petition and held that the sale of the properties in Village Devanoor fetched Rs. 12,500/ and which were purchased by the appellant in village Davanoor and the sale was therefore valid. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The sale of the property in village Devanauta was sufficient to satisfy the amount mentioned in the sale proclamation but a few days after the sale had already taken place. The sale was therefore not complete. [675 C] (ii) The sale in village Devganoor was sufficient to meet the claim of the decree holder. [652 F] (iii) The sale was not complete. The sale certificate was also not issued. The decree holder was not entitled to challenge the validity of the sale. [653 B]
1187: The petitioners were the owners of certain shares in a certain house and were shareholders. They went to Pakistan on August 14, 1952, and took possession of the house. On March 23, 1954, they went to Pakistan but the time when they did so did not appear. They went there to Pakistan but as a result of the orders made under section 7 of the Act of 1950, the properties were declared evacuee property. Thereafter, other proceedings were taken under the Act of 1951 for declaring them evacuee property. The petitioners challenged the validity of the order dated August 14, 1951, made under the Act as violating their fundamental right to hold property to wit, their shares in the properties covered by the orders. The High Court held that the order was a nullity as the notice under section 7 had been issued to the petitioners and that it was not necessary to decide whether the petitioners were entitled to hold the property or not. Held, that the order of the Custodian was not a nullity as it could be challenged before the competent officer. The order of the Central Government under section 8(2) of the Act was an order made under section 11 of the Act and therefore the petitioners ' rights were not affected by the order. The order did not affect the petitioners ' shares in the property. The order was not a mere direction to the Custodian to determine the share of each shareholder in the property but it was a direction to the person who was holding the share. The order merely directed the Custodian to take action under section 10(1)(b) of the , for determining the shares of each share holder in the property and to divide the share between the two shares. The order also provided that the order shall contain the particulars of the property which is to be declared evacuee property and the shares of the persons who are to be declared evacuees. The order further provided that the property should be valued separately and that the amount due to the evacuee should be determined. The order thus made a complete answer to all the questions raised before it. The order, however, did not affect any of the petitioners. The order only gave the Custodian the power to determine the shares of any of the persons entitled to the shares. 862: The respondents were the workmen of the appellant Mills. The dispute arose out of their dismissal from service and the respondents claimed that they were entitled to be paid compensation for the short working or closure of the Mills on certain days during the period between November 1, 1951, and July 13, 1952. The Industrial Court held that the respondents had not been able to prove that they were not liable to pay compensation for the alleged short working or closing of the Mills. On appeal by special leave: Held, (i) that the decision in Digambar Ramachandra 's case was not applicable to the present case because the dispute related to a matter which was outside the scope of Standing Orders framed under section 26 of the Bombay Electricity Act, 1946, and the claim was barred by limitation. (ii)The decision in Digamber Ramachandra vs Khandesh Mills Ltd., ; applied only to cases where there was no dispute as to the employment of the workmen. The respondents did not raise any dispute at all with regard to the employment before the Industrial Court. (iii)The award made by the Industrial Court was binding on the parties and it could not be modified or set aside by the High Court.
3771: The respondents, Indian Goods Supplying Co., a partnership firm in Bombay, filed a suit against the appellants for recovery of demurrage on the ground that the Port Trust was not entitled to charge demurrage. The appellants contended that the Port trust was not entitled under section 43B(IA) and had no right to recover demurrage for the period during which the goods were detained by the Customs authorities. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant was not entitled either to claim demurrage or to claim the amount of demurrecharge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Port Trust is not entitled to collect demurrage in the circumstances of this case. [638E] (2) Section 43B(I)(a) provides that if any goods are detained by the port Trust for analysis or testing, the importer shall be entitled to claim the value thereof from the Customs Department. [639F G] (3) The Port Trusts Act, 1879, does not contain any provision for payment of demurrages. The Port Trust has been constituted under the Act and is a statutory body corporate. It is not bound to pay demurrage levied on the imported goods. The Port Trusts have been entrusted with the duty to ensure that the goods are delivered at the proper time and place. The Port trust is also responsible for the loss sustained by it because of delay in delivery of the goods. [640G H; 641A]
